comments.content: Output safety / fallback cleanup bug: if `originalPath == outPath`, `File.Copy` throws ("source and destination must not be the same") and the catch then calls `File.Delete(outPath)` — which deletes the user's source document. Separately, when `ReviseInPlace` throws, the partially-edited `outPath` is left in place and `WordprocessingDocument.Create` refuses to overwrite existing files, so the documented "guaranteed fallback" silently fails. Guard against `PathsEqual(originalPath, outPath)` and delete the partial output in the second catch as well.

Leading-insertion position bug: the comment claims a null anchor inserts at the body start, but `body.InsertBefore(para, sect)` puts the paragraph immediately before the section properties — which is the LAST direct child of the body, not the first. `body.Append` likewise appends to the end. New leading content silently lands at the document tail. Insert before the first body child instead.

Non-text run fidelity loss: `UnwrapHyperlinks` permanently removes `w:hyperlink` wrappers so rejecting a revision cannot restore hyperlink targets (only the rPr/Hyperlink style remains). `MarkParagraphDeleted` / `ReviseParagraph` also rebuild runs containing any text using `RunWithText`, which drops `w:sym`, `w:drawing`, `w:footnoteReference`, `w:noBreakHyphen` (mapped to plain `-`), `w:tab`/`w:posTab` distinctions, field-code runs (`w:instrText` / `w:fldChar`), and SDT/customXml content. `InnerRuns` likewise ignores existing `w:ins` / `w:del` wrappers, so the diff is computed against an "accepted" view of the source. Consider preserving hyperlink wrappers around the inserted/deleted runs (they are legal inside `w:ins`/`w:del`) and emitting untouched run children verbatim instead of reconstructing them from `RunText`.

Table-row revisions are not structural: a row "deletion" only wraps the text of each cell paragraph in `w:del` — the row itself is never marked via `<w:trPr><w:del .../>`, so accepting the revision leaves a visibly-empty row in the table. Conversely, row-count changes are emitted by `InsertRevisedParagraph` as ordinary body paragraphs (not new `w:tr` rows with cell paragraphs), and the cell-count mismatch fallback deletes the row and inserts a plain paragraph — destroying the table structure entirely. Use `w:trPr/w:del`/`w:ins` on the row for deletions, and construct real `w:tr` rows (with cells) when the diff asks for a new or replaced row.

Unbounded LCS allocation for paragraph-level diff: `DiffList` always materializes an `(n+1)*(m+1)` `int` matrix with no size cap, unlike `DiffText` which limits itself to 4M cells. With untrusted or large documents (paragraph counts in the tens of thousands), `int[n+1, m+1]` can exceed available memory and crash the process — also a denial-of-service surface if the CLI is fed arbitrary JSON. Apply the same `MaxCells` cap (or fall back to a coarse replace opcode) as `DiffText` does.

The global :focus-visible rule sets `border-radius: var(--r-sm)` on every element that gains keyboard focus. Because the property is applied to the element itself (not the outline), it mutates the element's actual border-radius — any element without an explicit radius will snap from 0 → 8px on focus and back on blur (visible jank on native <button>/<select>/<a>), and elements with custom radii (e.g., pill-shaped `.nm-tag` at 9999px) will be overridden while focus is visible. Remove the border-radius from this rule so the outline shape follows each element's own radius in modern browsers; if a uniform focus shape is desired, scope it to a specific selector rather than every focused element.

Two `:root { ... }` blocks are declared separately — the original theme-token block at the top, and a second one (`color-scheme: light`) mid-file near the scrollbar section. Both apply via cascade merging, but splitting them forces future edits to mentally combine the cascade and complicates adding new theme tokens (which `:root` block do they belong in?). Merge the `color-scheme: light` declaration into the top `:root` block as a single source of truth.

comments.content: The comment promises "保 16px 起跳防 macOS Safari 自动 zoom", but the override only enforces this floor at `large` (17px) and `xlarge` (19px). At `standard`, `.text-xs` resolves to 13px and `.text-sm` to 15px, so any textarea/input inheriting those classes still falls below the 16px threshold and triggers iOS/macOS Safari's viewport zoom on focus. Add a `standard`-tier override (or raise the standard floor for `text-xs/sm`) to honor the comment's stated intent.

`* { scrollbar-width: thin; scrollbar-color: var(--t6) transparent }` (and the matching `*::-webkit-scrollbar-*` rules) is an unusually broad selector for a stylesheet shared between the main window and the widget. It leaks into any shadow DOM, iframe, or future nested scrollable that wants its own scrollbar look, and creates specificity conflicts that are hard to debug later. Scope these to a top-level container (e.g., `html, body` plus a `:host` for the widget runtime) unless global application is intentional.

`.md-body li br { display: none }` deliberately swallows every `
` inside list items (to suppress the single-break gap that remark-breaks injects between list entries), but it also eats legitimate intra-item line breaks — multi-line task descriptions, wrapped code references, soft line breaks the author meant to preserve. The comment acknowledges this trade-off but it silently mutates rendered content. Narrow it to only the break remark-breaks injects between items (e.g., `:last-child`) so genuine intra-item breaks still render.

System theme change is not reactive after load. The inline script reads `prefers-color-scheme` exactly once at parse time. If the user has stored `"system"` as their preference and later switches their OS theme (e.g., from light to dark at dusk), the `.dark` class on `<html>` will never be updated by this script, causing a state desync between the stored preference and the rendered theme unless something else (e.g., a React effect) attaches a `matchMedia` change listener. Consider adding `matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)').addEventListener('change', ...)` here or explicitly documenting that React owns this after mount.

The `catch (e)` block silently swallows all errors with only a comment. While this is intentional for benign localStorage failures (private mode, quota, disabled storage), it hides genuinely unexpected runtime errors and provides no signal for production telemetry. Consider narrowing the try block around just the localStorage/matchMedia access and at minimum logging `console.warn(e)` so failures are visible during development without surfacing to end users.

The `<title>` is left as the boilerplate `"Tauri + React + Typescript"`. This leaks framework/internal stack information to end users (browser tab title, bookmarks, screen readers, OS notifications) and is not localized. Replace it with the actual product name (and ideally read it from the same source the in-app title component uses) before shipping.

comments.content: The config uses `export default` (ESM syntax). PostCSS will only treat this file as a valid ESM config if the project's `package.json` has `"type": "module"` or the file is renamed to `postcss.config.mjs` / `postcss.config.cjs`. Otherwise, loading this file will throw `SyntaxError: Unexpected token 'export'` at build time. If the project is CommonJS, change to `module.exports = { ... }`; otherwise the current ESM form is fine.

comments.content: Filter logic contradicts the documented policy: the header comment states "*-text.svg 字标不拷" (text wordmarks not copied), but the colors filter only excludes '-brand-color.svg'. Files like 'foo-text-color.svg' end with '-color.svg' and are NOT '-brand-color.svg', so they are included as colors. This is a real semantic gap between intent and behavior — either tighten the filter to also exclude '-text(-cn)?-color.svg', or update the comment to reflect that colored text variants are deliberately kept.

Destructive rmSync on dest with no path sanity check: `rmSync(dest, { recursive: true, force: true })` will silently wipe any directory the resolved `dest` points to, including following symlinks. If `src/assets/providers/lobe` were ever replaced with a symlink (or if `root` were ever computed from an unexpected cwd), this could delete unrelated files. Resolve and assert `dest` is inside the repo root and not a symlink before wiping, or use `rmSync(dest, { recursive: true, force: true })` after an explicit realpath check.

comments.content: Copy loop has no per-file error handling: a single unreadable/missing source file (e.g., race during reinstall, permission issue) aborts cpSync and leaves a half-populated assets directory, silently shipping an incomplete icon set. Wrap the copy in try/catch (or use cpSync's `errorOnExist` and accumulate failures), and either continue with a warning or rethrow after reporting all failures so the run is idempotent and diagnosable.

Vendored SVGs are copied with zero content validation: every file from node_modules is trusted as-is, so if the upstream @lobehub/icons-static-svg package is ever compromised (or a malicious version is installed) and ships SVGs with embedded `<script>`, `on*` event handlers, or `<foreignObject>` payloads, those files end up shipped as static assets and rendered by browsers. At minimum, scan each file for `<script`, `onerror`, `onload`, or `javascript:` patterns before copying, or document the vendor trust assumption in a comment so reviewers know the risk is accepted.

readFileSync and JSON.parse have no try/catch. If src-tauri/Cargo.toml or package.json is missing/unreadable, or package.json contains malformed JSON, the script aborts with a raw Node stack trace (e.g., `SyntaxError: Unexpected token ...`) instead of the friendly `[sync-version] ...` messages elsewhere in the script. Wrap the I/O + parse in try/catch and emit a clear localized error (e.g., `无法读取 <path>: <err.message>`) so contributors can diagnose without reading V8 internals.

comments.content: If the process is killed (or `renameSync` throws, e.g., `EPERM`/`EBUSY` on Windows) between `writeFileSync` and `renameSync`, `package.json.tmp` is left on disk and is never cleaned up. Subsequent runs overwrite it so it usually self-heals, but a failure during the rename leaves a stale artifact alongside a now-out-of-sync `package.json`. Add a `try/finally` so the tmp file is removed on failure, and consider removing any pre-existing `package.json.tmp` at the start of the script before writing a new one.

The comment claims the tmp+rename dance is for crash safety (`中断/盘满不会留下截断的 package.json`), but `writeFileSync` does not `fsync` the data to disk before `renameSync`. On a power loss between write and rename, the filesystem can rename the inode while the data blocks have not been flushed, leaving a renamed-but-empty/zero-length `package.json` after recovery — i.e., the very truncation the comment promises to prevent. For full crash safety, write through a `FileHandle`, call `handle.sync()` before `close()`, then rename. This is likely overkill for a build script invoked by `prebuild`, but the comment should not overstate the guarantee as it does today.

Module-level `.read_text()` calls turn a missing or unreadable source file into a collection-time `FileNotFoundError` stack trace, defeating the careful per-test guidance the rest of the suite provides ("Rust 侧改 src-tauri/src/error.rs, 前端同步 src/lib/errorHandler.ts"). Move the reads inside helper functions (or wrap in a fixture with a clear skip/fail message) so a missing file produces a per-test failure with actionable diagnostics instead of crashing `pytest --collect`.

comments.content: All three parsers locate regions with bare `str.index()` on hand-written anchors (`ENUM_HEADER`, `"\n}"`, `TS_TYPE_HEADER`, `"; "`, `"= ["`, `"]"`) and a hand-computed `+ 2` offset to skip past `= `. If the source format drifts — derive attribute split across lines, `= [` loses its space, a `//` comment lands between `export type ...` and `;` — pytest aborts with a raw `ValueError` stack trace, so the real cause ("someone reformatted the file") is hidden behind the same kind of crash that a missing file would produce. Wrap each anchor lookup in a helper that raises a descriptive `pytest.fail()` (or `assert` with a clear message) naming the anchor that was not found.

`registered_plugins` only matches `tauri_plugin_xxx::init`. Modern tauri plugins are commonly registered with `tauri_plugin_xxx::Builder::new()...build()` (e.g. `tauri_plugin_log::Builder::new().build()`); those `.plugin(...)` calls will be silently dropped from the registered set, and `test_plugin_calls_have_registered_plugin` will then falsely fail with "plugin not registered" on a correct codebase. Either generalise the regex (e.g. accept `tauri_plugin_(\w+)::(?:init|Builder)`) or also scan inside `.plugin(...)` argument lists.

The closure emit regex `(?<![\w.])emit\("..."` has no awareness of comments, doc-comments (`/// calls emit("foo") …`) or raw string literals (e.g. `r"emit("foo")"`). All of those populate `backend` with events that are never actually emitted at runtime, so `test_listened_events_have_emitter` will pass even when a real `emit(...)` has been removed/commented out, masking listener-without-emitter bugs. Consider stripping Rust line/doc comments and raw strings before scanning, or restricting matches to inside `fn`/`let emit =` blocks.

`frontend_invokes` only matches a hard-coded double-quoted literal with at most one generic level: `<[^>]*>` rejects nested generics such as `invoke<Promise<MyType>>("foo")`; template literals (`invoke(\`cmd_${id}\`)`), single quotes, and indirect dispatch (`const c = "foo"; invoke(c)`) are all skipped. The whole point of this audit is to catch "frontend calls an unregistered command" at lint time, so silently dropping these patterns means real production invokes against unregistered commands become false negatives. Either broaden the regex to accept single quotes and template literals, or add a fallback AST-based scan.

`registered_commands` calls `re.search(r"generate_handler!\[(.*?)\]\s*\)", ...)` with a non-greedy `.*?`, which stops at the FIRST `]`. If `lib.rs` ever wires two `tauri::generate_handler![...]` blocks (e.g. one for the main window and another behind a feature flag, or two `.invoke_handler(...)` chains), every command inside the second block silently disappears from the registered set, and `test_registered_but_uncalled_warn_only` will then spuriously warn about real commands while `test_frontend_invokes_all_registered` will be unable to verify them. Use `re.findall` over `generate_handler!\[([^\]]*)\]` (or a proper bracket-balanced scan) instead.

`emit_to` regex `\.emit_to\(\s*"[^"]*"\s*,\s*"([^"]+)"` insists the first argument is a double-quoted literal. Real code commonly targets a specific window via `app.emit_to(&label, "event", payload)` or `app.emit_to(window.label(), "event", payload)` — none of those match, so legitimate backend emitters are dropped from `backend`. Combined with finding #2 above, this skews both `test_listened_events_have_emitter` and `test_backend_emits_have_listener_warn_only` toward false negatives. Make the first argument optional/non-literal, e.g. `\.emit_to\(\s*("[^"]*"|[^,]+?)\s*,\s*"([^"]+)"`.

strip_comments_and_strings treats everything between backticks as opaque string content and replaces it with spaces, including `${...}` interpolation expressions. Code like `` `result: ${eval(input)}` `` has the `eval(input)` body erased to whitespace, so EVAL_RE never matches it. Template-literal interpolation is very common in modern TS/TSX (dynamic class names, tagged-template helpers, error-format helpers, inline i18n), so this is a realistic false-negative path the audit does not catch. The header enumerates the regex-literal limitation but not this one — only WebView runtime CSP stands between an audit miss and a blocked execution. Consider tracking `${...}` nesting with a small stack inside the backtick branch and re-entering normal scanning for the expression body until the matching `}` closes it.

INDIRECT_RE enumerates only `(0,eval)`, `window.eval`, `globalThis.eval`, `self.eval`, and there is no eval-side equivalent of ALIAS_RE (which exists only for `Function`). Real obfuscation routes that slip past the audit:
1. `var e = eval; e('x')` — aliasing; `eval;` does not match EVAL_RE (needs `(`), and `e(` matches nothing.
2. `globalThis['eval']('x')` / `window["eval"]('x')` — computed access; the `'eval'`/`"eval"` literal is stripped to whitespace by the stripper, leaving `globalThis[  ]('x')` with no `eval` token at all, so neither EVAL_RE nor INDIRECT_RE fires.
3. `eval?.('x')` — optional chaining; `\beval\s*\(` requires `(` directly after `eval` and `\s*` does not match `?.`.
4. `Reflect.apply(eval, this, ['x'])` / `Function.prototype.constructor.call(...)` — reflective invocation.
Each of these is a reachable way to execute `eval`, so the indirect-form detector under-covers relative to its stated goal. Consider adding patterns for `\b\w+\s*=\s*eval\b` (alias), `(?:\bwindow\b|\bglobalThis\b|\bself\b|\bglobal\b)\s*\[\s*['"`]eval['"`]\s*\]` (computed), `\beval\s*\?\s*\(`, and `Reflect\s*\.\s*(?:apply|construct)\s*\([^,]*\beval\b`.

comments.content: `SabotageStore::upsert` simulates concurrency by mutating `updated_at` inside the *same* thread, before delegating to `MemStore::upsert`, and relies on MemStore's specific lock-acquisition order to trigger the 409 path. The inline comment flags the fragility, but the actual risk is silent false-positive: if `MemStore::upsert` ever wraps the whole operation in a single lock (or changes the compare order), the test still asserts 409 even though the conflict path is no longer being exercised — masking regressions in the most important write-safety guarantee. Replace the sequential trick with a real concurrent writer (a separate thread that bumps `updated_at` while the handler is sleeping in `MemStore::load`), or at minimum inject the mutation through a hook that MemStore exposes for tests.

`SlowStore` implements only `load`, `upsert`, and `event_hub` — `notify_change` is missing. If `TaskStore::notify_change` has a default impl that does nothing, `change_log_line` audit events and SSE `tasks-changed` notifications are silently dropped for this fixture, creating a coverage gap for the change-logging path. If it has no default, the test won't compile at all. Either add `fn notify_change(&self, op: &str, task: &db::Task) { self.inner.notify_change(op, task) }` (mirroring `SabotageStore`) or, if the default no-op is intentional, document it on the trait so future fakes don't silently lose events.

`Box::leak(Box::new(tauri::test::mock_app())).handle().clone()` permanently leaks the entire mock Tauri runtime for the life of the test process; combined with the cloned `AppHandle` (which is internally an `Arc`) passed into `api_stop_for_exit`, every internal mock-app reference stays reachable forever and accumulates across repeated test invocations and any future process-level teardown assertions. Hoist the mock app into a `once_cell`/`LazyLock` (or `std::sync::OnceLock`) at module scope so it is constructed once and reused, or accept the leak explicitly with a brief comment justifying why a `'static` `AppHandle` is required (so a future reader can revisit the decision).

Mutex held across blocking joins in `api_stop_locked`. The `state.0` guard passed in as `&mut Option<RunningApi>` is held by the caller (`api_stop_impl` / `rotate_apply`) for the entire duration of this call. The body blocks on `h.join()` (accept thread — comment cites ~400ms worst case) and then `stop_sse_writers(...)` (comment cites `SSE_STOP_JOIN_TIMEOUT` = 5s). Any concurrent `api_start` / `api_status` / `api_rotate_token` trying to take `state.0` is serialized behind this for up to ~5.4s, directly contradicting the file-level invariant that the lock only covers short in-memory mutations. Restructure to set the shutdown flag and grab the join handles under the lock, then drop the guard before doing the joins.

File I/O and port bind performed under `state.0` mutex in `api_rotate_token` Err recovery. The inner `Ok(mut g) => { ... }` block holds the mutex guard across two `std::fs::read_to_string(&path)` calls AND `api_start_locked(...)` (which binds `API_PORT` and spawns threads). This directly violates the module's documented convention "文件 I/O 一律在锁释放后做" and re-introduces the very serialization the design was meant to avoid. Drop the guard, do the file I/O and start_api outside the lock, then re-acquire to merge the new `RunningApi` into the Option — accepting the small TOCTOU window, since the alternative is blocking all API commands on filesystem + bind latency.

TOCTOU window between `service_present` re-check and `write_enabled_flag` in `api_start`. The comment itself admits "复核≠原子". Between `service_present(&state) != Some(false)` and `write_enabled_flag(&app)`, a concurrent `api_stop` (or a second `api_start` that took a fresh instance) can flip `state.0` such that the flag ends up describing the opposite of the in-memory truth. The comment says this is self-healing on next manual toggle, but a single race flips the persisted state for every subsequent boot until the user notices. Either (a) drop the re-check and accept the worst-case, or (b) make the in-memory state itself authoritative (e.g. record the decision in `ApiState` under the same lock as the `Option` mutation, and write the flag in a single follow-up that re-reads with no intervening command surface — not achievable with the current two-phase design).

Symmetric TOCTOU in `api_status` between `service_present` re-check and `clear_enabled_flag`. Same defect as `api_start`: between the re-check and the flag clear, a concurrent `api_start` may have already bound the port and written its own flag, in which case this clear silently undoes the user's just-issued start, persisting as "disabled" until the next manual toggle. The inline comment acknowledges "误清后果可由用户手动开关自愈" — that's documenting a known correctness bug, not solving it.

Lock-poisoning errors are flattened to `String` at every site (api_start, api_status, api_stop_impl, rotate_apply, api_rotate_token recovery). The pattern `state.0.lock().map_err(|e| { eprintln!(...); e.to_string() })?` discards the `PoisonError<MutexGuard<...>>` payload (which carries the inner guard, the original mutex error context, and backtrace hooks) and yields a bare `e` that then gets re-wrapped by `CommandError::HttpStartFailed` / `CommandError::Internal` / `?` propagation as opaque text. Preserve the typed error — either introduce a `CommandError::MutexPoisoned { location: &'static str }` variant that carries structured info, or at minimum keep `e` typed until the boundary rather than calling `.to_string()` at the lock site. This also affects `service_present`'s `None` return: callers compare `None != Some(false)` (true → writes flag) or `None != Some(true)` (true → clears flag), so a poisoned mutex silently drives both branches in opposite directions across the file.

`service_present` returns `Option<bool>` but `None` (poisoned lock) is interpreted inconsistently by its two callers. In `api_start`, `service_present != Some(false)` is true when poisoned → flag is WRITTEN. In `api_status`, `service_present != Some(true)` is also true when poisoned → flag is CLEARED. So a single poisoned mutex produces opposite file mutations depending on which command happens to run. This isn't just inconsistency — it's a correctness bug: poisoning should be conservative (refuse to mutate persisted state), not opportunistic. Make `service_present` return `Result<bool, CommandError>` and have callers short-circuit (skip the file I/O entirely) when the lock can't be inspected, or convert poisoning to a hard error.

Unconditional token clone in `api_rotate_token` even on the NotRunning path. `rotate_apply(&app, &state, token.clone())` always heap-allocates the UUID-derived String (32 chars) so it can move into `api_start_locked`, but on `RotateOutcome::NotRunning` the parameter is dropped unused. Switch `rotate_apply` to take `Option<String>` (only clone / move in the running branch), or branch in the caller: read token file under lock only if `g.is_some()`, otherwise write-only-update. Marginal allocation cost, but it's in a security-sensitive code path called by the UI on every rotate click.

Commit/SSE consistency gap: `notify_change` is a separate default method, not part of `upsert`. The documented real-time guarantee depends on every caller remembering to invoke it after a successful commit. An omitted call leaves SSE clients permanently stale; a call made before commit (or after a failed one) announces uncommitted state. Enforce post-commit notification inside the store (e.g., invoke it at the end of `upsert` on success) or return the broadcast result so callers can't accidentally skip it.

Sync-to-async bridge safety: `load`/`upsert` use `tauri::async_runtime::block_on`, guarded only by a thread-local Tokio-handle check that panics on violation. This is a fragile cross-layer contract that will bring down a request worker (and potentially the whole app if panic=abort) if any future caller runs on a Tokio task, in an async command handler, or from a Tauri callback. Either model the trait as async, or isolate the bridge behind a dedicated blocking pool and return an error instead of panicking when the invariant is violated.

Duplicate task IDs in a batch are silently last-writer-wins. The conflict loop checks every entry against the pre-write state, and the apply loop then writes in input order. Two entries with identical `id` both pass the baseline check (they each see the original row), and the second `g[i] = t` silently overwrites the first with no warning. Either reject duplicate IDs in the input or document and enforce a deterministic merge order.

Database errors are flattened to `String` at the trait boundary, discarding the underlying error type/source. The HTTP layer has to rely on message-prefix matching (e.g. `db::CONFLICT_ERR_PREFIX`) to decide between 409 Conflict and 500, and loses backtraces. Preserve a typed error (custom enum with `Conflict`, `Storage`, etc.) and convert to the transport-level representation only at the handler edge.

comments.content: MemStore methods use `lock().unwrap()`, so any prior panic while the lock is held poisons the mutex and turns subsequent ordinary reads/writes into another panic — even though the trait returns `Result`. Recover with `PoisonError::into_inner` (logging the poisoning) or propagate the error to callers instead of panicking.

The trim+empty-check logic is duplicated between `take_trimmed_string` (lines 11-14) and `check_field` (lines 26-29). Both implement the same pattern of `str::trim` followed by an empty check. If trim semantics ever need to evolve (e.g. handling Unicode whitespace, NFC normalization, or stripping control characters), both sites must be updated in lockstep or the two helpers will silently drift. Consider extracting a shared private helper such as `fn trim_view(s: Option<&str>) -> Option<&str> { s.map(str::trim).filter(|t| !t.is_empty()) }` so both functions delegate to it; the optimization comment in `check_field` (avoiding `to_owned`) is preserved because the helper returns a borrowed view.

`check_field` returns `Option<String>` where `Some(msg)` denotes an error and `None` denotes either "input absent" or "input valid" — both success paths are collapsed into the same `None`. This is documented, but it is easy to invert at a call site (e.g. `if check_field(...).is_none() { return error }` would be wrong). For a `pub(crate)` helper that consolidates 5 templates this is acceptable, but the API would be harder to misuse as `Result<(), String>` or a small typed enum (e.g. `enum CheckOutcome { Skipped, Ok, TooLong(String) }`). Worth weighing against the cost of updating the 5 call sites.

Silent u128→i64 truncation in `now_ms`. `as_millis()` returns u128; the bare `as i64` cast silently drops the high bits once the timestamp exceeds i64::MAX (~year 2262), turning real times into negative or wrapped values with no signal — exactly the kind of silent truncation the checklist calls out. Use `i64::try_from(d.as_millis()).unwrap_or(i64::MAX)` (or document an explicit overflow policy).

        .map(|d| i64::try_from(d.as_millis()).unwrap_or(i64::MAX))

comments.content: `over_limit` measures length in Unicode scalar values via `chars().count()`, but the caps are aliased from `crate::bot::MAX_*` and the bot side may enforce `bytes().len()` (or grapheme-cluster count via `unicode-segmentation`). A payload that passes the bot check can be rejected here, or vice versa, splitting the contract across crates. Either align the counting strategy through a shared helper or document the divergence explicitly.

`let _ = req.respond(...)` silently swallows transport errors in both `internal_err` and the 409 branch of `upsert_err`. A client disconnect or socket failure during the error response itself leaves no log entry and no metric, so 'silent 500s/409s' can hide a class of production issues — a textbook swallowed `Result`. Capture the result and route failures through the same `ratelimit::log_line` path.

comments.content: `UpdateReq` models archive/delete as two independent `Option<bool>` fields, which makes `{archived: true, deleted: true}` (and other ambiguous combinations) representable in the request shape and forces downstream code to re-validate and disambiguate. Per the type-design rule, model this with a single `state: Option<TaskLifecycleState>` enum (or tagged request variants) so invalid states are unrepresentable at the deserializer.

The pre-epoch branch in `now_ms` writes its diagnostic via `eprintln!`, while every other diagnostic in this module flows through `super::ratelimit::log_line(log, ...)`. The clock anomaly will never reach the api.log file alongside the other entries, making correlation harder in post-mortems. Route through the same `log_line` path (e.g. by accepting a `log: &Option<PathBuf>` parameter or via a shared logger).

comments.content: Inconsistent mutex-poison handling. Only `trace_id_for_session` defends against a poisoned guard (logs `[mutex_poisoned]` and recovers via `into_inner()`); every other accessor in this file returns a borrowed `Mutex` / `tokio::Mutex` and relies on callers doing `.lock().unwrap()` or `.lock().await` — a single panic-holding guard anywhere in the process will cascade into spurious panics in all the other tables (`skill_runs`, `artifact_registry`, `confirms`, `sched_running`, `stop_registry`, `chat_running`, `exec_running`, `pending`, `question_waiters`, `ask_contexts`, `subagent_stops`). Pick one policy (either "panic is fine — callers handle it" or "recover-and-log everywhere") and apply it uniformly, ideally by extracting a small `lock_or_log` helper that wraps `.lock()` + poison logging next to the one already used here.

Split-state hazard between managed `AppState` and `FALLBACK` is silent. `ext()` quietly routes to `FALLBACK` whenever `try_state` returns `None`; the existing comment on `stop_registry` already calls out that registering a guard through one `AppHandle` while `/stop` reads through another (one managed, one falling back) breaks stop semantics, and the same trap applies to `pending`, `artifact_registry`, `chat_running`, `exec_running`, `sched_running`, `subagent_stops`, `trace_registry`, `confirms`, `question_waiters`, `ask_contexts` — i.e. *every* table. Because the split is invisible (no log, no error type, just two `&'static`-shaped maps), production failures will look like "guard didn't fire / entry never arrived". Consider one of: (a) refuse silently to fall back and return an error / log at the boundary so a misconfigured test or bootstrap path is loud, (b) add a debug assertion that the accessor's `app` matches the one used to register, or (c) require every accessor to take the same canonical `AppHandle` and only fall back in explicitly-tagged test paths. As-is, this is an intentional fail-open that masks configuration bugs across the whole state layer.

History-lock poisoning is silently swallowed (`if let Ok(...)`) inside `broadcast()`. If `history` is ever poisoned, the event is broadcast live, persisted to disk (`next_id` is committed), and clients receive it — but it never enters the replay buffer. A reconnecting client with `Last-Event-ID` = (this id - 1) will skip this event forever, silently desyncing from the live stream. The file's own contract (`id 契约`) requires history to be authoritative for dedup; this branch violates it without any log or recovery. Either abort the broadcast with `return` (and roll the id back, like the atomic_write failure path), or explicitly log + record in a parallel journal.

`db::atomic_write` (filesystem rename) executes while `self.clients` mutex is held. This couples every broadcast's wall-clock cost to disk I/O latency — under antivirus scans, network filesystem stalls, or even transient filesystem contention, the `clients` lock will block all concurrent SSE registrations (`sse_connect` takes the same lock) and any subsequent broadcast. The "human-rate" cost claim does not hold when I/O is held under the broadcast critical section. Move persistence outside the `clients` critical section (e.g., write id after releasing the lock via a separate counter state, or use a background flusher keyed off `next_id` periodically).

The `clients` lock poison recovery uses `e.into_inner()`, which returns the inner `MutexGuard` — bypassing the poison flag but NOT validating that the guarded `Vec<(SyncSender, Weak)>` is in a logically consistent state. If a previous holder panicked mid-mutation (e.g., between `try_send` and `clients.remove(i)`), the vec may contain stale senders that have already been observed-failed by some other path, or partial updates. Subsequent broadcasts would push to / remove entries in a vec whose invariants are unverified. Either fail closed (`return` with diagnostic, mirroring the atomic_write failure path) or document why the vec's mutation pattern is panic-safe.

`EventHub.clients`, `EventHub.history`, and `EventHub.next_id` are all `pub`. This lets external code (e.g., the `sse.rs` writer, tests, or future refactors) bypass `broadcast()` / `replay()` / `last_id()` and mutate state directly, breaking the documented invariants (id monotonicity inside `clients` lock, history FIFO, hub_id stability). Keep fields private; expose only the `broadcast`/`replay`/`last_id`/`hub_id` API that already exists.

`escape_for_log` does `s.replace("| ", "|  ").chars()` which allocates a full intermediate `String` solely to iterate over characters; for every logged payload this is an extra O(n) heap clone on the write hot path. The inline comment even admits "旧实现的 `| ` → `|  ` 双空格补位在逐字符臂下由 `|`→`||` 语义覆盖", yet the code still performs the replace — the doc comment and the inline comment directly contradict each other (function header says replace is the rule; inline comment says it's redundant). Either drop the `.replace(...)` (and fix the misleading trailing comment), or implement the 2-char lookahead in the loop without allocating a throwaway `String`. The subsequent `escaped.chars().count()` followed by `escaped.chars().take(max)` is also two extra O(n) passes; a single forward pass tracking remaining budget avoids both.

`read_log_tail` discards the original `std::io::Error` via `format!("读取日志失败：{e}")` and stuffs a string into `CommandError::IoError`. The error kind/source chain is lost, which makes `err.kind()` / `e.source()` unavailable downstream and weakens any post-mortem classification. Wrap the original error (e.g. `io::Error::from(e)` or `io::Error::new(e.kind(), ...)`) so callers can still branch on `ErrorKind` and the OS-level cause survives.

comments.content: `read_log_tail` materializes the whole `bot.log` (up to the 5 MiB rotation cap) into a `String`, then `lines.collect()` allocates a `Vec<&str>`, then `lines[len-limit..].to_vec()` allocates *another* `Vec<&str>`, then `reverse()` + `join("\n")` does a final allocation. This is three O(n) Vec passes plus a full file read on every UI poll. A reverse-byte-chunk tail read (`BufReader::new(file).lines()` walking back from EOF, or `rsplit('\n').take(limit)` over a single `read_to_end`) eliminates both the whole-file buffer and the duplicate Vec.

Lock-poison recovery at `BOT_LOG_LOCK` only `eprintln!`s and silently resumes via `e.into_inner()`. The whole point of this lock (per the comment above) is to prevent the audit and bot audit appenders from interleaving bytes on `bot.log`. After any panic inside a previous holder the mutex is poisoned, the invariant is gone, and concurrent appenders can corrupt the file — but the only signal is a stderr line, no `audit_event!` is written for post-mortem correlation. At minimum, mirror the poisoning into the audit log (e.g. `audit_event!(..., "bot_log_lock_poisoned", err => &e)`) and consider refusing to write rather than silently producing potentially-garbled entries.

`write_event` reached from a `#[tauri::command]` violates the BOT_LOG_LOCK contract: the doc on `BOT_LOG_LOCK` says "持锁跨越整段阻塞文件 IO（rotate + open + chmod + write），不得在 tokio worker / 延迟敏感路径上直接调用", yet this command dispatches on Tauri's async runtime and synchronously runs `rotate_log_if_large` + `open` + `chmod` + `writeln` while holding the global mutex, blocking the worker. Either move the synchronous work into a `std::thread::spawn` (or `tauri::async_runtime::spawn_blocking`) before invoking `write_event`, or split write_event into a lock-free append path guarded by `spawn_blocking`. Same hazard applies to any caller of `audit_event!` / `write_event_with_error` from a `#[tauri::command]` or async task.

Silent mutex-poison recovery discards the invariant the lock was meant to protect: `e.into_inner()` lets a second writer proceed after a first holder panicked mid-write, so two threads can race `writeln!` into `bot.log` and produce interleaved/garbled lines, plus bypass the rotate/chmod ordering the lock guarantees. The same pattern is used on `BOT_LOG_TEST_LOCK`. Prefer propagating the poison (`unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())` -> `.lock().unwrap()` plus a clear panic in release) or, if recovery is intentional, at minimum document the data-corruption risk and surface a counter/metric so silent interleaving is observable.

chmod failure only `eprintln`s and returns `Ok`, so when chmod cannot tighten perms (unsupported FS, EPERM on a parent dir owned by another user, etc.) the file keeps its old mode (potentially world-readable under umask 0644) and continues to accumulate user commands, file paths, and tool output readable by other accounts on the host. stderr is also commonly redirected/buffered by launchers, making this regression invisible. Surface the failure to the caller (`Result<(), AuditError>`) and at minimum gate further writes / fall back to a perms-restricted temp file when chmod fails.

Every audit event reopens the log file (with `OpenOptions::create+append`) and re-runs `chmod`, and `write_at` also invokes `rotate_log_if_large` while holding `BOT_LOG_LOCK`. Under per-step audit volume this multiplies syscalls, widens the global lock window for every event, and serialises all writers behind the chmod+rotate syscalls even when nothing needs rotating. Keep a long-lived `Mutex<File>` (or `RwLock<File>` with the mutex only guarding close-on-rotate) and move rotate+open into a separate path so steady-state writes are a single locked append.

`format_event_line` is declared `pub` with `#[cfg_attr(not(test), allow(dead_code))]` — the doc says "测试用，不碰磁盘". Public visibility invites production callers to bypass `BOT_LOG_LOCK` / `rotate_log_if_large` / `chmod` / file persistence entirely (it just builds a string). Either gate it with `#[cfg(test)]` (and keep an internal `pub(crate)` helper for tests that need it via a non-public path), or rename/move it to a `pub(crate) fn format_event_line_for_test` so misuse is a compile error outside `mod tests`.

base_url_is_safe treats `http://attacker.com@127.0.0.1` as safe because the host resolves to a loopback address. The safety guarantee depends entirely on `base_url_is_safe` and the actual HTTP client (reqwest) agreeing on URL parsing — any divergence (e.g., a layer in between that splits on `@` and uses the left half as host, or a custom userinfo-display path that misleads operators) becomes a SSRF / data-exfiltration vector to `attacker.com`. Either reject userinfo-bearing URLs outright (simpler invariant), or document this strict contract here and verify the same `url::Url::host_str()` path is used everywhere the base URL is later consumed. The current test only proves the function's view, not the end-to-end behavior.
comments.existing_code:
// 安全：userinfo 不影响连接目标——host 解析后确为回环
    assert!(base_url_is_safe("http://attacker.com@127.0.0.1"));

comments.content: The comment "truncate_for_log 是 escape_for_log 的别名" is unverifiable from this file: the two are re-exported as separate items (`pub(crate) use audit::{escape_for_log, truncate_for_log};`) and this `mod.rs` has no `pub use ... as ...` or `pub fn truncate_for_log = escape_for_log` binding. If they really are aliases the alias lives in `audit.rs`, but if not this comment misleads readers about the relationship. Verify and either remove the "别名" claim or add an inline pointer (e.g. `pub use audit::truncate_for_log as escape_for_log;`) so the claim is enforced by the compiler.

Re-exporting Tauri's internal macro-generated identifiers (`__cmd__*`, `__tauri_command_name_*`) at the crate boundary via `pub use` leaks Tauri implementation details into `crate::bot::config::*`. If `bot.rs`'s facade genuinely needs them, they should at minimum be `pub(crate) use` so they don't escape to external consumers; otherwise this facade is wider than necessary and changes in Tauri macro output (versions, item names) become breaking API changes for this crate's public surface.

`bot_log_read_fail_audit_line_written` deletes a shared `bot.log` file at `exe.parent().join("bot.log")` (target/debug/deps/) after asserting on its contents. Multiple test binaries in the same target directory run serially per-binary but may share this path, and the silent `let _ = std::fs::remove_file(&log)` swallows the error. The `BOT_LOG_TEST_LOCK` only protects within one process — cross-process there is no synchronization. Either (a) move the audit log to a per-test tempdir for this assertion, or (b) explicitly check the error from `remove_file` and avoid the silent swallow, so future failures are visible.

The `bypass_llm_switch_defaults_true_and_honors_explicit_false` test, when run, writes/overwrites a real bot-config.json at `dir.path().join("bot-config.json")`, and the `read_bypass_llm_switch_at` / `read_memory_control_at` / `read_memory_tuning_at` paths are the production read kernel. If the production reader resolves the path relative to `crate::bot::config::io::config_path()` instead of taking the path as a pure argument, the test would mutate the real user config. The test relies on a "pure path parameter" kernel; verify that `read_bypass_llm_switch` (the non-`_at` variant exposed at line 56) does not accidentally call `read_bypass_llm_switch_at` with a path that resolves to the user's real config dir — otherwise tests can corrupt production config. This is a structural risk even if the current implementation is correct.

Dead/no-op code in the `None` arm: `if let Some(evo) = obj.get_mut("memoryTuning") { let _ = evo; }` binds `evo` to a `&mut serde_json::Value` and immediately discards it — the conditional has no side effect, so the next line `obj.remove("memoryTuning")` already covers both branches. Looks like an incomplete edit (the pattern suggests intent to mutate `evo` first — e.g. log/migrate its contents). Either drop the dead `if let` block or implement the intended logic.

CONFIG_WRITE_LOCK is held across blocking keyring I/O. `migrate_legacy_key` calls `keyring::has_api_key()` and `keyring::write_api_key(&k)` while the lock is held (same pattern in `strip_verified_keys` / `migrate_search_keys` / `migrate_mcp_server_secrets_locked`). The header comment claims the lock only guards RMW file writes, but in practice lock duration scales with keyring backend latency (e.g. macOS Keychain prompts, Windows Credential Manager, libsecret dbus round-trips). This serializes every config write behind the slowest path and risks re-entrancy if any keyring call ever fires the audit logger from a callback. Either do keyring IO before acquiring the lock (commit in-memory only, then re-verify under lock), or split into per-resource locks.

`write_memory_tuning_at` takes its own `TUNING_WRITE_LOCK` that is independent of `CONFIG_WRITE_LOCK`, so it is not synchronized with `update_config_file` / `add_allowed_dir` / `migrate_*` (which write the same file under `CONFIG_WRITE_LOCK`). Two concurrent writers — e.g. one RMW-updating `evolution` and one RMW-updating `memoryTuning` — both read the same JSON snapshot, then the last writer silently overwrites the other's unrelated field. The header comment defers this as a follow-up, but until it's fixed this is a real last-writer-wins data-loss race on `bot-config.json`. Fold `TUNING_WRITE_LOCK` into `CONFIG_WRITE_LOCK`, or use a single shared lock for the whole config file.

`add_allowed_dir` only `.trim()`s the user-supplied dir before persisting it into `cfg.allowed_dirs` — no `Path::canonicalize`, no absolute-path enforcement, no rejection of `..` segments / null bytes / symlink hops. Path-traversal or relative inputs (e.g. `../etc`, `~/passwd`, whitespace tricks) get persisted verbatim and later trusted by FS-whitelist enforcement downstream. Validate via canonicalize (or at minimum: require absolute path, reject `..`/null segments, normalize separators) before persisting, and surface a typed error to the caller instead of silently writing the raw string.

Inconsistent audit coverage on plaintext-key strip. `migrate_search_keys` emits `config.search_key_migrated` and `add_allowed_dir` emits `config.plaintext_key_stripped`, but `migrate_legacy_key` silently strips `api_key` (the most sensitive credential) on success with no audit row at all. For a security-relevant operation, emit a `config.api_key_migrated` audit event after the successful `write_config_atomic`, mirroring the `drop(_g); for slot in migrated_slots { audit_event!(...) }` pattern in `migrate_search_keys`. This both improves forensic traceability and makes the three strip paths uniformly observable.

Mutex poisoning recovery silently absorbs panics from concurrent writers. If a thread panics inside the RMW window (during `store.load()`, `db::prepare_for_upsert`, the field mutations, or `store.upsert()`), the next writer calling `e.into_inner()` proceeds as if nothing happened. Each thread re-loads from DB so data is not directly corrupted, but the original panic is swallowed, the root-cause bug is hidden, and the same panic will recur on every subsequent request - turning a recoverable bug into an indefinite silent degradation. Treat poisoning as a hard failure (return 500 / `Err(...)` out of the labeled block) so it is visible to operators and to the calling handler instead of masked by an `eprintln!` line.

Note: this pattern is repeated identically in `update_task` and `delete_task`; the same fix should be applied to all three call sites.

`API_RMW_LOCK` is held across both `store.load()` and `store.upsert()`, so wall-clock DB I/O latency is fully serialized across every concurrent API writer - even when the in-memory mutation is microseconds. With `MAX_WORKERS=64` the achievable write throughput collapses to `1 / (load_latency + mutate + upsert_latency)` instead of overlapping. The code already populates `expected_updated_at` on create, so optimistic concurrency is available: take the lock only across the brief mutate window (or none at all), and let the store reject a stale snapshot with a 409 - the global mutex then stops being on the critical I/O path.

`list_tasks` calls `query_param` four times. Each call performs a full `url::form_urlencoded::parse(query.as_bytes())` over the raw query string, walking the bytes and percent-decoding each pair. A single parse into a small map (or a single linear scan that records only the keys we care about) is both clearer and cheaper, and avoids the subtle `Some("1".into())` allocation per call.

The `task` (resp. `t`) struct is cloned solely so `store.upsert(vec![task.clone()])` can take ownership while the original is later returned as `Ok(task)` (resp. `Ok(t)`). The clone is wasted on the failure path (the original is dropped anyway), and even on success the clone copies the entire `Task` (which carries `note`, `tags`, `files`, `subtasks`, `schedule`, etc.) for no semantic reason. Either move the struct into the upsert and re-load it (one extra DB read per success - cheap relative to the wasted full clone), or change `TaskStore::upsert` to accept `&[db::Task]` so the in-memory mutation can stay borrow-only.

Replacement for the previous comment on this block (the prior suggestion_code rendered with stray markup). The substantive finding is unchanged: `path.strip_prefix("/api/tasks/")` returns the raw URL tail without URL-decoding, without a length cap, and without a character whitelist. The `id` is forwarded to `get_task`/`update_task`/`delete_task` and is propagated to the SSE emitter and the log line. A crafted request such as a 64KB id or a `%00...` blob is passed through unchanged, letting a single request burn CPU/RAM in the handler, in SSE subject interpolation, and in any logging that doesn't bound its input. Cap the length (UUIDs are 36 chars; anything longer is by definition invalid) and reject empty ids.

Static array indexed by `slot.index()` panics if any future `KeySlot` variant maps to an index >= 3. `KeySlot::index()` in `types.rs` currently returns 0/1/2 for Llm/Tavily/Brave, but that invariant is implicit — adding a fourth variant will compile cleanly and then panic at runtime the first time `migrate_legacy_keyring_entry` runs. Consider replacing the hardcoded `[AtomicBool; 3]` with a `HashMap<KeySlot, AtomicBool>` or attaching the migrated flag to the slot itself, and assert in tests that the array length matches the variant count.

Silent orphan in legacy migration: when `new_entry.set_password(&old)` succeeds but `old_entry.delete_credential()` fails, the v0 legacy entry is silently left behind (`let _ = ...`). On subsequent calls `migrate_legacy_keyring_entry` early-returns as soon as it observes a non-empty v1 entry, never retrying the v0 cleanup — so the orphan survives indefinitely until the user explicitly clears the key (which goes through `delete_api_key_at`). Across upgrades this lets stale v0 credentials accumulate per slot. Either schedule a best-effort v0 cleanup pass on each `read_key_of_slot` even when v1 is non-empty, or write a WARN audit when the v0 delete fails so the inconsistency is visible.

Comment/contract mismatch: the doc-comment promises `classify_get_password` maps failures to "结构化变体" so the frontend can hint by code, but the implementation collapses every `keyring::Error` (including `NoEntry`, `PlatformFailure`, etc.) into a single `CommandError::KeyringError(format!(...))` String. `CommandError` only has one `KeyringError(String)` variant, so all keychain errors surface to the frontend as the single error code `KEYRING_ERROR` — 'not configured' is indistinguishable from 'keychain locked' or 'permission denied'. The companion `classify_has_key` correctly preserves `NoEntry → Ok(false)`; `classify_get_password` should likewise distinguish at least `NoEntry` so that callers like `read_search_key` (which currently relies on a separate `has_*` call) can rely on a single read. Either introduce a structured `KeyringError` variant with a cause enum, or split the function into two: one returning `Result<Option<String>, _>` where `None` means unconfigured.

TOCTOU race in `migrate_plaintext_key_if_system`: `p.exists()` is checked, then later the file is opened via `read_key_file_from` and the path is mutated (`key_entry.set_password` then `std::fs::remove_file`). A concurrent process (or a second instance of the app started in parallel) can delete or rewrite the plaintext file between the `exists()` check and the read, causing a `NotFound` to leak through `read_key_file_from` or — worse — letting the file be deleted between a successful read and the subsequent `remove_file`, leaving a stale plaintext copy alongside the just-populated v1 entry. Prefer opening the file directly (treating `NotFound` as 'no migration needed') rather than pre-checking with `exists()`, or wrap the read/remove in a lock file.

Inconsistent error reporting for keyring events: legacy `delete_credential` failure is reported via `eprintln!` to stderr, while every other keyring lifecycle event in this module (`keyring_fallback_plaintext`, `keyring_fallback_chmod_failed`, `keyring_migrated_from_plaintext`, `keyring_service_migrated`) flows through `crate::audit::write_warn_audit_to`. For a security-sensitive module whose failure modes need to be diagnosable from `bot.log`, this means a v0 cleanup failure is invisible to the audit pipeline and only shows up on the terminal — bypassing the structured event tags that the rest of the module uses. Route the failure through `write_warn_audit_to` with a dedicated tag (e.g., `keyring_legacy_cleanup_failed`).

Shutdown can miss a concurrently connecting client. `sse_connect` publishes its sender into `hub.clients` before acquiring `SSE_WRITERS`, while this function releases the registry lock before setting any stop flags. A request already dispatched by the accept thread can therefore register after this scan and keep the retired hub (and itself) alive indefinitely. Use a lifecycle gate shared by client admission and writer registration, mark the hub as stopping under that gate, and set all flags before releasing it.

Discarding this `flush()` error can keep a dead buffered connection alive: the writer continues waiting for events/heartbeats, its `_alive` token remains strong, and it occupies an SSE client slot until later traffic or service shutdown. Treat replay flush failure as fatal, and apply the same error check to the keepalive flush below.

comments.content: `debug_assert!` for lock invariants is compiled out under `--release`. If a caller invokes `migrate_config_file_locked` without holding `CONFIG_WRITE_LOCK` in a release build, the assertion is silently dropped and the function runs against unlocked state — racing with `load_config` / `bot_set_config` and potentially corrupting `write_config_atomic`. Either make it a real `assert!`/explicit precondition check, or rename/privatize so only the `#[cfg(test)]` shim and the single locked caller can reach it.

Check-then-act race: `SCHEMA_MIGRATION_CHECKED.load(...)` runs before `try_lock`, so two concurrent callers can both pass the outer gate. The lock holder then performs the migration and sets the flag; the second caller hits `WouldBlock` and returns `Ok(())` assuming the holder did the work — but if the holder's migration *fails* (the `Err` branch leaves the flag unset per the documented contract) the WouldBlock caller silently skips the next chance to retry. Additionally, the `try_lock` fallback silently drops migration without an audit/log line, so a misordered caller (e.g., `load_config` invoked inside an RMW section without first calling `migrate_bot_config_schema_locked`) silently skips the schema bump. Suggest either (a) keeping a small "migration-attempted-this-process" flag separate from "migration-succeeded", or (b) recording the deferred attempt so the next call retries deterministically.

Recovery from `TryLockError::Poisoned` silently reuses the inner guard and continues. A poisoned mutex almost always means the previous holder panicked — silently swallowing that masks real bugs (state corruption, partial writes during the panic). Use `lock()`/`try_lock()` only on a recovered-from-poison mutex after an explicit audit event so the corruption is observable, and avoid keeping the inner guard if you can't prove the protected state is still consistent.

Schema migration re-serializes and writes the *entire* JSON whenever `schemaVersion` is missing/stale. The doc comment says the plaintext `apiKey` field is cleared by `migrate_legacy_key` / `migrate_search_keys`, but the ordering is unenforced — if a future caller wires this migration after the key cleanup, or runs it independently (e.g., during a manual recovery), the freshly-written file still contains the plaintext credential. Either (a) explicitly invoke the key-cleanup migration inside this function before write, or (b) document the contract as `must_run_after(key_cleanup)` and add a unit test that asserts ordering.

All IO/serde errors are flattened to `String` via `e.to_string()`, discarding the original `io::Error` kind (`NotFound`, `PermissionDenied`, …) and the serde error chain (line/column). This makes diagnosing disk-full vs. permission-denied vs. malformed-JSON indistinguishable in user-facing messages. Wrap with `thiserror`/`anyhow` at this boundary or use `map_err(|e| format!("read_to_string({path:?}): {e}"))` to preserve context.

`derive_legacy_fields_from_active` claims (per the doc) to back-fill the "four legacy fields" (`base_url`, `model`, `max_tokens`, `api_provider`) used by `bot_model_loop`, but it only writes `base_url` and `model`. If any caller reads `cfg.max_tokens` directly instead of going through `effective_inference`, they get the *global* value rather than the active entry's `max_tokens` — diverging from the active entry's effective inference. Either derive `cfg.max_tokens` from the active entry as well (matching the base_url/model pattern), or explicitly state in the doc that `cfg.max_tokens` is intentionally a global-only field and audit every reader accordingly.

`resolve_top_p` does not take a `provider` parameter while `resolve_temperature` does, even though both live next to each other and the doc comment explicitly enumerates per-protocol temperature bounds. This asymmetry forces callers (and reviewers) to remember that `top_p` happens to share a single bound (`0..=1`) across both protocols today — and any future change (e.g., a vendor that allows `top_p > 1`) becomes a silent foot-gun. Take `provider: ApiProvider` for symmetry even if it's unused, so the API shape doesn't drift.

`SCHEMA_MIGRATION_CHECKED` uses `Ordering::SeqCst` on every `migrate_bot_config_schema` entry (the hot path on every `load_config` until first success). Since this is a one-shot latch with no synchronization coupling to *other* data (the real protection is `CONFIG_WRITE_LOCK` plus the double-check inside it), `Ordering::Relaxed` is sufficient and avoids the SeqCst fence cost.

comments.content: `spawn_blocking` 的 JoinHandle 在 `.await.unwrap_or_default()` 处把三种性质截然不同的失败吞成空 Vec：(1) spawn_blocking 内部 `load_config` panic；(2) JoinError（线程被取消/关闭）；(3) 配置里没有 `mcp_servers` 字段（`unwrap_or_default()`）。下游 `servers.into_iter().find(...)` 命中 `None` 时统一报「MCP 服务器已被删除」——配置读取故障被伪装成业务状态，模型会按错误的因果链路重发请求，排障与审计均受影响。应区分错误源，至少 spawn_blocking/JoinError 走 error 通道，「配置缺失」单独文案。

远端调用 `Err`（连接拒绝、超时、协议错误等）一律包成 `ToolResult::ok`，仅靠首字「MCP」规避 severity classifier 把 error 当 warn 的副作用。这意味着所有 MCP 失败都不会出现在错误指标/告警/dashboard 里，问题被埋进 ok 文本。建议：(a) 跟 registry 协商，让 severity classifier 接受带前缀的 error 标签（结构化标记），不要靠首字符 hack；(b) 在此之前，至少在返回文本里附上机器可识别的失败类型，让下游能 grep 出 MCP 失败率。

`build_mounted_tools` 是热路径（每轮模型循环 + 每次 dispatch 反查都要跑一遍），`used` HashSet 与 `out` Vec 没有按总工具数预分配容量。HashSet 在元素数较多时 rehash 开销可观，Vec 多次扩容会 memcpy。预先统计 `servers.iter().map(|(_,_,t)| t.len()).sum()` 一次性给出容量 hint，把扩容次数从 ~log(n) 降到 0。

Lost-update race: `bot_set_active_model` does an unlocked load → modify → write. The comment on `bot_set_config` explicitly warns that an unlocked load before a locked write creates a lost-update window (concurrent `persist_last_run`/evolution writes can be silently overwritten). This function never acquires `lock_config_write()` at all, so concurrent `bot_set_config` calls, evolution writes, or two rapid `bot_set_active_model` invocations can race and silently destroy each other's edits (settings-page changes, `verified_vendors`, etc.). Acquire the same write lock used in `bot_set_config` around the read-modify-write.

Verification-flag injection via full config replacement: `prune_verified_vendors` never checks `disk.verified_vendors.contains(v)`. The retain closure only verifies that the vendor's (protocol, base_url) signature is consistent between incoming and disk, so any vendor the frontend includes in `incoming.verified_vendors` whose entries already match in both maps will survive — even if it was never tested. This bypasses the stated "test-only" path documented on `bot_test_connection`. The in-file test `prune_verified_vendors_drops_overwritten_missing_and_url_changed` actually demonstrates this: disk has no verified vendors, yet `DeepSeek` is retained because its signature is consistent. Require `disk.verified_vendors.contains(v)` before retaining, or restrict `verified_vendors` mutations to the test command.

Non-atomic credential/config coordination. In `bot_set_config` all keyring writes (api_key, vendor_key, tavily/brave) run *before* `lock_config_write()` and `write_bot_config_file_locked`, so a config-write failure or a concurrent save leaves credentials already changed while `verified_vendors`/config still describe the old state — the opposite of the documented fail-closed intent. `bot_clear_vendor_key` then separately updates `verified_vendors` and deletes the key without any cross-lock, so an in-flight `bot_test_connection` that read the vendor key before deletion can complete after the delete and re-add the vendor to `verified_vendors`, leaving a vendor flagged verified with no key. Additionally `bot_clear_api_key` never invalidates `verified_vendors` for vendors that had no vendor-specific key and relied on the global fallback. Stage all credential mutations under the same config lock and gate verified-flag changes on the same epoch/keyring state used by the probe.

Credential-bearing probe trusts caller-supplied destination. `bot_test_connection` accepts arbitrary `base_url`, `api_format`, and `vendor` from the IPC caller, loads the matching stored credential (vendor key or global fallback), and attaches it as `Authorization: Bearer` / `x-api-key` to a GET against the caller-supplied URL. There is no scheme/host allow-list, no binding to the vendor's persisted endpoint, and `api_format` is only branched on the literal `"anthropic"` — any other value silently gets Bearer auth with no warning. A compromised renderer (or any untrusted IPC caller) can exfiltrate stored credentials to any host. Validate the URL (scheme, allow-listed host or at minimum non-loopback/non-link-local) and require `vendor`'s persisted base_url to match before attaching credentials; treat unknown `api_format` as an error rather than a default.

Keyring errors silently coerced to "no key". Both branches use `keyring::read_api_key().unwrap_or_default()`, discarding locked-keychain / permission-denied / backend-unavailable errors. This contradicts the project's own policy documented on `bot_get_config` ("keyring 真实故障透传 Err，不吞成未配置") and the doc-comment on this function ("全局主 key 读不到（未配置 / 故障）按无 key 探活"). The practical consequence: a locked keychain makes the probe send no credentials, the server returns 401, and `verified_vendors.retain(|x| x != v)` then incorrectly removes the vendor from the verified list — turning an actionable KeyringError into a false-negative authorization decision. Propagate the keyring error with `?` (matching `has_vendor_key`/`has_api_key` earlier in the file) and let the caller decide.

Authorization ordering: the per-tool rule gate (deny/ask) and `skill_on_step` side-effects run *before* the subagent whitelist, so a forbidden tool can still trigger user confirmation prompts and mutate skill counters/records before being rejected. Move the `subagent_ctx` whitelist (and the budget acquire) ahead of `tool_rule_gate`/`skill_on_step`, or ensure they no-op for non-whitelisted names. Also verify the `use_skill` exemption at lines 271/280 cannot indirectly execute a tool that the deny rule blocks.

Cancellation-/panic-unsafe call/return balance: `tool.call` is emitted at function entry but there is no RAII guard (or scoped future combinator) to ensure `tool.return` is written if the future is dropped/panicked during `ask_user_confirm`, the tool body, `execute_mcp_tool`, `trace_sink` recording, or `skill_on_step_post`. Today only the manually-listed early returns are paired; any other abrupt exit leaves a dangling call in the audit log and an inconsistent skill step state. Wrap the post-`tool.call` body in a guard that always emits a final `tool.return` (or use a `defer`-style helper) keyed by the trace's `tool_call_id`.

Sensitive data in audit previews: `args_preview` (tool.call), `preview` (tool.return), and `parse_args` stderr logging (escape_for_log(args,200)) persist up to 80/200 chars of tool input and output without redaction. Tools commonly handle file contents, secrets, tokens, URLs, or PII; writing them to bot.log leaks them to anyone with log access and to log shipping pipelines. Apply redaction (regex on key names, content-type allow/deny) at the `audit::write_event` boundary or strip previews for tools that touch credentials, and downgrade `parse_args` error logging to the structured audit channel so it can be redacted.

Result/Option mapped to misleading status: `commit_and_report` maps `db_upsert_for` errors to `ToolResult::ok` with empty `refs`. Any consumer that decides domain success from `result.status` (skill post-hook, future pipeline stages, UI caches, automation that polls) will treat failed persistence as committed; only the textual error and a single audit event flag the failure. Either return `ToolResult::warn`/`error` so the semantic outcome is observable, or change every `ToolResult::status` consumer to consult the audit stream/result text first.

Trace span diverges from audit policy: `turn: trace.turn.unwrap_or(0) as i64` writes `turn=0` for every scheduler/background call that has no model-loop context, contradicting `trace_kv` which deliberately omits the field to avoid misleading `turn=0`. Additionally `ok` is derived from a text classifier (`!tool_call_failed`) instead of `result.status`, while the paired `tool.return` audit event uses `AuditLevel::from_tool_status(result.status)` — so a single call can have an `Error` audit level yet `ok=true` (or vice versa) in the span. Either make `SpanRecord` accept `Option<i64>` for `turn`, or stop emitting spans for non-model-loop traces; and drive `ok` from `result.status` (the same source the audit event uses) so the two records always agree.

Interactive default + caller-provided session_id without a guard: `execute_tool` hard-codes `interactive=true` and accepts a raw `session_id` while having no StopGuard to bind it; `traced_impl` likewise defaults `interactive` to `true` when `stop` is `None`. The comment claims "无 StopGuard 时按交互执行处理（DSL 调度器只在聊天上下文里跑）", but the type system does not enforce that. A background caller using `execute_tool` (or passing `None` to `execute_tool_with_stop`) will be treated as interactive, can block on `ask_user_confirm`, and any mismatched `session_id` will be accepted for subagent context lookups (`tool_guard::subagent_ctx(session_id)`) and trace attribution. Either default `interactive=false` (ask_user_confirm fails closed in non-interactive mode) and require an explicit guard for chat-context calls, or have a single internal API that derives both `session_id` and `interactive` from a canonical source.

Allowlist is not an execution boundary. `npx -y @scope/pkg`, `uvx pkg`, `docker run --mount /`, `python script.py` all run arbitrary code/containers; combined with attacker-controlled args (only length-bounded, not shape-checked), checking argv[0] alone gives no real protection. Either treat config as fully trusted or block dangerous arg patterns / use a tighter launcher registry.

`env`/`headers` are documented as secrets but the struct derives `Debug`, so any `format!("{:?}", cfg)`, panic message, error chain, or test assertion prints plaintext secrets. `skip_serializing` only gates disk; add a manual `impl Debug` that redacts env/headers (e.g., prints map length or `<redacted>`).

Two SSRF gaps here: (1) only lexical host is checked — a public-looking domain can resolve (or rebind) to a private IP, and reqwest follows redirects by default, so a 30x to 127.0.0.1 bypasses this gate; ensure the connection layer resolves the destination IP, rejects reserved ranges, and pins/blocks cross-host redirects. (2) The validator accepts URL userinfo (`http://user:pass@host`) and `McpServerConfig.url` is serialized to bot-config.json, leaking embedded credentials to disk — reject any parsed `username`/`password` or mark the field secret.

comments.content: `starts_with("gpt-5")` is unanchored: a hypothetical `gpt-50`, `gpt-500`, or `gpt-5x` would silently inherit the `reasoning_effort` protocol even if OpenAI ships such a model without one. Same hazard for `starts_with("o1")` matching `o10`/`o11`. Anchor to the version segment (`starts_with("gpt-5-") || m == "gpt-5"`, or `split('-').next() == Some("gpt-5")`) so unknown releases fall through to the safe `None` branch instead of picking up a wrong wire protocol.

Either fail closed — return `None` from `glm_version` on unrecognized separators so the caller's `_ =>` unknown-model branch fires — or explicitly require one of the documented separators before trusting the version.

comments.content: OpenOptions.mode(0o600) 只在文件创建时被采用；tmp 文件若已存在（例如上次写流程在 rename 之前崩溃留下），create(true).truncate(true) 会复用旧 inode 并跳过 mode，于是 rename 之后的目标文件继承旧权限（可能 0644），直接破坏本模块声称的「0600 不变式」和注释里的「无 chmod 窗口」承诺。建议：要么 `.create_new(true)` 拒绝复用旧文件（AlreadyExists 时先删再建），要么 open 后用 `f.set_permissions(Permissions::from_mode(0o600))` 显式 chmod 兜底；并在测试中加一条「预先以 0644 创建 tmp，再触发写」的回归。

tmp+rename 的「原子写」假设在断电/进程崩溃下并不成立：write_all 落 page cache 但未 fsync，rename 也未对 tmp 或父目录做 sync_all，rename 仍可能把未刷盘的 0 字节/截断内容置换到目标文件，造成服务器条目静默丢失。System 路径有「写后读回」兜底，但 PlaintextFile 路径没有读回校验。建议：rename 前对 tmp 调 `File::sync_all()`，并对父目录 fd 调 `sync_all()`（Linux 关键），使 tmp 内容持久化后才发生 inode 切换。

本模块设计文档与降级路径都用 `crate::audit::write_event` 记录敏感事件（`mcp.secret_fallback_plaintext`），但 hydrate 读路径上的 keychain 读取失败**只走 stderr**——与同函数里声明的「WARN（连接会失败、状态点红可见）」以及文件头注释的审计承诺口径不一致。运维侧无法在审计日志里发现持续性的 keychain 故障。建议：在此处补 `crate::audit::write_event(app, AuditLevel::Warn, "mcp.secret_read_failed", &[("server_id", s.id.clone())])`；同时确认 `AuditLevel::Warn` 在文件里有公开变体可用（与 `warn_fallback_once` 同口径）。

写后端的 `fallback_lock` 已在此函数体内释放，但缓存更新 (`cache_put`) 紧跟其后且**未与写操作在同一临界区**：并发 hydrate 在这两步之间命中旧缓存会得到旧值并应用到 cfg，而此时磁盘已是新值——cache 与 backend 短暂不一致，可能让 hydrate 把已被覆盖的旧 env/headers 注入到刚保存的服务器实例上。建议：要么把 cache_put 移入 `write_backend`（与 PlaintextFile 的 fallback_lock 临界区同生灭），要么显式走「先 cache 后 backend，失败回滚 cache」的乐观路径，避免「磁盘是新的、内存是旧的」窗口。

命中 cache 的「热路径」用 `s.env = secrets.env; s.headers = secrets.headers;` 是零拷贝移动；但 cache miss 成功路径里却先 `.clone()` 两次 BTreeMap 再 `or_insert(Some(secrets))`——每台服务器多分配两份 BTreeMap，且与文件设计目标「高频读不敲 keychain」下的 init/load 路径直接相关。建议：用 `std::mem::take` 取出原 map（前提 secrets 之后可弃），或 `let env = std::mem::replace(&mut secrets.env, BTreeMap::new())` 后将「空壳」插缓存；亦可在 cache 里直接存一个标志位 `enum CacheEntry { None, Present { env, headers } }` 避免双克隆。

`bot_effective_params` returns `CommandResult<...>` but the function unconditionally wraps in `Ok(...)`. If `load_config` returns a `Result`, the error is silently swallowed and the user sees defaults without any indication of failure (e.g., corrupted `bot-config.json`). If it returns `BotConfig` directly, the `CommandResult` wrapper is dead and misleading. Either propagate the load error so the settings UI can surface it, or drop the `CommandResult` wrapper since the function cannot fail.

Hardcoded-only entries' display values are string literals in `param_value` rather than references to constants — this recreates the exact 「展示的默认值」与「实际生效值」漂 problem the module-level docstring warns against. If `schedule.scan_secs` is ever changed from 30 to 60 in code, the table's `default: "30"` and the panel's `value: "30"` will silently desynchronize. Bind these literals to `pub const`s (e.g., `SCHEDULE_SCAN_SECS: u32 = 30`) and use them in both the `ParamDef::default` and `param_value`.

Sync filesystem syscalls inside an async fn on the Tauri runtime. `extract_path_check` walks every task and calls `std::fs::canonicalize` for each bound file on the async worker thread; with N tasks and M bound files this becomes N×M blocking syscalls that stall concurrent commands/events. Either short-circuit by comparing lexical path prefixes before canonicalizing, or move the whole bound-files scan into `spawn_blocking` (matching the `sanitize_task_files_arg` pattern already in this file).

`resolve_owner` is `async` but invokes the synchronous Tauri command `crate::db::people_list` directly on the async runtime. The comment acknowledges this, but it still blocks the worker for any I/O `people_list` performs (state lookup, file read, etc.) on every edit_task call. Wrap the lookup in `tokio::task::spawn_blocking` (or an equivalent helper) like the other bot tools do for sync syscalls.
