comments.content: Both `app.emit` results are dropped via `let _ =`. If the broadcast fails (channel full, listener gone, runtime issue), widgets stay stale with no audit/log signal — this is the sole mutation broadcast path for create/edit/complete/delete/archive flows, so silent loss means UI desync until next reload. At minimum log failures via `audit_log`; ideally surface as a recoverable error to the caller.

Silent fallthrough: `column` accepts only the literal string `"doing"`; anything else (including `"done"`, `"todo"`, typo, or LLM mis-naming) is created as `Todo` with no feedback. Inconsistent with `tool_edit_task` (line ~890) which uses `parse::<TaskStatus>()` and properly honors `"done"`. A model sending `"column":"done"` will get a Todo task and no error. Either reject invalid values explicitly, or use `TaskStatus::from_str` here too — and if the intent really is "create only as Todo/Doing", document/return the coerced value so the model can react.

monthly 日 / weekly 索引未做边界检查：例如 `monthly:99:00` 会渲染为「每月99日 00:00」、`weekly:9:08:00` 因 `["一".."日"].get(8)` 返回 None 而整体静默回退到「weird」分支、而 `weekly:0:08:00` 会 `checked_sub(1)` 失败同样回退。仅展示用途影响小，但解析口径与上游 `bot_scheduler::occurrence_after` 校验不一致；若将来同格式串被编辑器复用，会原样继承此缺口。建议在解析处加 (1..=31)/(1..=7) 边界或显式返回 None 触发未知格式回退。

冗余 DB 加载：交叉校验触发时连续两次 `active_tasks`（一次在 line 708 找 id、二次在 line 717 经 `find_task_by_keyword` 再走一遍 `active_tasks`），同窗格连续操作不同卡时会被放大。建议把第一次 `active_tasks` 的结果保存下来复用，或者把 `find_task_by_keyword` 改成接受已加载列表的纯函数版本。
trigger_reload 文档承诺「失败只记审计不回滚配置」，但 spawn 体里 reload_from_config 的结果被直接丢弃，既不写审计也不记日志；同时 JoinHandle 也被丢弃，应用关停时重载可能被中途打断，留下半连接/未释放的 socket。把 JoinHandle 存下来用 abort_handle + 收尾审计，至少与文档一致。

CONFIG_WRITE_LOCK（std::sync::Mutex，同步阻塞）在整段 RMW 内持有，期间既会执行 migrate_mcp_server_secrets_locked（keyring 写 + 文件读 + 文件写），用户闭包里还会调用 store_server_secrets/purge_server_secrets。macOS/Windows 的 keyring 系统调用在冷启动/credential prompt 期间可阻塞数百 ms，期间所有配置写者（add_allowed_dir / bot_set_config / 其他 MCP save）都被串行化。即使设计有意如此（锁内才能防止迁移读旧明文），仍应在文档里标注「写盘热路径会阻塞其他写者」，避免后续误以为可以无脑并发。

编辑路径下 store_server_secrets 先于 upsert_in_config 执行且若 upsert 失败补偿被故意跳过——但 store_server_secrets 已经把 keyring 里这个 id 对应的 env/headers 覆盖成「新值」。若 upsert_in_config 因为超上限等业务规则失败，配置文件仍保留旧 env/headers，但 keyring 已写入新值，下一次 reload_from_config 把两者合并时会得到混合态（旧 env + 新 secret）。建议编辑路径下也采取"upsert 成功后再 store_server_secrets"，或者在 upsert 失败时把 keyring 回滚到 pre_existing 的旧值。

column 参数仅识别 `"doing"`，其它任意字符串（含 `"done"`、`"review"`、空串、模型笔误的 `"do"`）一律静默回退 `TaskStatus::Todo`——模型拿不到任何反馈。`tool_edit_task` 用的是 `parse::<TaskStatus>()`（更宽松但至少报错），两套口径不一致。建议要么统一走 `TaskStatus::from_str`（非法值走 ok 通道回写给模型），要么保持显式三选一并补一个 `Some(other)` 分支返回「不支持的列 {other}」让模型纠正。

mcp_status 在未取任何锁的情况下调用 load_config（其内部会触发 schema 迁移 + hydrate_mcp_servers 从 keyring 读 secret），同时与 shared() 的 manager 内存态合并读。一个并发 in-flight 的 with_locked_config 写者已经写完 keyring 但还没原子替换配置文件时，mcp_status 会读到「旧结构 + 新 secret」的混合视图再与尚未重载的连接槽合并。原子 rename 保证文件不会被撕裂但不能保证 reader 与 writer 的视图一致；如果设置页依赖这个状态做下一步操作（启停/查看工具），会有明显的瞬态不一致。建议至少在读侧加 CONFIG_WRITE_LOCK 读路径，或在 writer 端把「写 keyring」推迟到 write_bot_config_file_locked 成功之后。

toggle 的审计只写入了 set_enabled_in_config 之后的最终状态（toggled 里是 new state），从审计日志无法重建「旧 enabled → 新 enabled」的转移，只能看到事件名 + 当前值。需要在闭包里捕获切换前的 enabled 值（set_enabled_in_config 之前），并在 audit 调用里同时输出 prev / new；或者改用结构化审计字段（如 prev_enabled / new_enabled）。

Race: the check–remove–spawn–insert sequence is not serialized per server. Two concurrent callers (different cfg snapshots, or `call_tool` racing `reload_from_config`) can both pass the fingerprint gate, each spawn its own subprocess, and the second `slots().insert(...)` clobbers the first — or, worse, resurrects a server that reload already removed. The `mark_down` path (see comment below) can likewise overwrite a freshly reconnected slot for the same id. Add per-id in-flight guards (e.g. a `Mutex<HashMap<String, Arc<tokio::sync::Mutex<()>>>>`) or a generation counter on the slot that `ensure_connected`/`mark_down` re-check before mutating.

`mark_down` unconditionally overwrites whatever is in the slot. If a concurrent thread just reconnected with a different config (or the user removed/disabled the server), this stale failure writes `Down` over the fresh `Connected` slot or resurrects a server that should be gone — wiping out a working connection until the next reload. Gate `mark_down` on the slot's current fingerprint (and on the slot being present at all), or skip the write entirely when the slot is no longer "ours".

`Slot::Down` carries no fingerprint, so `ensure_connected`'s fast path can't tell whether the cached failure corresponds to the current `cfg`. Every retry respawns unconditionally even when nothing relevant changed, and `connected_service` cannot distinguish "stale failure" from "current failure" — which is also why `mark_down` overwrites blindly above. Add `fingerprint: u64` to `Down`, populate it on insertion, and have `ensure_connected` / `mark_down` re-check it under the per-id guard.

Silent argument-shape loss: `args.as_object().cloned()` returns `None` for any non-object JSON (array, string, bool, number). A caller passing the wrong shape therefore invokes the tool with no arguments — possibly triggering defaults, no-op behaviour, or side effects — instead of receiving a typed validation error. Reject non-object values explicitly, treating only JSON `null` (and the absence of `args`) as "no arguments".

Only `TransportClosed`/`TransportSend` mark the slot Down. The bare `Err(_)` branch (which includes timeouts and protocol-level errors) leaves the slot `Connected`, so subsequent `call_tool`/`list_all_tools` keep retrying against the same broken service until config changes or a transport-level error finally fires. Mark Down (subject to the fingerprint guard) on repeated protocol errors and on the first timeout, or at minimum force a disconnect+lazy reconnect when this branch is reached.

The comment says "unwrap 让其响亮暴露" (let it surface loudly) but the implementation silently recovers from poison via `unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())`. If a panic ever does occur inside a guarded section, the corrupted `HashMap` is then observed by every subsequent locker without any surface signal. Either change the call sites to `.lock().expect("McpManager slots poisoned")` (or `.unwrap()`) to match the documented intent, or update the comment to reflect that poison is intentionally tolerated and accept the resulting loss of invariants. The same contradiction appears in `stderr_ring`, `stderr_tail_snapshot`, and `prune_stderr`.

`serde_json::to_value(cfg).unwrap_or(serde_json::Value::Null)` collapses every serialization failure into `Value::Null`, so all un-serializable configs hash identically and silently skip reconnects. If a future field on `McpServerConfig` (e.g. a non-string map key, a custom `Serialize` impl) breaks serialization, every server gets pinned to its first observed fingerprint. Hash the fields you actually care about manually, or at minimum `debug_assert!(value.is_object())` / `.expect("McpServerConfig is serializable")` so a regression fails loudly in dev.

Arbitrary child stderr lines are concatenated into the error string returned by `ensure_connected`/`call_tool`, surfaced through `McpSlotStatus.error`, and recorded in audit events. A server can echo values from `cfg.env` / header tokens (or anything else) into stderr; this path neither redacts secrets nor restricts which consumer sees the diagnostic. Either sanitize the joined tail (strip `key=value`, bearer tokens, common credential patterns), or restrict stderr-tail visibility to dev / logs and document exactly which surfaces may see it.

The 20-line ring buffer caps only the line count, not the per-line byte size. `BufReader::lines()` allocates the entire line into memory and the loop ignores `next_line()` errors — so (a) a child emitting one very long line (or no `\n` at all) balloons `VecDeque` entries and the same bytes are then copied verbatim into `format_with_stderr_tail` / audit / IPC; (b) a non-UTF-8 byte sequence returns `Err` from `next_line()`, the loop terminates, and all subsequent stderr from that child is silently discarded. Truncate each entry (e.g. to 4 KiB) on push, and on the error path log + continue (or use `read_until(b'\n', ...)` with a max-buffer cap) instead of dropping the reader.

`MAX_TOOLS_PER_SERVER` only caps the tool *count*; each `Tool`'s description, name, and input JSON Schema can be arbitrarily large, and `mounted()` clones every one of them into a snapshot exposed via the registry every model turn (per the file's own comment). A misbehaving or malicious server can publish a single huge schema that explodes the model context and memory. Add a per-snapshot byte budget in addition to the count cap — either truncate each tool's `description`/`input_schema` to N KiB, or sum a serialized-bytes cap and drop the tail.

The HTTP branch delegates all egress protection to `http_url_is_public` and disables redirects, but `reqwest::Client::builder()` still honors `HTTP_PROXY`/`HTTPS_PROXY`/`NO_PROXY` by default, and the URL check is performed before `reqwest` resolves DNS. Confirm the helper (a) rejects DNS names that resolve to loopback / private / link-local addresses, including IPv4-mapped IPv6 (`::ffff:127.0.0.1`), and (b) the resolved peer is pinned against the URL host — otherwise DNS-rebinding can still hit a private address. If the helper is purely textual, pre-resolve via `tokio::net::lookup_host`, re-check, and `.resolve(...)` against the reqwest client.

`TokioChildProcess::builder(cmd).spawn()` ultimately calls the synchronous `std::process::Command::spawn` (fork/exec on Unix, `CreateProcessW` on Windows) directly inside an async function. On a slow fork (large address space, seccomp filters) or a busy AV on Windows this can briefly block the tokio worker thread, stalling unrelated tasks on that worker. Run the spawn through `tokio::task::spawn_blocking(|| cmd.spawn())` and build the `TokioChildProcess` from the returned `Child`.

`reload_from_config` awaits each `ensure_connected` serially, and each one carries two stacked 10s timeouts (initialize + tool discovery). One hung server stalls every subsequent server for up to ~20s, so startup / reload latency is bounded by `Σ timeouts`, not by the worst server. Drive the loop via `futures::future::join_all` (or a bounded `buffer_unordered(N)`) and emit `mcp-status-changed` once after the batch, so a single misbehaving MCP can't dominate the reload.

`ensure_connected` returns `Ok(())` both for fresh connections and for the fingerprint-equal fast-path no-op, but `mcp.connected` is audited unconditionally on every reload — producing duplicate audit entries for servers whose config didn't actually change. Have `ensure_connected` return a richer result (e.g. `bool` or an enum distinguishing "already connected" from "just connected") and gate the audit event on the transition.

`McpSlotStatus.state` is an unrestricted `String` representing a fixed tri-state ("connected"/"down"/"absent"); a typo at any consumer will compile and serialize silently. Replace with `pub enum McpSlotState { Connected, Down, Absent }` and `#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]` on the enum so the wire format stays identical while the type system enforces exhaustive handling.

`mcp-status-changed` is emitted at the end of every `reload_from_config` regardless of whether any state actually changed, causing redundant UI refresh and potential refetch storms on no-op reloads. Track a "did anything change" flag (any disconnect, new connect, fingerprint change, or Down transition) and only emit when at least one transition happened.

`shutdown_all` calls `tauri::async_runtime::block_on` from what its docstring says is a synchronous cleanup context. If this is ever invoked from inside an async context (a Tauri lifecycle callback, a `tokio::main`, or even a Tauri command handler), it will panic with "Cannot drop a runtime in a context where blocking is not allowed" — exactly the opposite of the "sync wrapper" intent. Either drive the shutdown via `tauri::async_runtime::spawn` and await on the join handle, or detect a runtime context (e.g. via `tokio::runtime::Handle::try_current()`) and skip when one is already active.

Fallback for missing/unreadable vendor key may leak an unrelated vendor's credential into the override entry's base_url: `crate::bot::read_llm_key(api_provider, active_model_id, models_by_provider)` does NOT return the global main key — it first resolves the *currently active* model's vendor and uses that vendor's key (keyring.rs::read_llm_key ~640). So a per-card override whose vendor key fails to read (or never existed) gets the active vendor's key sent to the override entry's endpoint, which can be a different provider entirely. The comment "全局 key 兜底" is therefore inaccurate; use `crate::bot::read_api_key()` (or a small wrapper that explicitly walks vendor → global main key → vendor-of-selected-entry) instead.

`#[derive(Debug, Clone)]` on `ResolvedModel` exposes `api_key` (cleartext) through any future `dbg!` / `{:?}` / `unwrap()` panic message that includes this struct, and through log crates that auto-format Debug. `BotConfig` deliberately avoids `Debug` for this reason; `ResolvedModel` should redact `api_key` (custom Debug that prints `api_key: "<redacted, len=N>"`) or drop the derive. Combined with the fallback bug above, this is a realistic leak path.

Entry lookup ignores `api_provider`: the function searches `models_by_provider.openai` first, then `anthropic`, regardless of which protocol the caller passed in. The codebase elsewhere treats `entry_id` as globally unique (crypto.randomUUID), but a hand-edited or imported `bot-config.json` with the same `id` in both lists silently picks the OpenAI entry even when the caller passed `Anthropic`. At minimum this should assert uniqueness or scope the search to the requested provider; alternatively require `entry_id` to be protocol-qualified.

`resolve_model_override` returns `Result<_, String>` but propagates `read_vendor_key` / `read_llm_key` errors via `?` (which already produce `CommandError`) by calling `e.to_string()`. The original keyring error message — including the underlying keyring crate error — is preserved only in a flattened string, which makes UI diagnostics and triage harder when the entry lives behind secret-service. Prefer returning `CommandError` directly so the frontend hint logic can match against structured variants (KeyringError / InvalidArgument) the same way other config commands do.

comments.content: String-typed fields that already have a runtime enum (`api_provider`, `perm_mode`) bypass the type system in the persisted format: every reader (`ApiProvider::from_cfg`, `PermMode::from_cfg`) does defensive string→enum fallback, and the same fallback exists in the frontend. The same applies to `ToolRule.action` (allow/ask/deny) and `ui_font_size`. A typed enum with `#[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")]` would prevent invalid values from being persisted and eliminate the scattered "非法值 → 安全默认" paths.

`evolution: Option<serde_json::Value>` round-trip relies on every code path that produces a `BotConfig` re-reading the existing on-disk value before writing — otherwise the block is silently dropped on next serialize (the comment at the field declaration acknowledges this, and the `skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none"` makes the loss worse because a forgotten hydrate looks indistinguishable from "user never set it"). Add a defensive `serde_json::Value` default that round-trips through `Default::default()` (`#[serde(default)]` without `skip_serializing_if`) or wrap evolution behind a dedicated config struct that owns its on-disk presence so other code paths can't accidentally clobber it.

`MAX_TITLE` / `MAX_NOTE` / `MAX_KEYWORD` / `MAX_SUBTASK_TEXT` / `MAX_DUE` / `MAX_TAGS` / `MAX_TAG_LEN` are task-card field limits, not bot-config limits. They are declared here, exported via `super::types` from `bot/config/mod.rs`, and re-used from `db/tasks.rs`. The module-level docstring for `types.rs` even calls this out ("7 个字段上限常量（MAX_TITLE/NOTE/...）") but the grouping is misleading — every future reader will look in this file for bot-config limits and end up hunting for the task module that owns them. Move them to a dedicated module (e.g. `db/tasks::limits` or `bot/config/limits.rs` if they truly belong to bot config).

The unit tests in `model_override_tests` rely on `run_with_keychain_guard` to avoid a 3-second hang on macOS when the keychain is locked. The guard returns `None` when the timeout elapses and the test silently `eprintln!`s a skip and `return`s — which means none of the assertions in that branch run and CI gets a green test with no real coverage. For tests that are *meant* to fail (e.g. `resolve_rejects_missing_and_disabled`), the "missing" branch bails out before its `assert!(m.is_err())` and silently passes. Either skip the whole module when `run_with_keychain_guard` reports None (so coverage is visibly absent) or assert the guards actually ran before asserting the result, otherwise these tests can never fail in a locked-keychain environment.

The doc comment for `KeySlot::Llm` says the LLM keyring entry is the existing one and remains unchanged ("既有条目，不动"). That is true for the *storage slot*, but the *resolution policy* was changed by `read_llm_key`: previously the LLM key was a single global key; now it is "active model's vendor key → global main key". Tasks cards / per-model override still funnel through `read_llm_key` and will pick up the active vendor's key, which contradicts the comment's promise that existing users see "zero migration". Document the policy change explicitly on the LLM slot and on `resolve_model_override`.

Screenshot filename race: `chrono::Utc::now().timestamp_millis()` truncates to millisecond precision, so two concurrent `tool_screenshot` invocations within the same millisecond produce identical `wm-screen-<ts>.png` names and silently overwrite each other on disk. The later caller reports a path/file that no longer corresponds to its own screenshot (and any concurrent model consumption of the older path gets corrupt bytes). Append a sub-millisecond counter, atomic file create (`create_new`), or a random suffix to `screenshot_filename` so collisions cannot overwrite an existing artifact.

DNS rebinding / TOCTOU between validation and browser open: `ensure_public_http_url` resolves the host once and rejects loopback/private IPs, but the validated URL string is then handed to `app.opener().open_url`, where the OS browser performs its own (typically later) DNS lookup. An attacker-controlled DNS record that returns a public IP at validation time and a private/loopback IP at browser-open time will bypass the public-net gate and open an internal address. The sandbox comment promises "DNS 解析后拒绝本机/内网/保留地址", so this gap undermines that guarantee — pin the resolved IP into the URL or use a host allowlist/canonical name rather than relying on re-resolution by the browser.

PowerShell command-injection fragility on Windows screenshot: the output path is interpolated into a single-quoted PowerShell string with only `'` → `''` escaping. This happens to be safe today (single-quoted PS strings ignore `$`, backticks, parens, semicolons), but the safety relies entirely on (a) staying single-quoted and (b) keeping the single-quote escape in place — any future edit to a double-quoted string, an interpolated subexpression (`"$($x)"`), or removing the escape turns this into a shell/PS injection sink that executes attacker-controlled path text as PowerShell. Refactor to pass the path via `-ArgumentList` or `-File` with a script that reads `$args[0]`, so the path is bound as a data argument instead of concatenated into the script source.

Cancellation/timeout unsafety on `spawn_blocking` tasks: the `spawn_blocking` JoinHandles for screenshot (line 236) and clipboard_write (around line 151) are awaited unconditionally with no timeout, cancellation token, or shared-cancellation observation. If the outer future is cancelled (request timeout, app shutdown, model abort), the OS-side work continues to completion — `screencapture`/PowerShell still writes the PNG, and the clipboard plugin still overwrites the system clipboard — but the caller never receives the path/result and the side effects are invisible to it. That can leave orphan artifacts in `AI_Gen_Files` and surprise-mutate the user's clipboard. Wrap the `await` in `tokio::time::timeout` / `select!` with cancellation, or at minimum log a warning when the blocking task outlives the caller.

Audit log may exfiltrate secrets via URL/path arguments: `audit_log` records the full URL (`escape_for_log` only truncates/escapes — it does not redact query-string tokens like `?token=`, `?api_key=`, `?code=`, OAuth `?state=`, pre-signed S3 URLs, etc.) and the full canonical filesystem path revealed by `reveal_path`. Both are written verbatim to the audit log on every successful call, which is a credential/PII leak vector — auth-bearing URLs and absolute user paths can land in any log shipper downstream. Strip/replace query strings (keep only scheme://host/path) before logging URLs, and consider hashing or shortening paths that may point into sensitive directories (e.g., SSH keys, browser profiles, cloud creds).

Time-zone inconsistency: `register` stamps `registered_at` with `chrono::Local::now().timestamp_millis()` while `confirm_artifact_batch` stamps `updated_at` with `chrono::Utc::now().timestamp_millis()`. Both are millisecond Unix epochs but anchored to different clocks — they cannot be compared meaningfully (a user in UTC+8 will see `updated_at` numerically smaller than `registered_at` even when it came later). Pick one zone (UTC is the conventional choice for persisted timestamps) and use it consistently.
comments.suggestion_code: registered_at: chrono::Utc::now().timestamp_millis(),
comments.existing_code: registered_at: chrono::Local::now().timestamp_millis(),

This is an editing residue, not a comment. Rewrite to a coherent sentence explaining the invariant being tested.

comments.content: Path-validation strength is bounded by `gen_dir(&app)`. The current code is fail-closed (when `gen` resolves to `None` from `canonicalize` failing, every path is rejected), which is safe — but the symmetric risk is that a misconfigured `gen_dir` returning `/` (or any directory that canonicalizes to the filesystem root) trivially turns `canon.starts_with(gen)` into a no-op and lets every path through. Make sure the invariant is enforced where `gen_dir` itself resolves the directory, not here: e.g., refuse root/empty values upstream, so this file can rely on `gen` being a non-trivial prefix.

`confirm_artifact_batch` is `async` but the per-path validation does `std::fs::canonicalize(p)` synchronously inside the `for p in &paths` loop on the async runtime. Each canonicalize performs filesystem syscalls (stat + symlink resolution); a slow/network mount or many paths can block the runtime worker. For consistency with the spawn_blocking discipline used a few lines below for `open_db`, move the per-path canonicalize + filter into `tauri::async_runtime::spawn_blocking` (or `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`) and return the validated `Vec<TaskFile>`.

Two consecutive full clones of `next` on the success path: `vec![next.clone()]` into `db_upsert` and `vec![next.clone()]` into `broadcast_after_mutation`. Move `next` into one of the calls (e.g. broadcast takes ownership) and pass the other by reference/cloned as needed, eliminating one redundant struct copy. While here, `files` could be preallocated with `Vec::with_capacity(paths.len())` since the upper bound is known.

`is_error` classification passes empty tool name. `crate::audit::tool_call_failed("", &text)` is called with an empty string for the tool name argument. If the function inspects the name for per-tool failure semantics (e.g., only flagging specific tools as failures, or excluding certain error-text-only results), passing "" silently misclassifies every tool result. The block currently has access to `tool_use_id`; the matched tool_use's `name` (from the `emitted_tool_use_ids` tracking step) should be threaded through so `tool_call_failed` gets the actual tool name it was designed to inspect. As-is, this is either a silent misclassification or a misuse of the audit API.

Silent data loss: `_skipped_images` count is discarded by the public API. The internal `convert_all` correctly counts non-data-URL images it has to drop (Anthropic only accepts base64 inline images), but the public `openai_msgs_to_anthropic` throws this counter away with `_skipped_images`. Callers (chat loop, planner) cannot log a user-visible warning when an image the user attached (e.g. an `https://` URL pasted in) is silently dropped before reaching Anthropic. Either propagate the count in the return type or log it locally here so silent image loss is observable.

URL normalization runs `strip_suffix` at most once and doesn't guard against empty input. (a) `strip_suffix("/v1/messages").or_else(...)` only fires one branch — so an input like `…/v1/messages/v1/messages` strips down to `…/v1/messages` (still ends with `/v1/messages`) and then re-appends `/v1/messages` only if it ends with `/v1` (it doesn't), producing the broken `…/v1/messages/v1/messages` back. A loop / iterative strip is needed for misconfigured gateways that double the path. (b) An empty / whitespace-only `base_url` falls through to `format!("{b}/v1/messages")` = `"/v1/messages"` — a relative URL that reqwest will reject. Add an empty check and reject early.

`apply_anthropic_thinking` trusts the caller to clamp `budget`. The function blindly writes whatever `budget` it receives into the request body. The comment defers all validation to `reasoning::resolve` — but this is a public function and any future caller (a test, a new code path, a future feature flag) that forgets the clamp will silently send an invalid body (`budget_tokens < 1024` or `>= max_tokens`) that Anthropic rejects upstream with no local signal. Add at minimum a debug_assert that the budget is in-range, or return a `Result` so misuse fails fast at the call site instead of as a 400 in production.

Stream-error messages are silently truncated to 200 chars with no marker. `msg.chars().take(200).collect()` drops everything past 200 codepoints and the user-facing error path sees no indication of truncation. Anthropic error payloads commonly include structured detail (token counts, the offending parameter value, retry-after hints, internal request IDs) past the first 200 chars — losing them makes debugging upstream rejections much harder. Either lengthen the cap, or append an ellipsis / truncation marker so the receiving log / UI can tell the message was clipped.

`existed` check OR's `is_dir` and `is_file`. If `canonical` resolves to a directory (e.g., user passes a directory path that survives `resolve_writable` because the parent is writable), `existed = true` triggers the "覆盖已存在文件" confirmation branch, then `atomic_write` fails with `IsADirectory` (an opaque IO error). The intent appears to be "is there an existing file to overwrite" — should be `is_file` only (and `resolve_writable` should arguably reject directory targets as a separate hardening).

Per-tool `Allow` ToolRuleAction bypasses the whitelist check **and** the `perm_mode` triage entirely — it only emits an audit log. In `resolve_with_perm`, an `allow` rule for any tool means the model can read **any** canonical-resolvable path (including symlink-resolved escapes that fall outside every whitelist dir) without user confirmation. The comment says "rule_allow = 单工具 yolo" so this appears intentional, but worth confirming: (a) rule persistence/sanitization is hardened, (b) rule auth requires the same trust level as `perm_mode=Yolo`, and (c) `Deny` rules should still take precedence over an `Allow` for a different tool if a future refactor reorders checks.

Same per-tool `Allow` bypass exists in the **write** path: a single `allow` rule for `edit_file` / `write_file` lets the model write to any path the OS resolves, completely sidestepping `writable_dirs` and the `ask_user_confirm` danger prompt. The "覆盖已存在文件" sub-prompt is also bypassed by an Allow rule because `existed` branch sits above this check (actually below — `resolve_writable` returns before the existed check, but the cover-prompt logic still runs and emits its own confirmation). Verify the comment "与读侧同语义" matches the actual UX: does the user expect a per-tool Allow to mean "no whitelist, no confirm, ever" for writes? If yes, document it; if no, also gate the cover-prompt behind `rule.allow`.

`tool_rule_for` calls `crate::bot::load_config(app)` synchronously on every path resolution, and is invoked from both `resolve_with_perm` and `resolve_writable` (which run inside Tauri async commands). If `load_config` does sync filesystem IO without going through `spawn_blocking`, it will block the Tauri async runtime — exactly the class of bug the rest of this file goes to lengths to avoid. Worth verifying `load_config` is `async` or wrapping the call in `spawn_blocking_io`.

`write_before_snapshot` silently returns `None` on `create_dir_all` failure or `atomic_write` failure, emitting only an audit event. The caller (`edit_file` / `write_file`) treats `None` as "no rollback snapshot" but does not surface this to the user — the tool result still says "已修改 / 已覆盖" with no indication that rollback is unavailable. For a feature whose user-facing promise is "回滚证据链", this is a degraded state worth flagging in the tool output (or at least the audit log entry should include the user/agent-visible identity, not just an internal error code).

`expand_tilde` only handles `~`, `~/...`, `~\...`. The Unix shorthand `~username/...` (other user's home) is passed through verbatim and becomes a literal `~username/...` path that `canonicalize` will reject (ENOENT) — confusing error path. If LLM-generated input ever includes `~root/...` or `~admin/...` the user sees a generic "路径不存在" rather than the actual cause. Either explicitly reject with a clearer message, or implement `getpwnam`-based expansion (Unix only) — at minimum, surface the unhandled form.

`strip_verbatim` only handles the canonical `\\?\` verbatim prefix. Windows also uses DOS device paths `\\.\COM1`, `\\.\pipe\foo` which can appear from `GetFinalPathNameByHandle` for some file types — though `canonicalize` typically doesn't surface these for normal files. More importantly, the function returns the original `p` on no-match by `PathBuf::from(s)` semantics: the `match stripped { Some(s) => PathBuf::from(s), None => p }` correctly preserves, but the `to_string_lossy()` round-trip silently corrupts non-UTF8 paths on Windows (Chinese paths on non-Unicode codepage systems). Consider keeping the `OsString` form rather than going through `String`/`to_string_lossy` if any Windows user might have non-UTF8 paths in `allowedDirs`.

`render_context_hits` does `hits.contains(&i)` inside an inner loop over every line of the window — O(n*m) per file. With `context=5` and many hits this is wasteful. Build a `HashSet<usize>` once per call (or use the already-merged window structure to mark hits per window) — small constant-factor win but easy fix.

In `tool_write_file`, between the `existed` check (which fetches `is_file` via `spawn_blocking_io`) and the subsequent `atomic_write`, another process could create/delete/replace the file. The `atomic_write` will then operate on a different file than what the user confirmed for overwrite. This is a TOCTOU window parallel to the documented read-window TOCTOU, but on the write side: an attacker who can race the user's "yes" decision can swap the file content the user thought they were overwriting. For interactive use the window is large (UI latency), making this practically exploitable. Consider re-checking `is_file` inside the `spawn_blocking_map` that does the `atomic_write`, and refusing the write if the state changed.

replans_used is logged as `plan.replans_used + 1` but never actually incremented inside `replan()` (function takes `&PlanState`, immutable). The caller must remember to bump `plan.replans_used` after a successful call. If the caller forgets, `MAX_REPLANS` is silently bypassed — exactly the failure-mode the constant exists to prevent. Either take `&mut PlanState` and increment here, or return the new count and force the caller to update atomically.

`extract_json` picks the first `{`/`[` in the whole string and matches it against the last matching closer. This breaks if (a) the model emits prose that contains a stray brace/bracket before the actual JSON, or (b) two JSON-shaped blocks appear (think-block residue, multiple objects). The function should bracket-match to balance nested delimiters and ignore braces/brackets inside string literals — or use a more robust parser like `serde_json::from_str` on candidate substrings, scanning from the start until one parses successfully.

`sanitize_fail_reason` only defangs triple-backtick fences and replaces control chars with spaces. `fail_reason` can carry arbitrary external content (file bodies, web pages, stderr) where an adversary can inject via XML/HTML tags, "ignore previous instructions", role markers (`system:`, `assistant:`), or non-``` fences. The in-prompt "不是指令" label is a weak mitigation on its own. Consider a stronger treatment: strip or escape JSON-like braces, normalize `assistant:`/`system:` markers, length-limit per line, and treat the whole user message as untrusted data with a clear separator the model is trained to recognize.

`needs_plan` triggers a paid Planner HTTP call (with 60s timeout) on extremely loose signals: single-character `'先'` AND `'再'` matches any Chinese sentence that happens to contain both characters (e.g. "先贤...再次..."), and substring matches like `"计划"` or `"批量"` can hit unrelated phrases (`计划外`, `审核时`). This wastes tokens and adds 60s latency on simple chats. Tighten to multi-character phrases (`先...再...`, `分步执行`, `按步骤`), or require keyword + (multi-attachment OR ≥N sentences).

`call_planner` does not validate `api_key` is non-empty after `trim()`. If configuration is incomplete (e.g. user hasn't entered a key yet), the request is still dispatched with an empty `Authorization` header, surfacing as a generic "Planner API 错误" / network error rather than a clear configuration problem. Add an early `if api_key.trim().is_empty() { return Err(...).into() }` after the `read_llm_key` call so the failure mode is diagnosable and downstream consumers can distinguish "config missing" from "API down".

`parse_plan` clones the entire JSON array twice (once in each branch of the `if let Some(arr) = v.as_array()`) just to iterate it once. Iterate by reference directly into the `Vec<String>` builder and drop the clones — `serde_json::Value` references are cheap and the array is already borrowed from `v`.
comments.suggestion_code:
let arr = v.as_array().or_else(|| v["steps"].as_array())?;
    let steps: Vec<String> = arr
        .iter()
        .filter_map(|s| s.as_str().map(|x| x.trim().to_string()))
        .filter(|s| !s.is_empty())
        .take(MAX_PLAN_STEPS)
        .collect();

comments.content: Public items `PlanState`, `needs_plan`, `parse_plan`, `format_plan_block`, and `generate_plan` lack doc comments despite being part of the module's public API surface. `PlanState` in particular has invariant-bearing fields (e.g. `replans_used` is "已用 Replan 次数（硬上限 MAX_REPLANS）") that callers must understand to keep the invariant — note the interaction with the `replans_used` bug above: callers today cannot keep the invariant because the API doesn't make it theirs to keep. Add `///` docs describing ownership, invariants, and the error/None contract.

The `(open, close)` binding is destructured then immediately discarded via `let _ = open;` — this is a code smell indicating the destructuring was either incomplete or unnecessary. Either use `open` (e.g. assert start byte matches opening), or collapse into a single local. Right now a future reader has to convince themselves `open` is intentionally unused.

spawn_subagent_locked writes upsert_tasks then insert_subagent without a transaction. If insert_subagent fails after the card has been written (constraint violation, lock conflict, mid-call I/O error), the task card is left in Doing with no SubagentRow referencing it — the orphan card then drives check_subagent_locked / finalize_card_locked into their `TaskNotFound` branches and stays stuck in Doing forever. Wrap both writes in conn.transaction() the same way run_subagent's setup block already does, so commit/rollback is atomic.

cancel_subagent_locked does update_subagent_status then conditionally upsert_tasks (the Doing→Todo revert) without a transaction. If the second write fails after the row is already Cancelled, the subagent row says Cancelled but the card stays in Doing, leaving the front-end a stuck 'in-progress' card and confusing the watcher / auto-finalize paths that key off card.column. Same fix as the spawn core: wrap both writes in a single conn.transaction() so they commit together or roll back together.

wait_slot_cancellable calls gate().notify.notify_one() on every failed-acquisition iteration, immediately before the 50ms sleep. With N queued waiters this becomes an O(N) wake-up storm per 50ms tick on top of the retry work — each waiter immediately wakes another waiter that will also fail (or worse, wakes the just-acquired waiter). Only notify when global state actually changed (e.g., a slot was released), ideally from inside GateTicket::drop, so the wake-up is targeted at a real transition instead of a retry pulse. The 50ms backoff alone already guarantees the fairness claim in the surrounding comment.

The watcher JoinHandle is held as a bare `let watcher = tauri::async_runtime::spawn(...)` for the entire body of run_subagent — through stop-token registration, the model loop's await, and the wall-timeout branch — and only wrapped in `_watcher = AbortOnDrop(watcher)` at the very end. If anything in that gap panics or early-returns (ChatGuard acquire failure, stop-token insert failure, run_model_loop returning Err before the timeout, a future edit adding an `?` somewhere), the JoinHandle is dropped without ever calling AbortOnDrop and the 2s polling loop leaks — repeatedly opening DB connections and pumping stop tokens — until the AppHandle itself is dropped. Wrap the JoinHandle immediately after spawn, or move both spawn and guard into a tighter scope so the abort guard always pairs with the spawn.

tool_spawn_subagent parses each budget field with `.as_u64().unwrap_or(DEFAULT as u64) as u32`. The trailing `as u32` silently truncates any u64 above u32::MAX (e.g., `5000000000` becomes `705032704`; `2^32` becomes `0`), and the truncated value then flows into SubagentBudget::clamped(). When clamping only floors at 1 (e.g., the tool_calls path), a large attacker-controlled JSON value can collapse to the floor rather than the cap, producing a useless 1-shot sub-agent instead of the documented default. Use checked/try_into casts so oversized values degrade to the documented defaults instead of wrapping.

comments.content: After tokio::time::timeout fires, the code calls `stop.force_stop()` followed by a hard-coded `tokio::time::sleep(750ms)`. In-flight work spawned via spawn_blocking (model loop's Python/MCP/external-tool calls) does NOT honor future cancellation and only stops when its own StopToken polling hits; 750ms is a guess that may be too short for a long streaming response or a large file write, leaving the comment's stated invariant ('no orphan processes') un-enforced. Make the grace budget-derived (e.g., `min(budget/4, 2s)`) or poll until the tool_guard registry reports zero in-flight guards / stop tokens, so the cleanup actually waits for the work to drain.

Mutex poison recovery via `e.into_inner()` silently discards the panic context. If a thread panicked while mutating the protected HashSet (or while holding DB_WRITE_LOCK mid-transaction), the in-memory state may be inconsistent yet every subsequent caller proceeds as if the lock were healthy — the same swallow pattern is repeated in ChatGuard::acquire/drop, ExecGuard::acquire/drop, chat_guard_is_held, create_exec_session, and persist_exec_reply. At minimum propagate the poison (return Err or re-panic) so the inconsistency surfaces, or document an explicit invariant that the protected state is recoverable after a panic.
Same poison-swallowing pattern as ChatGuard; a panicked writer leaves the running set in an undefined state and acquire/drop will silently keep operating on it.

DB_WRITE_LOCK is a global writer mutex; a panic mid-write poisons it and `e.into_inner()` recovers the lock without aborting the in-flight SQL transaction the panicking thread may have left half-done. Subsequent transactions inside this guard will then operate against potentially corrupted rows. Wrap the transaction in a `Transaction::set_rollback_on_drop` style guard and let the poison propagate instead of swallowing it.

`chat_execute_tasks` runs every supplied task_id sequentially with no per-task or overall timeout. Each iteration can invoke up to 50 rounds of LLM with full tool execution, and the only stop check sits between cards. A long batch combined with slow skills will occupy the runtime worker indefinitely and `/stop` cannot interrupt a card already in flight. Cap `task_ids.len()` at the call sites, wrap each per-card call in `tokio::time::timeout`, and consider a global deadline.

`bot_chat` has no function-level deadline. Only individual HTTP requests inside `run_model_loop` carry timeouts; the plan generator, memory injection, history-truncate-and-summarize call, image attachment, and any awaited LLM step can each stall indefinitely. While ChatGuard is held this also blocks the user's session from making further progress. Wrap the orchestration body in `tokio::time::timeout` and surface a typed `CommandError` on expiry so the caller can react and the guards still drop.

`register_exec_session` and `register_ask_context` are paired with explicit unregister calls on the normal return path, but neither has a Drop-based counterpart. A panic (or any future `?` added between registration and unregister) leaks the `sid -> origin` mapping in `AppState` for the rest of the process lifetime, and stale ask contexts will let `ask_user` fire from already-failed runs. Wrap both in small RAII guards so cleanup runs on panic/early-return paths.

`summarize_http` builds the request URL via `format!("{}/chat/completions", base_url.trim_end_matches('/'))` with no validation that `base_url` is a well-formed http(s) URL. A model-library override entry with an empty/relative/malformed base_url (or one already containing `chat/completions`) produces a malformed request that is surfaced only as a generic `请求大模型失败` string, hiding the configuration error from both callers and the audit log. Validate the URL with `reqwest::Url::parse` before composing the path, and return a typed `CommandError::ConfigInvalid` for the failure mode.

Files exceeding `MAX_IMAGE_BYTES` (or empty) are silently skipped without incrementing `skipped` and without an audit log entry. That conflates "not in whitelist" with "too large / corrupt", so a poisoned `[附件文件]` block that references an oversized file looks identical to a missing one. Either count them separately or write an audit line so abuse is observable.

The `find("\n}\n")` boundary finder matches the first `}` at column 0 after the function header — but the body of `run_python` (and `py_gate_acquire_inner`) almost certainly contains nested matches/closures/helpers whose closing brace is at column 0. Truncating at that brace silently shortens the inspected region: if `py_gate_acquire()` happens to be called after a nested `}`, the assertion passes for the wrong reason; if the call is moved past such a brace the test falsely reports a regression. Use a brace-depth counter, or `syn`-based parsing, to locate the matching `}` of the function header.

The second `assert_eq!` requires `max_seen` to exactly equal `PY_RUN_MAX_CONCURRENT`. The accompanying comment admits this is "几乎必然" rather than deterministic: under CI load the first pair of threads can enter-and-exit (each holds the permit for 100 ms) before the next pair reaches `CUR.fetch_add`, in which case `max_seen` will be 1 and the test fails with a confusing "闸门退化" message even though the gate is correct. The first assertion (`max_seen <= PY_RUN_MAX_CONCURRENT`) is the actual safety invariant — the second one is a flaky heuristic at best and should either be weakened to `max_seen >= 2` or wrapped in a retry/deterministic scheduling harness.

`run_python_revisions` re-detects Python availability with `python_with_docx()` even though every caller first invokes the same function to decide whether to skip. Between the outer `if python_with_docx().is_none()` check and the helper call, the environment can change on shared CI runners (container teardown, apt installing python-docx in parallel jobs, PATH mutations from a sibling test), and the helper then `panic!`s instead of skipping cleanly. Pass the resolved interpreter path into the helper so detection happens exactly once and the panic disappears.

comments.content: `is_live_group_leader(u32::MAX - 1)` assumes the kernel will never allocate that PID to a live process during the test. On long-running CI containers, especially those near `pid_max` or that have already recycled PIDs after a prior fork-heavy run, that PID can legitimately be assigned and the test will report a false positive ("dead pid 被误判存活"). Spawn a child, capture its PID, then assert the helper rejects it after `wait()` — that exercises the real `getpgid`/`kill(pid, 0)` path without relying on PID arithmetic.

Blocking filesystem + DB I/O inside async `build_skill_block_for`. The leading comment claims "重活包 spawn_blocking" but the very first statement `let all = scan_skills(app);` performs a synchronous directory walk over all skills (and a `crate::db::open_db` + `load_all_skill_outcomes`) on the async runtime thread before the ONNX rank step is wrapped in `spawn_blocking_map`. This stalls the Tokio worker for the entire scan, which is exactly what `spawn_blocking` exists to avoid. Wrap the scan (or the whole `enabled` collection step) in `spawn_blocking` and `await` its result, then continue with the rank step.

DB failures are silently swallowed in `scan_skills`. Both `crate::db::open_db(app)` and `crate::db::load_all_skill_outcomes(&conn)` failures are dropped via `if let Ok(...)`, leaving the caller to see a successful skills list with empty badges and no diagnostic. A corrupt/locked DB then manifests as missing `last_outcome` entries with no log line to investigate. At minimum log via `eprintln!` / `tracing`, or surface the error so the SettingsPage can show a degraded-mode banner.

TOCTOU crash window in `skills_import`: `std::fs::create_dir(&dest)` succeeds, then `copy_dir_all` runs. If the process crashes, panics, or is killed between those two points, an empty `dest` directory is left on disk. The next import attempt hits the `SkillLoadFailed { reason: "同名技能已存在" }` error and the user has no way to distinguish "stale placeholder from a crashed prior import" from a real duplicate, while `skills_delete` would silently wipe whatever happened to be there. Either stage into a sibling temp dir (e.g., `dest.parent().join(format!(".{name}.tmp-XXXX"))`) and `rename` into place atomically, or at least store a `.importing` sentinel file that the startup scanner cleans up.

Filename dedup uses `to_string_lossy()` which silently corrupts non-UTF-8 byte sequences into identical `U+FFFD` strings. Two distinct skill directory names that differ only in invalid UTF-8 bytes (e.g., on NFS mounts, legacy HFS+, or any non-UTF-8 locale) will collide in the `seen` HashSet, silently dropping one skill from the listing without any warning. Convert to `OsString`/`PathBuf` for the dedup key, or compute the lossy name lazily only for display.

`registry_known_tools()` rebuilds a fresh `HashSet<String>` from `crate::bot::registry::tools_index()` for every directory entry in `scan_skill_dirs`. The registry is process-global and effectively static, but `scan_skill_dirs` runs on every `skills_list` / `build_skill_block` / `build_skill_block_for` call, and now also on every `build_skill_block_for` rank step. With N skills and M built-in tools this is O(N*M) wasted hashing + M*sizeof(String) per skill. Compute the set once at scan entry (e.g., `let known = registry_known_tools();` before the closure) and capture it by reference inside the closure.

Wildcard re-exports (`pub use ...::*`) flatten every public binding of eight submodules into this crate root. Any helper, error type, or internal struct marked `pub` inside any submodule becomes part of the `bot_skills` public API, which prevents the submodules from being refactored without potentially breaking downstream consumers and leaks implementation details that should remain private. Replace the glob re-exports with an explicit list of the symbols that are actually meant to be part of the subsystem's public API (e.g. `pub use files::{load_skill, SkillBody};`); this also gives you a single place to attach API-level documentation and version the surface.

The subsystem spans parsing, filesystem I/O, scheduling, and runtime execution, but no `bot_skills::Error` enum or `Result` alias is defined or re-exported here. Each submodule will surface its own error type, forcing callers to juggle multiple error kinds and write ad-hoc `From` conversions at every integration point. Consider adding a top-level error type (e.g. `#[derive(thiserror::Error)] pub enum Error { Parse(parse::Error), Io(#[from] std::io::Error), Runtime(runtime::Error), ... }`) and a `pub type Result<T> = std::result::Result<T, Error>;`, then re-export it so all of `bot_skills` shares one error boundary.

comments.content: Global `cfg` is used for reasoning model/provider instead of the resolved override. `model_for_reasoning` and `provider` (passed to `ReasoningEffort::resolve`) come from the global config, but when `model_override` is set, the actual request goes to `resolved.model`/`resolved.api_provider`. Reasoning effort mapping (OpenAiEffort vs AnthropicBudget vs GlmThinking) is model-family-specific, so resolving against the wrong model can produce the wrong reasoning wire flavor — e.g. an Anthropic override could end up sending a `reasoning_effort` field (OpenAI-only), and a GLM/o-series override could get the wrong budget gate. Use `resolved.as_ref().map(|r| r.model.clone()).unwrap_or(cfg.model.clone())` for `model_for_reasoning`, and use the resolved provider for reasoning resolution too.

Reasoning injection does not gate OpenAiEffort/GlmThinking by provider. The match on `http.reasoning` writes `reasoning_effort` and `thinking` blocks without checking `http.provider`. If reasoning was resolved as `OpenAiEffort` (e.g. for an OpenAI model) but the actual request goes to an Anthropic gateway (via override), an unrecognized `reasoning_effort` field is sent → risk of strict-gateway 400. Conversely, `AnthropicBudget` is gated to provider==Anthropic and silently dropped on Openai requests (which is correct, but the asymmetric handling for the other two flavors is the bug). Add provider guards like the existing Anthropic one.

Soft-warn remaining-budget message is mis-computed. The injected system message tells the model it still has `fuse_cap - soft_warn_at` calls left, but `function_calls_total` is already `>= soft_warn_at` at the moment of injection (the gate is `function_calls_total >= soft_warn_at`), so the true remaining budget is `fuse_cap - function_calls_total`. Misleads the model into thinking it has more capacity than it does, defeating the soft-warn's purpose of forcing convergence before the hard fuse (especially with low caps or after several rounds of in-flight calls).

`accumulate_tool_call_delta` failure audit conflates two distinct overflow types. The function returns false both when `delta.index > MAX_TOOL_CALL_INDEX` (DoS / malformed index) and when the per-call `arguments` byte cap is exceeded (adversarial / runaway arguments chunk). The caller logs every drop under `llm.tool_call_index_overflow` with `index/max` keys that make no sense for the arguments case, making it impossible to distinguish adversarial-arguments DoS from index-DoS when investigating incidents. Either split into two booleans/diagnostic values, or add a separate audit event for the arguments overflow path.

Possible usize overflow in arguments length check. `t.2.len() + args.len()` can overflow `usize` in pathological cases (debug builds panic, release builds silently wrap and let the cap be bypassed). Although `t.2.len()` is bounded by `MAX_TOOL_CALL_ARGUMENTS_BYTES` (1 MiB), a single adversarial SSE delta chunk larger than `usize::MAX - 1 MiB` could wrap. Add an early `if args.len() > MAX_TOOL_CALL_ARGUMENTS_BYTES { return false; }` before the sum — also saves the addition on every chunk and removes the overflow hazard entirely.

Per-round `msgs_chars` audit walks every message content string every round. This runs once per loop iteration (up to 50 rounds) and does `chars().count()` over every message content — O(n) over potentially 200K-char histories. After 50 rounds that's a noticeable steady-state cost in the streaming loop. Cache the running char total when messages are appended (mutate a counter alongside `msgs.push`), or skip the audit once it has already fired this conversation (one event is enough — the threshold is informational, not actionable).

`StreamEnd` comment is orphaned — the doc comment for `StreamEnd` (terminating sentinel types) sits above the next function's signature instead of immediately above the type. Move it back over the struct/enum definition it documents (or remove if the type is inlined elsewhere), otherwise readers will miss the meaning of the SSE termination markers.

comments.content: Expired `at:` tasks still execute. `stale_ids` is computed from the same `all` snapshot that feeds `due`, and `classify_due` returns `Run` for any past `at:` with `sched_last = None` (the `at_expired` branch is not consulted here). The "stale cleanup" block runs *after* `due` is returned, so the scheduler has already spawned `run_scheduled` for the expired task by the time the schedule is cleared. This directly violates the documented invariant "防重启后补跑过期任务" and the test comment that `at_expired` is responsible for cleanup. The `due` filter (or `classify_due` for `at:`) must consult `at_expired` and exclude such tasks, or the cleanup must run before dispatch.

Stale/missed cleanup defeats optimistic locking by resetting `expected_updated_at` to the freshly-loaded row's own `updated_at`. CAS is bypassed, so any concurrent edit between the initial `db_load` and the cleanup `db_load` (e.g. user changes `schedule` from a past `at:` to a future `at:`, or updates `sched_last` after a manual run) is silently clobbered: the schedule is force-cleared or `sched_last` is force-advanced. Workflow and job update paths correctly use the original row's `expected_updated_at`; the task path should do the same (carry `expected_updated_at = t.updated_at` from the first snapshot through to the upsert).

One-shot workflow `at:` is stranded on any non-Ok path. `sched_last` is recorded before `workflow_run` is called, and the schedule is only cleared on `Ok(_)`. When `workflow_run` returns `Err` (busy / DB error / invalid state), the function falls through the `Err` arm, which only writes an audit log. The row is now `sched_last = Some(...)` with a past `at:` schedule: `at_expired` returns `false` (because `sched_last` is `Some`), and `classify_due` for a past `at:` with `sched_last` set returns `NotDue`. The `at:` workflow is never retried and never cleaned up — silently dropped. On panic, runtime shutdown, or cancellation between the `sched_last` write and the clear call, the same stranding occurs. Add a matching `Err` cleanup, and consider rolling `sched_last` back if the `Ok` clear fails.

`finalize_job_run` silently discards every write it performs. The three DB calls (`record_job_run`, `update_job_run_state`, `delete_job_row`) and the auto-pause notification are all unchecked. Concrete consequences: (1) `record_job_run` failure means no history row exists even though the UI assumes it does; (2) `update_job_run_state` failure means `retry_at`/`retry_count`/`enabled` are not persisted, so a job that the function reports as "已排重试" or "已自动暂停" actually has none of those changes applied; (3) `delete_job_row` failure on an `at:` job leaves the row behind forever (combined with the stranding window above); (4) `delete_job_row` is unguarded — it does not respect the original `updated_at`, so a concurrent edit during a long LLM run (the original `job` snapshot is used) is unconditionally erased. At minimum, log every error with `audit_log`; ideally add CAS by `updated_at` for the `at:` delete and a fallback rollback if state persistence fails.

`SCHED_MAX_CONCURRENT` and `SCHED_TASK_TIMEOUT` only apply to task cards. `workflows_tick` and `jobs_tick` (lines ~600 and ~1075) spawn each due workflow/job with `tauri::async_runtime::spawn` and no semaphore, no timeout, and no shared guard acquired before permit acquisition. A burst (e.g. 50 one-shots all firing after a downtime) will spawn 50 concurrent long-running LLM executions, exhausting the LLM rate limit and memory; a single hung job will never be reaped and blocks all retries for that `job.id` (the `SchedGuard` is held for the full run). The task-side permit is also acquired *after* `find_due_tasks` returns, so each 30s tick re-spawns a duplicate task for every still-due item while the semaphore is saturated — duplicates queue unbounded, and on permit release the queued duplicates all run `SchedGuard::acquire` and only one proceeds, wasting runtime slots. Either (a) extend the semaphore/timeout to workflows and jobs, or (b) acquire `SchedGuard` before enqueuing so duplicates are dropped at spawn time, and add a `timeout` wrapper around `run_scheduled_job`/`run_scheduled_workflow`.

Frontmatter delimiters are matched as substrings rather than line-bounded fences: opening `strip_prefix("---")` accepts `---foo` and closing `body.find("\n---")` stops at the first newline followed by any `---` (e.g. a description or example value containing the literal `\n---`). When this happens, `intents` / `allowed_tools` / `params` are silently lost, mode falls back to the default, and the risk-derivation rule (low → auto) may flip execution semantics with no diagnostic. Anchor the delimiters to lines consisting solely of `---` (allow optional trailing whitespace) before slicing.

`strip_frontmatter` reuses the same substring match: `body.find("\n---")` plus `body[end + 4..]` will also mis-terminate when content contains `\n---`, and will leave any trailing characters on the closing delimiter (e.g. `---abc`) in the returned body. Use line-anchored matching identical to `parse_meta` so both functions agree on what counts as the end of frontmatter.

`parse_param_line` sets `required` and `default` independently even though the doc-comment says the two annotations are mutually exclusive. Downstream `start_skill` (runtime.rs:74-87) checks `default` before `required`, so a parameter declared `key: 说明（必填）（默认 X）` is silently treated as optional. Either reject this combination at parse time or document the precedence so authors are not surprised.

`extract_default`/`strip_annotations` anchor on `rest.find("默认")` (first occurrence). If a description contains a stray “默认” before the real `(默认 X)` marker — or before a parenthetical remark that does not start with “默认” — the parser either returns `None` (silent loss of the real default) or grabs a wrong inner substring (e.g. parses “行为” from `(默认行为)`). Search for the marker together with its surrounding parens, e.g. `rest.find("(默认")` / `rest.find("（默认")`, so the first candidate is at least inside an annotation-shaped parenthesis.

Duplicate frontmatter keys are silently merged: `intents` and `allowed_tools` accumulate with `push` on every match instead of replacing the previous block. Authors who paste two `intents:` blocks (or rely on the scheduler’s `allowed_tools` allowlist) will unknowingly widen the set, and the parser never reports the duplicate. Treat the second occurrence as a hard parse error or, at minimum, replace the prior collection.

`enabled` parses with `!matches!(..., "false"|"0"|"no")`, which means any other value — typos such as `ture`, `flase`, numeric `1.0`, or even garbage from a mis-split key/value — silently leaves the skill enabled. For a security-relevant flag whose default is already `true`, a permissive “anything-else = true” rule can ship a misconfigured skill. Require the affirmative value to match a known true token as well.

`allowed_tools` items are pushed without validation, even though the documentation says tool names follow the ASCII-alnum/`_` convention. A typo like `read_text-file` (hyphen) or an empty string after trimming will be stored verbatim; later the scheduler checks `allowed_tools.contains(&step.tool_name)`, so such noise widens the allowlist surface and silently diverges from the “author declares allowed tools” intent. Validate characters and ignore empty entries.

`parse_step_heading` accepts `0` as a valid step number (only `usize::parse` is checked). The downstream continuity check (`s.index != i + 1`) tolerates a leading 0 and then rejects later numbers, which still lets `Step 0` slip through and the parser keeps it. Per the DSL contract steps are 1-based; reject `0` explicitly so the error surfaces at the heading line rather than later.

Soft-warning remaining-budget is mis-computed. At this point `function_calls_total >= soft_warn_at`, so the true remaining budget is `fuse_cap - function_calls_total`, not `fuse_cap - soft_warn_at`. The message as written can mislead the model into thinking it has more capacity than it actually does, weakening the soft-warn's "converge before the hard fuse" purpose. Use `fuse_cap.saturating_sub(function_calls_total)` instead.

comments.content: `accumulate_tool_call_delta` returns false for two distinct failure modes (index > MAX and arguments byte overflow), but every drop is logged here as `llm.tool_call_index_overflow`. Operators cannot distinguish adversarial-arguments floods from index DoS attempts from this audit data. The function should return the reason (or use a separate `ToolCallOverflow { kind }` enum) so callers can log the right audit event.

Hot-path: tool-output truncation walks the entire `text` twice (once for `chars().count()`, once for `chars().take(cap).collect::<String>()`) and then a third time inside the `format!` of the truncation marker. For outputs up to 200K chars this is significant per-tool overhead. Compute `char_count` once, build the truncated `String` with `String::with_capacity(cap + marker.len())`, and pre-format the marker — or use a byte-level scan with char-boundary correction that tracks count while copying.

`t.2.len() + args.len()` can theoretically wrap on `usize` if `args.len()` is enormous (even though `t.2.len()` is bounded by MAX_TOOL_CALL_ARGUMENTS_BYTES = 1MB). An adversarial SSE chunk could send a delta large enough to wrap; in release builds the comparison would silently let the append proceed past the cap. Add an early `if args.len() > MAX_TOOL_CALL_ARGUMENTS_BYTES { return false; }` before the addition — overflow-safe and slightly cheaper.

`bot-tool-done` truncates `result` to 2000 chars but emits `args` in full. `args` can be up to MAX_TOOL_CALL_ARGUMENTS_BYTES (1MB), so each tool call ships a potentially huge JSON payload to the widget. Asymmetric with the 500-char truncation in the audit_log call right below. Apply a similar `args.chars().take(N).collect::<String>()` to the emit field, or extract a small helper.

Inconsistent provider gating in reasoning injection. The `OpenAiEffort` and `GlmThinking` branches write provider-specific fields (`reasoning_effort` / `thinking`) to `body` unconditionally, while the `AnthropicBudget` branch correctly gates on `http.provider == Anthropic`. If `reasoning.resolve()` ever returns the wrong wire type for the actual provider (e.g. a future model mapping returns `OpenAiEffort` for an Anthropic model, or `AnthropicBudget` for an OpenAI-compatible model), the request body would carry fields the receiving API doesn't recognize → strict gateways return 400 invalid params. Defense in depth: gate each branch on its matching provider, and emit an `audit_warn` on mismatch so the misconfiguration is observable instead of silently dropped or silently mis-sent.

Arguments overflow leaves the tool-call entry in an inconsistent state. The function mutates `t.0` (id) and `t.1` (name) BEFORE the arguments size check, so when the size guard trips, `id`/`name` are already populated but `arguments` stays empty; then the caller does `continue` past the `bot-tool` emit, so the widget never sees the tool start event. Downstream the `id` is non-empty (so the `call_synth_*` fallback is a no-op) and the partial entry is dispatched to `execute_tool` with empty arguments, producing a confusing, hard-to-diagnose tool failure. Fix: perform the size check first (returning false before mutating id/name) so a rejected delta leaves the entry pristine, OR roll back id/name on rejection, OR emit `bot-tool` for the new id before returning false.

Mutex poison recovery silently discards panic evidence. `e.into_inner()` returns the inner `MutexGuard` and clears the poison flag, so a subsequent panic that occurred mid-transaction (e.g., inside the INSERT loop) leaves the next caller proceeding against a DB whose state may be inconsistent (rusqlite's `Drop` for `Transaction` will roll back the in-flight tx, but nothing surfaces that to the caller). Because `_g` is held across `open_db` *and* the SQL transaction, a panic anywhere in this scope produces this risk. Prefer propagating `PoisonError` (return as a `CommandError`), or at minimum set a process-wide "db dirty" flag and refuse further writes until a checkpoint. Both `bot_history_save` and `bot_history_clear` have this same pattern.

Global `DB_WRITE_LOCK` is acquired *before* `super::open_db(&app)?`. Any cost in `open_db` (file I/O, schema bootstrap, WAL replay) is paid under the lock and serializes all history writers behind first-touch initialization. Open the connection first, then take the lock — or split into a per-connection cache so the lock only guards the actual write transaction.

`bot_history_save_inner` returns `Result<(), String>` and uses `.map_err(|e| e.to_string())` on every rusqlite call, which destroys the structured `rusqlite::Error` (and thus the SQLite extended code / constraint name) before the caller maps it into `CommandError::DbError`. Have the inner function return `rusqlite::Result<()>` so callers can preserve the original error context, classify constraint violations, etc.

Truncation assumes `messages` arrives in chronological order (oldest first). The slice `&messages[messages.len() - MAX_HISTORY_MSGS..]` keeps the last N entries, but the log message asserts "丢弃最旧 N 条" (drop oldest N). If the frontend ever passes the array newest-first, the wrong rows are discarded and the log line lies. Either document this ordering as a strict precondition on the public API, or truncate by sorting/filtering on a timestamp/id field within the row itself.

`bot_history_clear` deletes messages but, unlike `bot_history_save`, does NOT update `bot_sessions.updated_at`. After a clear, the session row still reflects the previous write time, which is inconsistent with `bot_history_save` and will cause the session to appear "more recent than it is" in any UI sorted by `updated_at`. Either intentionally document the asymmetry or touch `updated_at` here as well.

The test "rank_skills_truncates_to_top_k_and_keeps_rest" does not actually verify the truncation or tail-ordering contract — it only asserts `out.len() == 7` in both the empty-query fallback and the "ranked" path. Worse, `rank_skills("任务", ...)` calls the real `crate::memory::embed::embed_text` rather than the fake, so the assertion relies on ONNX being initialized for tests and the comment "借用 fake embed 全命中" is misleading. This contradicts the module-level claim "测试：embed_fn 注入式设计，不依赖 ONNX." comments.content: Rollback window has no RAII guard: `reopen_failed_run_for_rollback` flips a `Failed` run to `Running` and trusts the caller to invoke `restore_failed_run_after_rollback` later. If the rollback segment panics, returns early, or the surrounding future is dropped, the run is left in `Running` forever — `active_skill_run_for` will return it, the main loop will silently advance a run that should be terminal, and the state-machine invariant (`Running` ↔ tool execution allowed) is broken. Wrap the open/restore pair in a small RAII guard (e.g. `struct RollbackGuard { ... }` whose `Drop` calls `restore_failed_run_after_rollback`) so any panic path is closed safely.

`restore_failed_run_after_rollback` only restores when `state == Running && session_id matches`. If the rollback segment itself flips the run to `Failed` (because an inner tool step failed again), this guard is a safe no-op as the comment notes — but combined with the caller-controlled reopen it means there is no audit trail that the run ever passed through the rollback window. Consider recording a transient `end_reason` like "rollback-in-progress" during reopen so post-mortem logs can tell whether a `Failed` run ever went through the rollback path.

Registry keying is `name` but every accessor filters by `session_id`. Two sessions cannot run a skill of the same name concurrently: the second session's call to `active_skill_run_for` will either pick up the first session's still-active run (and the main loop will drive the wrong session's tool execution) or see a terminal run that the second session didn't start. Either key the map by `(name, session_id)` (composite key or separate per-session maps) or assert in `active_skill_run_for` that only one matching run exists per session_id, to make the cross-session collision detectable instead of silent.

Production test hooks `test_hook_insert_skill_run` / `test_hook_remove_skill_run` / `test_hook_skill_run_state` are `pub fn` with only `#[doc(hidden)]` and are not gated by `#[cfg(test)]`. The cfg-gated `test_insert_skill_run` / `test_remove_skill_run` / `test_skill_run_state` helpers right below suggest the intent was for both to be test-only. Accidental production use (or a buggy / malicious caller) silently inserts or removes live `SkillRun` records and corrupts the global registry. Gate them with `#[cfg(any(test, feature = "skill-test-hooks"))]` (or move the integration-test callsites onto the `#[cfg(test)]` helpers if they share a single test target) and gate the feature flag in `Cargo.toml`.

Every lock site silently recovers from mutex poisoning via `e.into_inner()` after a single `eprintln!`. This (a) drops the original panic payload into stderr without surfacing it through the app's structured logger, (b) leaves the mutex un-poisoned so a second poisoning in another thread does not escalate (subsequent panics are masked), and (c) hides the bug that caused the panic. Prefer propagating the error to the caller, or switching to `parking_lot::Mutex` (which does not poison), or at minimum re-poison after recovering the inner data so the next failure surfaces.

`load_skill_meta` collects the body from the full read text via `text.chars().take(MAX_SKILL_BODY).collect()`. `text` here is the full file contents (~potentially many MB on a misconfigured disk) — the `.chars().take(...)` then `.collect::<String>()` builds an intermediate UTF-8 string anyway because Rust `String` is UTF-8. For large files the read + allocation is O(N). Cap at `read_to_string` with a length check, or stream-collect into a preallocated `String`: `let mut body = String::with_capacity(MAX_SKILL_BODY); for c in text.chars().take(MAX_SKILL_BODY) { body.push(c); }` after early-returning if `text.len() > MAX_SKILL_BODY * 4` (rough UTF-8 worst-case).

`SkillState` carries a duplicate of `SkillMeta.mode` intent (`terminal_after_confirm` for non-resumable pause-then-confirm). The state machine has 6 states, but the `Paused + terminal_after_confirm` combination effectively models a third behaviour that consumers must remember to check alongside `state`. Consider making `Paused` carry the terminality flag in the variant itself (`Paused { terminal_after_confirm: bool }`) so invalid combinations (e.g. `terminal_after_confirm = true` on `Running`) become unrepresentable and pattern matches on `Paused` exhaust the flag.
