comments.content: `SkillRun::new` uses `chrono::Utc::now().timestamp_millis()` directly while the module exports `now_ms()` next to it (and `runtime.rs` / `scheduler.rs` import `state::now_ms` as their canonical timestamp source). The struct's own constructor bypasses the helper, so any future change to the timestamp source (e.g. swapping `chrono` for `std::time`, making it injectable for tests) must be applied in two places and the unit-test `test_run` helper uses a hard-coded `started_at_ms: 1000` that drifts away from production semantics. Use `now_ms()` here too.

`load_skill_meta` reads every fallback directory sequentially even after the first hit. Currently the early `return Ok(...)` after a successful read short-circuits, which is correct — but if a future change adds caching or a "prefer newest" heuristic, the loop must continue past the first match. Add a `// first hit wins; do not fall through` comment, or refactor the loop into an explicit `for ... { match read(...) { Ok => return, Err(NotFound) => continue, Err(_) => return Err } }` so the contract is enforced by the type system rather than an implicit early return.

Silent mutex-poison recovery on `DB_WRITE_LOCK`: a prior holder that panicked mid-SQL would leave the in-DB state (or surrounding invariants) potentially inconsistent, but the recovery via `into_inner()` discards the panic signal and lets subsequent writers proceed as if the critical section was clean. After a poison it would be safer to either bubble the original poison error to the caller, return a typed `CommandError::LockPoisoned`, or run an integrity check before continuing. The same pattern is repeated in `bot_session_delete` (lines 124-127) and `bot_session_rename` (lines 147-150).

Async/sync mismatch on blocking DB writes: `bot_session_create` and `bot_session_rename` are synchronous `#[tauri::command]` functions that open a SQLite connection and run INSERT/UPDATE under `DB_WRITE_LOCK` on the calling (main) thread, while `bot_session_delete` correctly uses `spawn_blocking`. Under contention these sync writers stall the Tauri main thread, block UI events, and serialize behind `open_db` disk I/O. Consider making create/rename `async` with `spawn_blocking` (or wrapping the whole flow in `spawn_blocking`) so they match the delete path.

`open_db` runs outside `DB_WRITE_LOCK`, breaking the documented invariant: the comment claims the lock's critical section only covers the SQL write, but `open_db` itself performs PRAGMA setup and idempotent DDL. If first-touch DDL is not strictly side-effect free when multiple writers race (e.g. concurrent first open + table creation), or if the same `DB_WRITE_LOCK` is supposed to serialize schema bootstrap across the module, the documented scope is fragile. Either move `open_db` inside the lock or guard schema bootstrap behind a one-shot `OnceLock`/`OnceCell` so the lock really only has to cover SQL writes.

`JoinError` from `spawn_blocking` is flattened to a formatted Chinese string, losing the underlying error chain and any panic payload from the blocking closure. If the inner task panics (e.g. the `unwrap()` inside the closure, or a future rusqlite change), only a localized status string surfaces — no machine-readable cause and no panic backtrace. Map the `JoinError` to a typed `CommandError` variant (e.g. `Internal`/`Join`) that preserves the `JoinError` (downcastable via `e.into_panic()`) and chain the original error when available.

Critical panic: when caller passes no `params` (or a non-object value like an array/string), `params = serde_json::Value::Null` is assigned, but the loop at lines 80-86 then indexes into it via `params[&p.key] = ...`. serde_json::Value's IndexMut panics with "cannot access a Null with an index" if the skill declares any param with a default (or even any provided key). Net effect: every `use_skill` call without `params` against a skill that has defaults panics the caller; this is the normal case (model may legitimately omit params). Initialize as an empty Object instead: `params = match params { Value::Object(m) => Value::Object(m), _ => Value::Object(Map::new()) };`

All `start_skill` errors (disabled/blacklist/conflict/missing-required-params) are surfaced as `ToolResult::ok(e, ...)`. The harness / main loop therefore cannot structurally distinguish a refused skill from a successful load — it sees the same OK envelope and the same Vec<UI artifact> shape, and the only signal is a Chinese error string inside the payload. If anything downstream ever branches on the success flag (e.g. stop-the-loop, redact prior tool history, mark turn as failed), it will silently treat refusal as success. Either propagate a typed `Err`/`ToolResult::err`, or at minimum return a distinct envelope (e.g. a leading sentinel like `__skill_load_error__:…`) so callers can match without parsing prose.

Audit-trail gap: this `find` filters on `state == Running` only. The step counter was already incremented by `step_check` (which only checks for `Paused`), so any state change between `step_check` and this post-hook — e.g. user /stop causing a concurrent `skill_finish` → `Terminated`, or `step_check` itself flipping `state` to `Failed` for max-steps/timeout — silently drops the failure record, the `actions` entry for this tool, and the post-execute state transition (so the `is_fail` branch never runs even when the tool errored). Net result: `step` is incremented, but neither an `actions[]` entry nor a `skill_step_fail` line is written, and the skill remains in whatever state the other path set, not necessarily Failed. Either widen the filter to `(Running || Paused)` and only run the state transition if `Running`, or always record an audit line for the step (success/fail) regardless of terminal state.

Mutex-poisoning recovery relies on `eprintln!` only and silently proceeds with `into_inner()`. Production deployments commonly drop stderr (Tauri bundled app, GUI subsystem, log-rotation captures only the audit log) — so a panic from any holder of `skill_runs` (e.g. mid-way through the `start_skill` switching loop, or after `r.state = SkillState::Completed` but before `runs.insert(...)`) leaves the registry in an inconsistent state, and there is zero record in `bot.log` / `audit_log_hook`. Either (a) emit a structured audit event before continuing so the inconsistency is at least visible, or (b) fail-fast / re-poison so the next caller sees the same panic and surfaces it. The current pattern actively hides state corruption.

`name` is passed straight from the model's `use_skill({"name": …})` payload to `load_skill_meta` with no validation (only `trim()` upstream). If `load_skill_meta` joins `name` into a filesystem path (e.g. `<skills_dir>/<name>/SKILL.md`), characters like `..`, `/`, `\\`, or absolute prefixes let a hostile or hallucinated model read arbitrary `.md` files inside the app data dir, and the body is then echoed straight back into the prompt at line ~245. Even if `load_skill_meta` rejects `..`, the contract is not enforced here — add a name-shape check (e.g. require `name` to match `[A-Za-z0-9_\-\u4e00-\u9fff]+`, reject anything containing `/`, `\`, `..`, NUL, or starting with `.`) before forwarding, so the safety gate is at the boundary rather than relying on a downstream file-path library.

Race window on rollback text: after dropping the registry mutex, `skill_finish` re-reads the SKILL.md via `load_skill_meta(app, &name)` to extract the rollback section. The SKILL.md on disk may have been modified or deleted since `start_skill` admitted the skill (external editor, hot-reload, multi-process restart), so the rollback text rendered into `rollback_hint` can disagree with the security gate that originally admitted the skill — or be silently empty even when the in-flight run's `meta.rollback == "auto"` justified the suggestion. Either capture the rollback section inside `start_skill` (or under the lock here using the cached `meta` if it carries a rollback blob) and stash it on the `SkillRun`, or guard the re-read with a "best-effort, may differ" annotation in the rendered text.

comments.content: `apply_conn_pragmas` discards the PRAGMA result rows. `journal_mode=WAL` and `synchronous=NORMAL` both return a row whose value is the *actual* mode that took effect; if WAL cannot be set (e.g. on a network FS, read-only mount, or when the file is not yet committed by another writer) the connection silently keeps the previous journal mode and the durability invariants the rest of the migration module relies on are violated without any signal. Run each PRAGMA via `query_row` and assert the returned value (e.g. `journal_mode == "wal"`), or at minimum log/return an error when the mode does not match.

`migrate_legacy_file_bindings` materializes the candidate rows via a plain `prepare`/`query_map`/`collect` and only afterwards calls `conn.transaction()`. The `SELECT` runs in an implicit read that is **not** part of the transaction's snapshot, so a concurrent writer that toggles a row's `files` column between the read and the `UPDATE` will either cause a duplicate `files` JSON write or cause the migration to miss a row whose `file_path` was just cleared — both break the idempotency guarantee this function advertises. Open the transaction first, prepare + execute the SELECT inside it (or use `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`), then iterate.

`migrate_data_json_file` swallows every failure (`read_to_string`, `from_str`, `prepare`, `query_map`, `transaction`, `upsert_tasks`, `commit`) as a bare `return false`, and the caller `migrate_data_json` does `let _ = migrate_data_json_file(...)`. Result: a corrupt or partially-written `data.json` is silently left in place, but a JSON that deserializes but fails to upsert also leaves the file intact with no log line, no error to surface, and no signal to the user that their data wasn't migrated. This is a real data-loss hazard. At minimum, log the underlying error (`eprintln!`, `log::warn!`, or whatever the project uses) on every `Err` path, and have `migrate_data_json` return a `Result<(), String>` so the caller can react.

`reset_bot_assigned_with` uses `SeqCst` for *both* the success and failure orderings of `compare_exchange` and the rollback `store`. The flag only needs to enforce "the winning thread's `exec()` happens-after every previous load of `done`", which is the classic `Acquire`/`Release` pair; `SeqCst` here overstates the synchronization contract and makes future readers wonder what global ordering is required. Use `Ordering::Acquire` for the success ordering and `Ordering::Relaxed` for the failure ordering of `compare_exchange`, and `Ordering::Release` for the rollback `store` (or `Relaxed` if failure doesn't need to publish anything to other threads — it only needs to be visible to the next caller, which an `Acquire` load on the next CAS will see regardless).

`migrate_data_json_file` deserializes the entire `data.json` and collects all existing IDs into a `HashSet<String>` before checking whether there is any missing task. For users with large legacy files and an already-up-to-date DB this is wasted I/O, parse time, and an unbounded `HashSet` allocation on the migration hot path. Cheap pre-check: after `file.exists()`, `metadata().len()` and/or `peek` the first few bytes; alternatively, do the cheap `existing.contains(&t.id)` filter while streaming, and bail out as soon as you have processed all tasks without finding a missing one — but never pay the full JSON parse if you don't need to. At a minimum, pre-size the `HashSet` with `HashSet::with_capacity(row_count_hint)` if you keep the current shape.

Every rusqlite error is collapsed through `.map_err(|e| e.to_string())`, discarding the typed `rusqlite::Error` (SQL state, error code, chained context) at the API boundary. The pattern is repeated in `ensure_brief_entries`, `brief_list_global`, `brief_list_card`, `brief_delete_workflow`, and `brief_delete_task` as well. Consider propagating `rusqlite::Error` (or a project error type) and converting at the Tauri command boundary with added context — that preserves the ability to match on constraint violations and log structured diagnostics.

comments.content: `kind` and `source` are exposed as raw `&str` with only loose string constants; the DDL has no CHECK constraint and `brief_insert` does not validate the values, so any caller can persist arbitrary strings. Downstream consumers (especially the LLM injection built from these rows) silently receive typos and misspellings, and a refactor that renames a variant won't be caught at the boundary. Model these as Rust enums (`BriefKind`, `BriefSource`) or at minimum add `CHECK(kind IN ('qa','rework','manual','clarify'))` / `CHECK(source IN ('user','agent','qa','system'))` to `BRIEF_DDL` so invalid values are rejected at the storage layer.

TOCTOU race in `people_ensure_placeholder`: the `COUNT(*) ... WHERE id = ?1` check and the subsequent `people_upsert_entry` call are not executed atomically. A concurrent real upsert for the same id between the SELECT and the INSERT will leave `count == 0` in this transaction's view, after which the placeholder write of `"未知成员"` will silently overwrite the real `name` (and any `avatar`) — directly violating the documented "已知 id 不覆盖" guarantee. The intent is best expressed as a single atomic statement, e.g. `INSERT OR IGNORE INTO people (id, name, is_self, updated_at) VALUES (?1, '未知成员', 0, ?2)`, which removes the check-then-act window entirely.

`people_upsert_cards` calls `people_upsert_entry` once per card, and each call goes through `conn.execute(...)` which re-prepares the same INSERT/ON CONFLICT statement on every iteration. For an envelope of N cards this is O(N) prepares plus O(N) fsyncs; a single `conn.prepare_cached(...)?` (or a precompiled statement held by `people_upsert_entry`) reused in a loop would be O(1) prepare. Beyond performance, the batch relies entirely on the caller wrapping it in a transaction per the "调用方负责事务/写锁" comment — without one, a mid-batch panic leaves a partially applied envelope, and `chrono::Utc::now()` is evaluated per row so `updated_at` drifts across cards that are logically a single unit. Consider an explicit `conn.transaction(|tx| { ... })` (or accepting one) plus a prepared statement.

All four internal helpers (`people_load`, `people_upsert_entry`, `people_upsert_cards`, `people_ensure_placeholder`) immediately map `rusqlite::Error` to `e.to_string()`, discarding the underlying `SqlState`, the offending SQL, and any column/index context. Per the project's error-handling guidance, errors should preserve the original cause and gain actionable context at the boundary (the `CommandResult` returned by `people_list`), not be flattened this early. Consider a dedicated `PeopleError` (or a `From<rusqlite::Error>` impl) so that, for instance, an `SQLITE_CONSTRAINT` on this upsert is distinguishable from an `SQLITE_BUSY` or an I/O failure at the tauri command boundary.

`brief_list_card` filters only on `task_id` and `brief_delete_task` runs `DELETE ... WHERE task_id = ?1` without joining/filtering on `workflow_id`. This silently relies on task_ids being globally unique across workflows. If two workflows ever share a task_id (short IDs, reused handles, imported/restructured tasks, or simply a caller bug), `brief_for_injection` will leak one workflow's history into another's prompt and `brief_delete_task` will silently delete the wrong rows. Either add `AND workflow_id = ?2` to both queries and thread `workflow_id` through the API, or document and enforce a uniqueness invariant on task_id generation at the call sites. The test suite does not exercise a same-task-id-across-workflows scenario, so the regression would not be caught today.

With the current `MAX_ENTRY_TEXT=200` and `MAX_ENTRY_REASON=80` the worst-case rendered line is ~288 chars so the bug doesn't materialize today, but if either constant grows (or reason formatting grows) the cap will start leaking. Either hard-truncate the over-cap line so the contract is always enforced, or `debug_assert!` the invariant `cap_chars >= 2 + MAX_ENTRY_TEXT + 5 + MAX_ENTRY_REASON + 1` so a future raise of the constants fails in tests instead of silently overshooting the prompt budget.

comments.content: Both public helpers flatten `rusqlite::Error` with `e.to_string()`, discarding the typed error variant (busy/locked, constraint violation, corruption, etc.) and any row context. Callers cannot branch on the real cause, and the message reveals nothing about which operation or column failed. Propagate `rusqlite::Error` (or wrap it in a crate error with `#[from]`) instead.

Enforce the binary representation at the storage layer with a `CHECK (rollback_attempted IN (0, 1))` constraint and reject unexpected values when decoding instead of using `v != 0`.

comments.content: Library-init `expect` panic in `http_client`'s fallback path. When both builder attempts fail, `OnceLock` initialization panics, crashing the whole bot runtime. The intent ("loud panic safer than an unconstrained client") is documented, but a production library should still avoid panicking on recoverable environment failures — consider returning a typed error from `http_client()` and propagating it from the call sites that already return `Result`.

Jina Reader fallback silently exfiltrates the user-provided `raw_url` to a third-party host (`r.jina.ai`) whenever direct extraction yields <100 chars. The comment acknowledges this but there is no explicit user opt-in / consent path, and only stderr logging records adoption vs non-adoption. For a tool whose threat model is otherwise strict (SSRF, redirect rejection, DNS pinning), consider gating the fallback behind a config flag, and/or redacting sensitive query/path/userinfo segments before submission.

`href_from_tag` does not validate that the delimiter after `href=` is actually an attribute quote — it accepts any first byte as the delimiter, so a tag like `<a href=javascript:...>` would treat `j` as the quote and extract garbage. For attribute safety, require the delimiter to be `"` or `'`, which also avoids matching malformed input.

`find_ci` does no tag-boundary check, so `<div` matches inside `<divider>`, `<diva class=...>`, or comments that weren't fully stripped. In `extract_main_content` this can mis-attribute spans to a `<div` that isn't actually a `<div` element. Consider using `find_tag_open` (which already enforces a whitespace/`>`/`/` boundary after the needle) for HTML tag detection, or add a post-match boundary check.

`web_search` does two linear scans over `domain_count` for every result (`iter().find(...)` then `iter_mut().find(...)`), giving O(n²) behavior across merged results. With `opts.count` capped at 10 the constant is small, but `domain_count` is a perfect fit for a `HashMap<String, usize>` (with `get` + `insert`) for clearer O(1) updates.

Phase 2c rollback unconditionally removes db_path-wal and db_path-shm, but the early guard at function start only checks `db_path.exists()` for the main file. If -wal/-shm sidecars pre-existed at the target location (e.g., from a prior partial import or a crash leaving orphan sidecars), Phase 2a/2b overwrote them with tmp_wal/tmp_shm, and this rollback then destroys whatever was there — including the pre-existing data. Extend the guard to also reject when the target sidecars exist (and snapshot their existence so rollback only deletes files this call actually created). The same pattern exists in the Phase 2b rollback and is the root reason a "fail-closed" import can destroy sidecars the user never asked us to touch.

The docstring claims "rename 覆盖目标" (rename overwrites target), but `std::fs::rename` on Windows returns an error when the destination file already exists rather than overwriting it. `atomic_write` therefore silently fails to overwrite existing files on Windows, contradicting the documented contract. Import/upgrade flows that depend on overwriting an existing file will fail closed on Windows for an entirely different reason than intended, and the file system will keep stale contents. Use a platform-aware atomic rename (e.g. Win32 `MoveFileExW` with `MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING`) or a dedicated crate that normalizes atomic-rename semantics.

`metadata` then `rename` is a check-then-act race, and `rotate_log_if_large` is `pub` and unsynchronized. More importantly, if the log writer holds an append handle (typical for tracing from another thread), that handle keeps writing into the inode that has just been renamed away, producing a log file with no path name that grows unbounded. Additionally `std::fs::rename(path, old)` on Windows refuses to overwrite an existing `.log.old`, silently disabling rotation when it would be most useful. Pair rotation with the writer's mutex (or have the writer observe the rename via the path lookup failing), and use a Windows-replaceable rename.

The atomic_write test only forces failure by making the destination a directory — a failure mode that triggers identically on every platform. The most relevant portability gap (`std::fs::rename` refusing to overwrite an existing FILE on Windows, which directly contradicts the docstring's "rename 覆盖目标" promise) is not exercised, and the test name's "NEW-5:不留 .tmp 垃圾" claim is not cross-checked for the overwrite path. Add a Windows-gated test where the destination already exists as a regular file with prior contents and assert the file is overwritten with no `.tmp` residue — this directly enforces the documented contract.

Phase 1 opens a transient `Connection` solely to issue `wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)` and then performs byte-level `std::fs::copy` on the main file. On Windows this is fragile: anti-virus software and external writers may still hold the file with sharing restrictions immediately after the SQLite handle drops, causing `fs::copy` to fail intermittently with sharing violations. Worse, any writer active during the byte-copy can produce a torn page at the end of the copied file — there is no MVCC snapshot guarantee. Using `rusqlite::backup::Backup` for the main file gives a crash-consistent snapshot and is portable across platforms and AV interference; -wal/-shm can still be byte-copied if preserving uncommitted transactions is the desired design (matching the current docstring intent).
`record_job_run` 的 INSERT 与裁剪 DELETE 分两次 `conn.execute()` 调用，未包裹在 `conn.transaction()` 中。若中间 panic、磁盘满或进程被中断，`scheduled_job_runs` 将无界增长，裁剪逻辑失效。建议在事务中执行：先 INSERT、再 DELETE，最后 `tx.commit()`。

`migrate_legacy_task_schedules` 在循环中执行多条 INSERT，最后一次性 UPDATE tasks.schedule/sched_last/enabled，全程未用 `conn.transaction()`。崩溃/中断可能造成「任务卡 schedule 已清空但 scheduled_jobs 行未生成」的中间态，破坏迁移的幂等契约（即使重跑也找不回已清空的字段）。建议把所有写入包到事务里。

`update_job_run_state` 注释明确放弃 RMW，但同一个作业可能被周期 tick 与 `retry_at` 触发的 tick 同时进入执行收尾（两者都到达 `jobs_tick` 后调用本函数）。两次写入会按最后写者胜的顺序覆盖 `last_status/retry_count/enabled`，结果难复现。同一条 SQL 还无条件 bump `updated_at`，会令持有 `expected_updated_at` 快照的 UI 并发编辑立即失效。建议：(1) 调度器侧用 per-job 串行化（互斥队列）保证单作业的执行收尾互斥；(2) `updated_at` 仅在实际状态发生迁移时 bump，而非每次调用都写。

comments.content: Bot-history rollback test is self-fulfilling: it manually creates the transaction and delete/insert sequence instead of calling the production save entry point, so it will pass even if the production entry point stops wrapping replacement writes atomically.

Pre-transaction reads rely solely on debug_assert!: `load_workflow` and `load_tasks_by_workflow` run BEFORE the transaction is opened. The only enforcement that `lock_db_write()` is held is a `debug_assert!`, which is compiled out in release. If any future caller forgets `lock_db_write()`, the read-modify-write window becomes a real TOCTOU: the `kept_task_ids` baseline, `expected_updated_at`, and `created_at` snapshot could all be stale relative to a concurrent writer, and the transaction would still commit. Consider either making `holding_db_write()` a runtime check (or having `workflow_save_locked` acquire the lock itself and assert before/after), or move the snapshot reads inside the transaction.

Cycle sentinel silently deletes cycle-bearing nodes on next save. `task_fp_at` returns a unique `__cycle__:<id>` fingerprint for any existing task that's part of a cycle, which can never match a draft (drafts reject cycles up front in `draft_fingerprints`). The result: any workflow whose existing `tasks` graph contains a cycle (via data corruption, an external writer, or a future regression that lets cycles slip into storage) will have those nodes deleted on the next canvas save with no warning surfaced. Consider either: (a) propagating the cycle condition as a typed error/warning so the caller can choose how to handle it, (b) treating the cycle fingerprint as still matching so the user is forced to break the cycle deliberately, or (c) at minimum logging an `audit_event` so the silent data loss is observable.

Event emit errors silently dropped (3 sites: workflow_save, workflow_import, workflow_delete). `let _ = app_emit.emit(...)` and `let _ = app_emit.emit_to(...)` discard every error — including a missing 'main' window or serialization failure — leaving the widget/menu potentially stale with zero observability. The "best-effort broadcast" design is documented, but at minimum route the result through `tracing` or `eprintln!` so that production desyncs become diagnosable. Also: the `serde_json::json!` macro will silently stringify any non-serializable `Task` (e.g. a future field added without `Serialize`), and you wouldn't notice until the UI is missing the change.

`Workflow.enabled` round-trip semantics are easy to misinterpret. The docstring says "None/Some(true) = 启用, Some(false) = 暂停", and storage maps `None→NULL`, `Some(false)→0`, `Some(true)→1`. The mapping itself is consistent, but the comment is misleading: NULL on disk does NOT mean "absent" — it carries the semantic meaning "enabled by default". Any frontend or downstream consumer that treats a JSON `null` for `enabled` as "unknown / not loaded" (a common default) will mis-render the toggle, and `upsert_workflow` silently writes NULL for enabled/schedule/sched_last on new rows with no UI hint. Consider an explicit tri-state enum (`Enabled`/`Disabled`/`Unset`) or, at minimum, sharpen the field doc to spell out "null means 'enabled', this is NOT an absence marker".

`workflow_set_schedule` docstring understates the SQL's effect. The comment "只动 schedule 字段；sched_last 由调度器维护" suggests only `schedule` is changed, but the SQL also writes `updated_at = ?3`. The behavior is reasonable (a modification timestamp should advance), but the comment is misleading and a future maintainer relying on it could write code that assumes `updated_at` is preserved across schedule-only edits (e.g. for incremental export/cache invalidation). Update the comment to mention `updated_at` is bumped.

Same emit pattern duplicated three times. The `let _ = app_emit.emit("tasks-changed", ());` + `emit_to("main", "tasks-updated", json!{...})` block appears verbatim in `workflow_save`, `workflow_import`, and `workflow_delete` (with only `upserts: []` vs `outcome.upserts` differing). Extract a small helper like `broadcast_tasks_changed(app, upserts: &[Task], deletes: &[String])` to keep the payload shape, the event names, and the error-handling decision in one place.

The unknown‑tool compatibility gate is broken. `unknown_tool_names` returns a deduplicated set that mixes main steps *and* rollback steps, and the comparison `unknown.len() >= steps.len()` then misclassifies valid plans (e.g. duplicate unknown tools in main steps, or unknown tools only in the rollback segment). In addition, the gate only checks the static `tools_index()`, ignoring the MCP fallback in `dispatch`, so skills that rely on MCP tools are prematurely terminated. Fix by counting how many *main* steps reference unknown tools (not a deduplicated name set) and by consulting a list of known MCP tools before treating an unknown name as fatal.

The per‑step state lookup is session‑scoped only; if a different skill for the same session is started while this scheduler is still running, `active_skill_run_for` will return the new run and the remaining steps will be advanced against the wrong run, corrupting the state machine and audit trail. Filter by `name` (or otherwise bind to the specific `SkillRun`) just like the wrapper does for params/allowed_tools.

`is_tool_failure_text` delegates to `audit::tool_call_failed` with an empty skill name. The classifier may rely on the skill context to disambiguate failure messages; passing `""` can lead to misclassification (e.g. a generic "失败" prefix being treated as a user‑initiated abort). Propagate the actual skill name (or a stable identifier) to the classifier.

Rollback steps bypass the `meta.allowed_tools` whitelist. The main loop enforces the whitelist before executing a step, but `run_rollback_segment_core` executes rollback tools unconditionally. If a skill declares a restrictive allowlist, the rollback segment can still invoke tools outside that list, violating the author‑declared policy. Apply the same `allowed_tools` check (or an explicit override flag) before each rollback tool invocation.

If a rollback step references `${params.*}` (as documented for normal steps), the value will not be resolved and the tool will be invoked with a literal placeholder. Pass the same `params` into the rollback path or merge them into the substitution context.

comments.content: Non-atomic status transition: `load → check → UPDATE` happens across three separate SQLite statements with no transaction and an unconditional `WHERE id=?1`. Two concurrent connections (e.g. runner + cancel signal, or two runner retries) can both observe the same pre-transition state, both pass `transition_allowed`, and the later UPDATE will overwrite a terminal state/timestamps (Running→Succeeded then Running→Failed; or queued→running then queued→cancelled), defeating the stated terminal immutability and idempotent polling contract. Fix by wrapping the read/check/write in a transaction and using a conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE id=?1 AND status=?expected_from`, returning `Err` when affected-rows is 0 (treat as lost transition).

Over-broad same-state bypass: the `row.status != to` guard makes every self-loop permitted, including Queued→Queued and Running→Running, which `transition_allowed` and the `transition_table_rejects_illegal_moves` test classify as illegal. Additionally, `COALESCE(?5, error)` rewrites the `error` column on a nominal same-state retry, so "terminal facts cannot be rewritten" is violated for the failure reason (and `started_at` can be back-stamped on a Running→Running call when the existing row lacked one). Constrain the exception to terminal→terminal only and never overwrite `error` on a no-op re-entry.

Silent enum fallback hides DB corruption: unknown `status` strings are mapped to `SubagentStatus::Failed` and unknown `profile` to `SubagentProfile::General`, returning `Ok(row)` with a fabricated domain value. The caller's state machine, retry logic, and profile-based tool whitelist will then operate on invented state — a corrupted row can be reported as Failed (triggering false failure paths), and a corrupt profile silently broadens tool access via the General mapping. Surface the corruption as a typed error (or an `Unknown` variant) instead of silently coercing.

Budget-clamp contract is unenforced at the persistence boundary. `SubagentBudget::max_turns`/`max_tool_calls`/`max_wall_seconds` are public fields, `clamped()` is opt-in, and `insert_subagent` writes `budget_json` as an opaque `Option<String>` without parsing or clamping. A row constructed directly (bypassing the documented spawn/task_patch path) can persist `maxTurns=0`, `maxTurns=u32::MAX`, or any wall value, breaking the safety budget that downstream runner/dispatch enforcement depends on. Either accept a typed `SubagentBudget` (call `clamped()` inside `insert_subagent`) or store a parsed struct and reject out-of-range values at write time.

Unconditional backfill writes lack lifecycle/version guards. `set_subagent_session` and `set_subagent_result` only check row existence, not its current status, so a stale or out-of-order runner can overwrite `session_id`/`result_json` on an already-terminal or cancelled row. Combined with the missing atomic update (see separate finding), two concurrent writers can race the same row and the second will silently clobber the first's session/result. Guard with a `WHERE id=? AND status NOT IN (terminal list)` (or an expected `status`) and check affected rows.

comments.content: Regex only matches the hyphenated 36-char UUID, but production task tools (bot/tools.rs: `uuid::Uuid::new_v4().simple().to_string()`) emit 32 hex chars without hyphens. `extract_task_id` therefore returns `None` for real task output, so `${stepN.id}` placeholders never resolve against actual `CompletedStep` data. The comment also mislabels the pattern as "v4" — the version nibble is unconstrained. Accept both forms and drop the misleading v4 claim, or document the limitation explicitly.

The byte-level `in_quotes` check only treats the placeholder as inside a JSON string when both neighbouring bytes are `"`. Common templates fail this heuristic — e.g. `{"note":"prefix ${step1.result}"}` (prev byte `f`), `{"note":"${step1.result} suffix"}` (next byte ` `), or any literal preceded by `\\"` / `: ` — so the replacement is inserted raw. A result containing `"`, `\`, or a newline then corrupts `args_json`, and `parse_args` (bot/dispatch.rs) silently downgrades the call to `Null` args, which downstream tools may execute with missing/empty parameters. The adjacent-byte check is structurally insufficient for JSON; replace it with a true JSON-string scanner that tracks string state and escape sequences.

comments.content: Each substitution stage consumes the previous stage's output (params → nested → by-index → prev). A `${...}` sequence returned from a `params` value or from a step's `result` is therefore re-scanned by later passes, so `params` is not actually static and step results are not actually literal. Concretely, `params = {"title": "${step1.result}"}` (legal per the key validator in parse.rs) expands step1's output into the next tool's args, and a result containing `${prev.id}` / `${params.*}` is interpreted in subsequent rounds. This breaks the documented "互不干扰" / 静态参数 contract and can leak context into tool arguments. Resolve every placeholder against the ORIGINAL `text` in one combined pass and never feed inserted values back into another `replace_ctx` call.

`serde_json::to_string(v).unwrap_or_default()` silently returns an empty string if serialization ever fails. For `&str` it cannot fail today, but the fallback turns any future regression into "produce structurally valid but empty JSON inside `args_json`", with no diagnostic. Drop the silent default and surface the invariant violation so the bug is caught at the boundary instead of producing downstream `Null` args.

The module's top-level comment declares the run grouping key as the composite `(workflow_id, run_started_at)`, but `wa_prune` selects and deletes by `run_started_at` alone (`SELECT DISTINCT run_started_at ... LIMIT ?`). This conflates runs from different workflows that happen to share a millisecond timestamp and lets the number of retained *runs* diverge from `keep_runs` (the query counts distinct timestamps, not distinct composite keys). It can also delete entries of an in-progress run for one workflow simply because an unrelated workflow started more recently. Use the composite key, e.g. `DELETE FROM workflow_audit WHERE (workflow_id, run_started_at) NOT IN (SELECT workflow_id, run_started_at FROM workflow_audit GROUP BY workflow_id, run_started_at ORDER BY MAX(created_at) DESC LIMIT ?1)`, or at minimum document and enforce the global-timestamp semantic intentionally.

`workflow_audit_export` reuses the display query's hard `limit = 500` cap and returns the truncated row count as if it were the full audit. For any workflow whose retained audit exceeds 500 entries (the retention default is only 20 *runs*; a single run can emit many events), the JSON file silently omits older events and the caller has no signal of truncation. Either stream the export, drop the cap, or include a `truncated: bool`/total-count field so the operator knows the archive is incomplete.

comments.content: The export path is validated in `spawn_blocking_map` but the actual `std::fs::write(&path, json)` runs synchronously on the async Tauri command. That (a) blocks the Tokio worker for the duration of the write proportional to JSON size and (b) creates a TOCTOU window: the destination can be replaced (e.g. symlink swap, file deleted/recreated) between the validation task and the write, so a write can land on a path that was never validated. Move the write into the same blocking task (open with `OpenOptions` + `write_all` after the path check, or pass the opened `File` handle across the spawn boundary) so validation and write are atomic relative to the caller and the runtime is not stalled.

comments.content: Settings update writes three key/value pairs in separate autocommit statements; if a later write fails (e.g., DB I/O error after the first two succeed), earlier settings remain persisted while the command returns an error, leaving configuration in a partially-updated state. Wrap the writes (and the final read used to build the returned view) in a single `Connection::unchecked_transaction` so all keys succeed or none do.

Getters bypass the setter's normalization. `node_acceptance_enabled` treats any string except "0" as true (so "false", "no", or garbage values become true), and `audit_retention_runs` accepts any in-range `u32` because clamping happens only on writes. Pre-existing or externally modified rows, plus any schema migration or manual DB edit, can change runtime acceptance and pruning behavior despite the documented "5..=100 / '0'|'1'" invariants. Apply the same canonical encoding and clamp on the read path.

The catch-all `_` arms in `node_acceptance_enabled`, `audit_retention_runs`, and (less critically) `review_model_id` collapse genuine SQLite failures — missing table, locked DB, I/O errors — into the documented default. The header comment only justifies falling back for missing rows / parse failures, so storage faults masquerade as ordinary "user did not set this" and propagate silently through `settings_view`. Surface DB errors to the caller (or at least log them) so a broken store does not silently flip critical runtime behavior.

`wa_prune` runs after the new retention value is already committed; a cleanup failure is only printed via `eprintln`, so users receive a successful response while old audit records continue to exceed the requested retention. If retention is treated as a compliance/policy guarantee, this leaves the system in an inconsistent state. Either roll back the new retention when pruning fails, or propagate the prune error to the caller (and consider including it in the audit event).

The audit event records the raw submitted `audit_retention_runs` rather than the clamped value actually stored and applied (`r.audit_retention_runs`). A request of e.g. 1000 will be audited as 1000 even though the database and pruning used 100, producing an audit trail that does not reflect the system's effective configuration and can mislead compliance review. Log the effective value (or both `requested` and `effective`) so the audit log matches reality.

comments.content: Mutex held across notification dispatch, audit log, and file I/O. The guard from `notify_state().lock()` spans `app.notification().builder()...show()` (which may involve IPC on macOS), `crate::bot::audit_log(...)` (likely disk write), and `save_state(app, state)` (file write). All blocking work is serialized behind a global mutex even though no current caller races for it — this is a fragile invariant and any one slow dispatch stalls the entire notifier. Consider dropping the lock between `plan_round` returning and the dispatch loop, or restructure state ownership so the heavy work happens outside the critical section (e.g., snapshot pending + flags, release lock, dispatch, re-acquire to write back).

Flag is set before notification delivery is confirmed. `plan_round` mutates `entry.h1 = true; entry.t0 = true` synchronously and returns the Pending; if the subsequent `notification().show()` fails (permission denied on macOS, Focus Assist / DND suppression on Windows, IPC error, transient system failure), the dedup flag is already set and the notification will never be retried. The audit log records the failure but the user receives nothing, with no backoff or retry path. Consider only marking the flag after a successful `show()` (i.e., move the flag mutation out of `plan_round` and apply it per-delivery inside `run_round`).

`save_state` failure leaves in-memory flags diverged from persisted state. Flags are updated, notifications dispatched, and then `save_state` is best-effort (logs on error and returns). If `atomic_write` fails (disk full, perms, transient I/O), the next restart will load the prior `false` flags and every still-active task within the T0_WINDOW will re-fire — there is no retry, no in-memory journal, and no reconciliation. Either persist before flipping flags, retry with bounded backoff, or coalesce unsaved transitions and persist them before the next scan.

comments.content: `load_state` corruption recovery loses dedup state and will spam notifications. Returning an empty HashMap on JSON parse error means a single corrupted/truncated `due-notify-state.json` causes every active task with `due` within 24h to re-fire its H1/T0 notification on the next scan. The comment frames this as intentional ("宁可重发不丢通知语义"), but the persistence layer is the only dedup mechanism, so any I/O blip (or a half-written file from a previous crash before `atomic_write` rename) translates directly into user-visible notification spam. Consider quarantining the corrupted file (rename to `.corrupt-{ts}`) and keeping a last-known-good snapshot, or at minimum log/metric the recovery so it's visible.

O(n*m) cleanup scan in `state.retain`. For each entry in `state` this does `valid.iter().any(...)` — a linear scan over the active list. With stale entries accumulated across upgrades or restores this is quadratic. Build a `HashSet<&str>` of valid IDs first and use `set.contains(id)` to make this O(n+m).

comments.content: No shutdown signal on the notifier task. The blanket `From<String>` / `From<&str>` impls silently funnel every string-shaped error into `CommandError::Internal`, which (a) makes `recoverable=false` regardless of root cause, (b) loses every semantic code the rest of the file is built around, and (c) provides no compile-time nudge toward the precise variants. `From<CommandError> for String` is a one-way lossy conversion that drops the stable code and recoverable flag and keeps only the human message. The doc comment acknowledges this and limits the use case to "tool→model boundary", but `From` impls are global and `?` will silently invoke this anywhere `Result<_, CommandError>` flows into `Result<_, String>`, erasing the very contract the rest of the file is built to enforce, with no compile-time guard. comments.content: check_export_path validates the *trimmed* path (so "/dir/foo.json " is validated as "/dir/foo.json"), but the callers in tasks_export/tasks_import pass the original untrimmed `path` to atomic_write/File::open. On Unix, trailing whitespace is a legal filename character, so a path with a trailing space passes the symlink-rejection check on the trimmed target while the actual file operated on is a different name — which can be a symlink to arbitrary content. The gate is also pure time-of-check; the actual open/write happens later in a different thread without O_NOFOLLOW or re-validation, so a symlink swap between gate and op also defeats the no-follow rule. Normalize and return the validated path from the gate (or strip and reuse), and reopen with O_NOFOLLOW + re-stat immediately before the file op.

load_tasks_by_workflow is documented as feeding workflow fingerprint diff/save, but the query lacks any ORDER BY clause. SQLite does not guarantee row order without ORDER BY, so the same DB state can produce different task orderings on different calls, producing nondeterministic fingerprints, spurious diffs, and broken change detection. load_all explicitly orders by `ord, rowid`; this function must mirror that (or use an appropriate workflow-scoped key).

comments.content: upsert_tasks is a public API whose correctness contract — that the caller holds DB_WRITE_LOCK and that bulk writes are atomic — is enforced only by debug_assert!, which is compiled out in release builds. Any external caller can invoke it without the write lock, defeating the SELECT-then-INSERT lost-update guard. The same is true for the sibling "_locked" helpers (task_set_column_locked, task_patch_locked, task_reorder_locked, delete_non_self_locked, import_tasks_conn): the suffix is a naming convention, not a runtime check. Either narrow visibility to pub(crate) so the contract is enforced by the module boundary and review, or upgrade the assertion to a runtime check that returns Err when the lock is not held.

`apply_one` calls `store::load_all(conn)` and runs two linear scans of every memory row on each invocation. When called inside `apply_from_consolidation`'s per-proposal loop this becomes O(M*N) full-table scans plus 2*M extra sweeps. Either hoist the `load_all` into a single `OnceCell<HashMap<...>>`/batch prelude in `apply_from_consolidation` and reuse it across proposals, or replace with targeted SQL lookups (`find_by_key_tag` for the key check and a `SELECT ... WHERE kind='lesson' AND content = ?` for the content check) so each proposal does at most one indexed probe.

When `embed_text` returns `None`, `apply_one` is invoked with `embedding=None`, which makes `store::insert_item`'s cosine similarity merge gate inert. In that path a near-duplicate of `p.suggestion.text` against an existing foreign-keyed memory is never detected, so `ConflictRefused` is impossible and the lesson silently overwrites nothing — but the audit/apply path still records `Applied` and writes the ledger. The current `evolution.embed_failed` warn is not enough: either skip such proposals (don't apply at all) or surface them as a distinct `EmbeddingUnavailable` outcome so they cannot bypass the anti-hijack check.

`unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())` recovers from a poisoned mutex by ignoring the panic and reusing the inner guard. After a writer panic the underlying state may be inconsistent — e.g. a SQL transaction aborted after appending a partial JSONL row, or vice versa. The current code prints a one-liner but never documents why post-panic state is safe to mutate; this is an undocumented invariant at a safety boundary. Either propagate the error (return `Err`) at the critical sections, or document explicitly which atomicity guarantee (SQLite transactions, JSONL lock pairing, etc.) covers the recovery.

`super::change::read_all(&cr_path).unwrap_or_default()` silently swallows IO/parse failures into an empty `rows`, so `unique_change_id_for` derives `chg-<pid>` (or similar) without seeing existing entries. The local `EVOLUTION_STORE_LOCK` only serializes within this process; another instance, the panel write path, or an external tool can still race. Result: collisions are only surfaced as an `append_change` error, and the apply has already counted the proposal as `Applied` in `report`. At minimum log the read failure and treat as a Warn audit, or hold the read-and-derive-inside-lock pattern with explicit error propagation.

`apply_one` collapses every non-`RefusedForeignMerge` `InsertOutcome` into `Applied`, so a `Merged` (existing lesson absorbed the new content via similarity merge) is reported identically to a fresh row. `report.applied` therefore counts both `Applied` (new row) and `Merged` (no new row, existing row updated), which is misleading for the apply summary, the bot.log line, and the `evolution.applied` audit event — all of which downstream consumers may use to gauge "how many new lessons landed". Model this as a distinct outcome variant (e.g. `ApplyOutcome::Merged { target_key }`) and surface it separately in the report.

TOCTOU race on the JSONL append path. `entry::read_all(&path)` is followed by per-iteration `entry::append(&path, &entry)` with no file locking, so two concurrent callers — e.g. `evolution::post_consolidation` racing with the "shadow 钩子" the doc comment explicitly says depends on this file — can both read the same baseline, both find no duplicate, and both append, silently breaking the dedup invariant that this whole function exists to enforce. Add a process-local `Mutex` (cheap, covers the same-process case the comment describes) or, better, an OS-level advisory lock (e.g. `fs2`/`fd-lock`) taken around the read–append window; failing that, re-read and dedup per-entry right before each append (still racy but at least narrows the window).

Partial-write semantics break the documented contract. If `entry::append` fails on the Nth proposal, entries 0..N-1 are already persisted on disk but the function returns `Err` with an incomplete `written` Vec (which is dropped at the `?`). The doc comment says "通知中心按此逐条落消息", so the caller (notification center) cannot tell which IDs were persisted: a naive retry can silently re-emit notifications for entries that already made it, and a naive rollback leaves the jsonl in a half-written state that may also trip the next call's `read_all`. Either build a tmp file in-memory and rename it onto `path` only after the whole batch succeeds (atomic-ish, also fixes the append-mid-line hazard), or document the partial-failure contract explicitly and return a typed error carrying the IDs that did get written.

Errors are flattened to `String` at the function boundary, dropping the original error source, the file path, and — most importantly for the "首行结构级损坏" case the comment explicitly warns about — the line/byte offset of the corruption. A caller seeing `Err("EOF while parsing a value")` cannot tell which jsonl line broke or where to look. Use a typed error (thiserror enum or `anyhow::Error`) and wrap with context: `.map_err(|e| CandidateError::Persist { path: path.clone(), source: e })?` so the structural-corruption incident the comment specifically guards against is actually diagnosable upstream.

evaluate_s2 unconditionally returns Allow and ignores the proposal (`_p`), so any proposal routed through this function — including irreversible ones — is approved. Safety relies entirely on an external caller-side filter that this function does not enforce or verify. Enforce the reversibility/impact invariant at the decision boundary itself (or at minimum, return a typed error/Result so callers must prove the pre-filter ran) rather than relying on a comment-documented invariant outside the API.

The loader honors externally configured `s2_active` even though evaluate_s2 is an allow-all placeholder. A misconfigured or tampered bot-config.json can flip the system into S2 and approve main-memory writes before any real policy exists. Either reject `s2_active` while the placeholder is in place, or require an explicit "policy_implemented" flag before honoring it.

This test explicitly asserts that high-impact proposals are approved by evaluate_s2. With the always-allow placeholder, any regression that removes the documented pre-filter would still pass. Add a test that exercises the irreversibility/impact guard at the actual decision boundary (or assert via a typed error/Result from evaluate_s2) so the safety invariant is enforced and verified, not just trusted.

A missing `activation_state` key, a non-object `evolution` value (e.g., a string or array), or any non-string state all collapse to S0 with at most an eprintln. Because the loader returns `ActivationState` rather than `Result`, callers cannot distinguish "deliberately unconfigured" from "config corrupted / wrong schema / unreadable file". Returning a `Result` with typed variants (or at least a richer tri-state) would make the contract explicit and prevent routing decisions from silently shifting on transient or malformed configuration.

The test is named `load_state_from_partial_json` but actually loads a fully populated valid JSON containing both required keys. Rename to reflect what it actually verifies, and add separate tests for genuinely partial JSON, malformed JSON, missing key, wrong-type `evolution` value, and unknown state string — these are the safety-critical fallback paths that determine whether routing silently changes.

rollback_count and pollution_survival_days assume each `mem_key` appears at most once in `applied` JSONL. Retries/reapplications silently inflate `rolled_back_total` (every absent row counts as a rollback) and `pollution_survival_days` only retains the last-seen timestamp per key in the HashMap. Either deduplicate by `mem_key` (keep latest `applied_at_ms`) or document that callers must guarantee uniqueness; current code has no enforcement and no test for this scenario.

Unchecked i64 subtraction `(now_ms - *at)` panics under overflow checks or wraps in release builds. Corrupted JSON with extreme timestamps can therefore yield a plausible positive age and pass the `days >= 0.0` guard, polluting the survival metric. Use `i64::checked_sub` (or `.saturating_sub`) and decide on a documented policy for invalid/future records (e.g. skip silently, but never let wrap survive).

comments.content: behavior_deviation trusts callers to validate inputs and enforce coverage. (a) Empty `hit_fractions` is treated as perfect 1.0 average, masking missing feedback. (b) `f64` fractions are not range/finite-checked — NaN propagates through `(1.0 - NaN).clamp(0.0, 1.0)` returning NaN, and values outside [0,1] silently bias the result (clamped). (c) `case_total` is only a zero-guard, so a short slice silently drops cases from the mean. Either validate inputs at the API boundary (reject non-finite / out-of-range, require `hit_fractions.len() == case_total` and unique case ids) or convert to `Result` and let the caller fix the upstream contract.

compute() does not bound its documented 0.0-1.0 ranges. `task_success_rate = case_passed / case_total` and `tool_call_efficiency = succeeded / total` silently produce values >1 when inputs are inconsistent. Likewise, `pollution_survival_days` is unbounded and has no associated sample-count field, so consumers cannot tell whether 0.0 means "no live lessons" or "all timestamps invalid". Clamp the rates or return `Result` when inputs violate documented ranges, and emit a `live_lessons_with_known_age` counter alongside the average.

Returning `Ok(Vec::new())` when the JSONL is absent makes a missing/unreadable source indistinguishable from a legitimately empty history. Downstream metrics then report `applied_total=0`, `rollback_rate=0`, `pollution_survival_days=0` as if data were complete. Either return a distinct error/sentinel (e.g. a `ReadOutcome { records, source_present }`) or require an explicit "no data" path at the caller; at minimum, log a warning so this condition is not silently hidden.

`#[serde(default)]` on `case_passed_placeholder` deserializes pre-existing JSONL rows as `false`, but those legacy rows almost certainly contain the same synthetic 100% task-success placeholder that this commit just learned to flag. Consumers trusting the new flag will therefore misinterpret historical reports as genuine metrics. Either re-tag legacy records on first read (treat rows without the field as `true`), version the schema, or document the silent downgrading prominently so callers do not mix old and new rows.

comments.content: `transition` returns `Result<(), String>`, collapsing three distinct failure modes (SameState, TerminalSource, IllegalTransition) into localized Chinese strings. Callers cannot pattern-match and tests have to use brittle `e.contains("非法")` / `e.contains("终态")` / `e.contains("未变")` assertions that break under i18n or copy edits. Introduce a `pub enum TransitionError { SameState, FromTerminal, Illegal { from, to } }` and `impl std::error::Error + Display`, so callers and tests can branch on the variant instead of substring-matching log strings.

The set of terminal states is encoded twice — implicitly by the absence of outgoing arms in the `can_transition` table, and explicitly via `ChangeStatus::is_terminal()` consumed at the top of `transition`. If a future contributor adds a new terminal variant and only updates one site, the safety guarantee holds but the error category becomes wrong (e.g. `transition(Rejected, X)` would report "非法 status 流转" instead of "终态不可流转"); in the other direction it can let a transition out of a supposed-terminal state through. Derive terminal-ness from a single source — e.g. have `can_transition` itself refuse to be called with a terminal `from`, or compute the terminal set once and check it in both places — and add a compile-time-ish test asserting `ChangeStatus::is_terminal()` matches `{Rejected, RolledBack, Expired}` exactly.

comments.content: `from == to` is checked before `from.is_terminal()`, so a terminal-to-self transition (e.g. `transition(Rejected, Rejected)`, `transition(Expired, Expired)`) reports "状态未变" rather than the more accurate "终态不可流转". The `transition_terminal_errors` test only covers `Rejected → Pending`, leaving the terminal-to-self mis-classification untested. Swap the order (terminal check first, same-state second) or add tests that pin down the chosen error category for terminal-to-self — otherwise the diagnostic contract drifts from what the doc-comment promises.

`append()` opens with `OpenOptions::create(true).append(true)` but never calls `sync_all()` / `sync_data()` and performs no explicit inter-process locking. Two concurrent appenders (e.g. Tauri command handler and a background worker) can interleave bytes mid-line and produce unparseable jsonl; a crash between `write_all` and flush can leave a truncated final line that silently halves the last record on the next read. The "锁契约" comment defers to an external contract — there is no defensive check, fsync, or temp-file rename-to-append here, so a single missing lock at any call site silently corrupts the file. Consider `fs2`/`fd_lock` for advisory locking, or append-and-rename via a sibling temp file.

`ChangeStatus` is a bare 9-state enum with only `is_terminal()` / `as_str()`. There is no `can_transition_to(&self, next: ChangeStatus) -> bool` (or builder/setter enforcing one) — any caller can persist any state into any record. The 9-state machine contract (`Pending → Shadowing → ShadowPassed → Approved → Canary → Active`, with `Rejected` / `RolledBack` / `Expired` as terminals) lives only in doc comments. Nothing prevents e.g. `Active → Pending`, a backward jump after rollback, or `Expired → Active`. With a `Mutex<ChangeRecord>` + setter, or a simple `validate_transition` helper called at every write site, you can make these impossible states unrepresentable.

The module doc claims hard-constraint `Pending → Approved → Applied` and that `AutoApplied` vs `HumanApproved` are tracked via `approval_source`, not `status`. However, there is no cross-field invariant. `serde::Deserialize` will happily rebuild `(status = Active, approval_source = Pending)`, `(status = Rejected, approval_source = HumanApproved)`, or `(status = Pending, rolled_back_at = Some(_))` from an existing jsonl line — and once persisted, downstream gating logic that trusts the contract will misbehave silently. Either add an explicit invariant check on load (rebuild into a typed state and reject impossible combos with a logged error), or wrap status+approval_source in an enum whose variants only admit legal pairings.

`read_all` delegates to `crate::evolution::read_jsonl(path, "changes")`, but the corruption-recovery contract assumed by the tests in this module — middle corrupt line silently skipped, first-line corruption triggering a backup file whose name ends in `.corrupt` and whose contents equal the original bytes — is not visible here. The module doc mentions a `.corrupt-<ts>` suffix while the locked-in test only requires `.corrupt`. A reviewer cannot confirm the delegate actually implements this contract from this file alone. If `read_jsonl` is correct, a brief cross-reference comment (or a one-line "see evolution::read_jsonl for corrupt-line policy") would make the contract self-documenting; otherwise the test suite here is testing behavior that the implementation may not actually provide.

Module-level doc contradicts itself about `schema_version`: it is listed under "构造时派生（不入 jsonl 即可）" (derivable at construction, persistence optional) and then immediately re-listed with "仍持久化以便未来 bump" (still persisted to allow future bumps). The locked-fields test asserts the field is present on the wire. Future maintainers reading the first half may add `#[serde(default)]` or remove the field, silently breaking compatibility with already-on-disk records; readers seeing only the second half will treat it as load-bearing. Either pick one phrasing or annotate with the version-bump convention explicitly (e.g. "当前 v1，缺字段 = 旧版派生 = 1，未来 bump 时在此处增加 enum 分支").

For jsonl append under load this is acceptable but the lack of buffering means each call is a syscall per record. More importantly, the current implementation allocates `line` then copies bytes into the file via `as_bytes()`; using a `BufWriter` (or `write_all` with a single small `Vec<u8>` buffer reused across calls) avoids repeated allocator churn when many records are flushed in sequence. Not critical at current scale but worth noting if `append` becomes hot.

The "theoretically unreachable" fallback uses `chrono::Utc::now().timestamp_millis()`, which is **not guaranteed unique** within the same millisecond. Two concurrent callers (panel toggle / shadow / apply CR all route through this per the docstring) can both exhaust 2..=9999 in the same millisecond and produce the **identical** `chg-<pid>-<ms>` suffix — reintroducing the exact "二次回滚永久卡死" bug class this function exists to prevent. Use a process-local `AtomicU64` counter, a UUID suffix, or `rand` — anything monotonic or with collision-grade randomness.

The docstring contract ("compliance=false 的 from_proposal 是终态 Rejected，流转即 Err") couples this to the status state-machine — if `status.rs` is ever refactored and lets a `Rejected`-status record traverse the chain, this line will silently flip compliance to `true`, masking the gate violation. Add an explicit re-check or `debug_assert!` so a future status-machine bug fails loudly instead of producing a non-compliant Active record.

`unique_change_id_for` is O(n × k) where k ≤ 9999: for every candidate suffix it does a fresh linear scan of `rows` via the `taken` closure. For a long-lived ledger this is unnecessarily slow. Build a `HashSet<&str>` of `change_id`s once, then probe in O(1) per candidate — total O(n + k).

During the four-step transition loop, `cr.status` advances (`Shadowing` → `ShadowPassed` → `Approved` → `Active`) while `cr.approval_source` stays `Pending` until the final statement overrides it to `AutoApplied`. The docstring claims these are "瞬时通过", but `cr` exists as a fully constructed `ChangeRecord` with each intermediate value — any `Drop` impl, log line, panic between assignments, or future refactor that exposes these states will observe a `status=Approved, approval_source=Pending` pair that is semantically wrong. Set `approval_source` as each step is committed (or document and `debug_assert!` that intermediates are never observed).

`created_at_ms` is copied verbatim from the proposal while `expires_at_ms` is derived from caller-supplied `now_ms`, with no validation that `now_ms >= created_at_ms`. The `expires_at_now_plus_ttl` test on line 92 explicitly demonstrates that an entry can be born with `expires_at_ms < created_at_ms` (creation at 1.7e12, now at 5000). A caller passing a stale, negative, or zero `now_ms` will silently produce an entry that is already expired relative to its creation timestamp — corrupting downstream retention/ranking logic. Either enforce the ordering at this boundary (panic, saturate, or return `Result`) or document the clock-anchor convention explicitly so callers cannot misuse it.

comments.content: Tests only verify `MemoryHint -> EvolutionLayer::Policy` and never assert the layer mapping for `ToolSchemaHint` or `PromptHint`. The `mk_proposal` fixture always uses `structured_patch: None`, so the silent-drop behavior flagged above is also untested. Add a table-driven test that asserts `layer` (and any expected structured-patch handling) for every `ProposalCategory` variant, plus one case with `structured_patch: Some(...)` to lock in whatever the intended behavior is.

Saturating to `i64::MAX` turns an out-of-range timestamp into an effective non-expiring entry, so the function no longer enforces its documented 14-day TTL. The test explicitly establishes this behavior for corrupt/adversarial values; if such a value reaches this helper, the candidate can remain pooled indefinitely and consume storage instead of being rejected/quarantined as invalid input. Validate persisted timestamps at the deserialization boundary and make this calculation fallible (or return a bounded fallback), rather than encoding overflow as “never expires.”

The 14-day TTL is never enforced: this helper only stores a deadline, and the current production code does not read `expires_at_ms` to transition `Pooled` entries to `Expired` (or otherwise expire them). Consequently, every ordinary entry remains pooled indefinitely as well. Add an expiration predicate and invoke it on the production load/consume paths; computing the timestamp alone does not implement the documented TTL.

The doc comment claims `record` contains "ChangeRecord + 5 个枚举" (ChangeRecord + 5 enums), but record.rs only defines 3 enums (ChangeStatus, ApprovalSource, EvolutionLayer). The other types in record.rs are ChangeRecord and EvalResult, both of which are structs, not enums. The description should be corrected to "ChangeRecord + EvalResult + 3 个枚举" or similar to accurately reflect the module's contents. This kind of structural mismatch is particularly important in a project where module structure is documented as a hard spec invariant.

Module-level header still advertises a `ShadowSink` trait abstraction and `MockShadowSink` (the four e2e tests are even described as using `MockShadowSink`), but the trait and mock were deleted — see the AppShadowSink doc at ~line 108 explicitly noting their removal. New readers will search for a trait and four e2e paths that do not exist; either restore the trait or rewrite this header to describe the actual two-function design (`shadow_apply_for_batch` test path + `shadow_apply_for_batch_with_app` production path).

The production entry point `shadow_apply_for_batch_with_app` is the only production caller, but every `#[tokio::test]` in this module exercises only `shadow_apply_for_batch` with `new_for_test`. The S0/S1/S2 routing (`S2Active → evaluate_s2 → Allow/Block`), the in-lock dedup against `ChangeStatus::Pending|Shadowing|ShadowPassed`, `unique_change_id_for` derivation, the `spawn_blocking` window holding `lock_evolution_store`, and the `evolution.not_reversible / evolution.blocked / evolution.shadow_dedup_hit` audit branches are all uncovered. Given this is documented as the only production path and carries the documented safety invariants (「本入口是生产唯一入口」), a dedicated e2e covering at least one happy-path S0 batch, one S2 Block batch, one S2 Allow batch, and one `is_reversible=false` proposal is required.

Global `TOTAL_WRITES` / `FAILED_WRITES` are `static AtomicU64` shared by both `shadow_apply_for_batch` and `shadow_apply_for_batch_with_app`, never reset in production. The threshold check at the end of both functions uses `TOTAL_WRITES.load()` (cumulative ratio across all batches and across both call paths), so a single historical failure batch keeps the `evolution.shadow_warning` audit firing on every subsequent healthy batch (cumulative failed/total stays > 5% forever), and the very first batch can spuriously alert if the cumulative rate from earlier runs is already above threshold. The check should use per-batch counters (locally incremented, then compared against `FAILURE_THRESHOLD`) rather than the global atomics, or the atomics should be reset to zero on each batch's evaluation.

`shadow_apply_for_batch` is `pub async` but performs synchronous filesystem IO (`sink.write_change` → `change::append_change`, an `open + writeln` syscall) directly on the calling task without `spawn_blocking`. The doc comment correctly flags it as test-only, but `pub async` exposes it to any future caller on the Tauri async runtime, which would pin a tokio worker exactly the way `shadow_apply_for_batch_with_app`'s comment warns against. Either downgrade it to a non-`async` synchronous `fn`, make it `pub(crate)`/`#[cfg(test)]`-gated, or wrap the write in `spawn_blocking` so the invariant holds regardless of caller.

`is_enabled` opens, reads, and JSON-parses the entire `bot-config.json` on every call with no caching. If invoked per-proposal or per-batch this is wasteful, and there is an inherent TOCTOU window versus a writer updating the file (a caller can read `enabled=false`, the file flips to `true`, and the in-flight call still treats shadow as off). Cache the parsed `ShadowConfig` once at startup (or memoize with a file-mtime check) and expose an explicit invalidation hook, or at minimum document that callers must take their own snapshot of `enabled` per dispatch.

The double space between `在` and `之后由` indicates a missing component name (likely an intermediate module/command name like `apply_from_*` or a phase label). comments.content: Rate cohort / denominator mismatch: only `candidate_generation_rate` is filtered to the observation window. `approval_rate` divides `promoted_count` (all proposals, ever) by `proposal_total` (all proposals, ever), and `rollback_rate` divides `rolled_back_count` (all ChangeRecords, ever) by `promoted_count` (proposals, ever). When a proposal owns multiple ChangeRecords, `rollback_rate` can exceed 1.0, and the lifetime vs. window semantics are undocumented. Pick one cohort (window-scoped or lifetime) and apply it consistently to all four metrics; if lifetime is intentional, rename fields and document it.

Survival join key identity: applications are indexed only by `mem_key` and the first occurrence wins. `AppliedRecord` also carries `proposal_id`, and `ChangeRecord` carries `proposal_id` and `change_id` — yet none are used. When a `mem_key` is reused across proposals or re-applied, every active change sharing that key is attributed the first applied timestamp, skewing the survival average. Either join on `(proposal_id, change_id)`/application-event identity, or enforce uniqueness of `mem_key` at write time; relying on `iter().find`-equivalent "first match" semantics hides a real data-integrity hazard.

Silent survival exclusions bias the average: active changes whose `mem_key` has no matching `AppliedRecord` (or has a future-dated `applied_at_ms`) are silently dropped from the mean, but `active_lessons` still counts all `Active` changes. A `pollution_survival_days` of `0.0` is therefore ambiguous (no active lessons vs. all matches missing vs. all future-dated), and the average is computed over a selected subset whose size is not surfaced. Track and expose `survival_skipped` (missing/future) separately so the metric's population is auditable, or fail loudly when an active change lacks an application record.

Behavior contract states "纯函数，输入相同 → 输出相同" but `derive_proposals_with` stamps every proposal with `chrono::Utc::now().timestamp_millis()`, so the full `Vec<EvolutionProposal>` is not reproducible across calls — only the `proposal_id` is stable. Tests only compare IDs and `len()`, hiding this nondeterminism. If downstream code relies on struct equality (e.g. snapshot tests, idempotent persistence) it will see a different `created_at_ms` every run. Either drop the pure claim, or pass `now_ms` from the caller (as `derive_lesson_proposal` already does).

The 5-item cap is a raw input-order truncation, which lets a leading run of Low-impact Distill or Medium-impact Merge proposals starve High-impact Contradiction proposals that the severity model is supposed to surface. Test `derive_caps_at_five` only checks length, not impact ordering. Either sort/filter by `impact` before truncating (High > Medium > Low) or document explicitly that order is FIFO and severity is not considered.

Proposal IDs are computed by joining arbitrary `String` ids with a literal `|` separator and no escaping, so two distinct sets can produce identical hash input. Example: `ids=["a|b","c"]` and `ids=["a","b|c"]` both sort to `["a","b|c"]` (different sort orders!) — `["a","b|c"]` joined with `|` is `"a|b|c"`, and `["a|b","c"]` joined is also `"a|b|c"`. Fix by length-prefixing each ref or using a separator that cannot appear in id strings (e.g. `\u{1F}`).

On 64-bit platforms, an `ids` vector larger than `u32::MAX` wraps silently and produces a wrong `occurrence_count` (e.g. `ids.len() == 0x1_0000_0001` becomes `1`).
