comments.content: Segment ③ walks `mark_human_applied` using the `cr.status` captured back in segment ①, then unconditionally writes `changes[pos] = cr.clone()`. If another caller mutates the same CR during segment ②'s apply window (e.g., `rollback_change_locked` flips status to `RolledBack`, or shadow/auto-apply advances it past Pending), segment ③ will silently overwrite that external status and resurrect a rolled-back CR. The re-`load_changes` here only re-locates by `change_id` — it never copies the file-side `status` back into `cr` before calling `mark_human_applied`. Fix: after re-loading, take `cr.status = changes[pos].status` (or skip the transition path entirely) so the write-back reflects the freshest persisted state.

Doc comment says "错误不阻塞回滚（mem_item 可能已不存在，例如重启后丢失）", but the function propagates real errors via `.map_err(...)` for both `open_db` and `delete_by_key_tag`. Only the `deleted == false` (row absent) path is silently tolerated. A transient SQLite error will therefore abort `rollback_change_locked` before the CR flips to `RolledBack`, leaving CR status and mem_item state inconsistent. Either change the doc comment to reflect "missing mem_item is non-blocking, other errors abort", or swallow non-existence errors and propagate only the rest.

`delete_by_ids` runs first; if it succeeds and then `rollback_applied` errors, the source mem_items are already gone but the apply-side lesson (key_tag `evo:<id>`) is left orphaned. The function returns the partial count and the caller (`delete_inner`) writes the proposal/CR as deleted, then propagates the error — so the user sees a failure but the lesson is permanently orphaned (still surfaced via injection_block, referring to a deleted proposal). Either run `rollback_applied` first (lesson first, refs second; on lesson failure nothing is changed), or commit both inside a single SQLite transaction so a mid-failure rolls both back.

Step ordering in `delete_inner` deletes the proposal line and pending CR rows before the optional cascade_source runs. If cascade_source fails (DB locked, disk full, SQLite busy), the function returns Err but the proposal and CRs are already gone — the next retry returns "proposal {id} 不存在" while orphan mem_items (source refs + lesson) remain in the DB, and the user has no visible way to retry the cleanup. Either reorder so cascade runs before the jsonl rewrites, or make the cascade failure a non-fatal warning (log + propagate only the proposal/CR deletion result) since the orphan mem_items are still recoverable from the proposal_id key_tag.

These two `#[tauri::command]` functions are declared sync (no `async fn`, no `spawn_blocking_map`) but call `read_derive_thresholds` / `set_derive_thresholds`, which perform file IO on the thresholds config file. They will block the tokio worker thread on every invocation, in contrast to every other evolution_* command in this file which routes blocking work through `crate::py::document::spawn_blocking_map`. Wrap them in `spawn_blocking_map` for consistency, or document the sync IO as intentional (and ensure the config IO is short/in-memory). Also note the inconsistency with `Result<_, String>` used everywhere else — only this pair uses the typed `CommandResult`.

DB_WRITE_LOCK held across the entire snapshot read. The mutex is acquired before open_db() and only released when the function returns, so every other DB-using caller (read or write) is blocked for the full duration of open_db + ensure_table + load_all. Holding a synchronous lock across I/O is also a cancellation hazard — if the surrounding task is dropped mid-query the lock is held until the JoinHandle is dropped without running the guard's Drop. For a read-only snapshot, prefer a short-lived lock just around the I/O call, or split into open + (lock + read + unlock) so other writers are not stalled.

Silent mutex poison recovery hides corruption. `e.into_inner()` after a poisoned MutexGuard unpoisons the lock and lets the function proceed as if the lock were healthy. The original panic may have occurred in the middle of a write transaction — at that point the on-disk state (or in-memory invariants protected by the same lock) can be inconsistent, and this recovery masks that fact from every later caller. At minimum, this should return an Err("mutex_poisoned") instead of forging ahead and emitting only an eprintln line.

String-prefixed type discriminator on ConflictRef. `ConflictRef.with` packs both the kind and the id into one String with prefixes `pool:` / `active:`, forcing every consumer (and tests) to substring-match instead of pattern-matching on the existing ConflictKind enum. Split into structured fields (`kind: ConflictKind, id: String`) and let serde produce the formatted string, or add a typed accessor like `ConflictRef::parse(&self) -> (ConflictKind, &str)`. Today the `change_id` test assertion `"active:chg-chg-1"` already shows the brittleness — change_id is "chg-" + proposal_id, but if `from_proposal` ever changes its id scheme the string encoding silently misroutes conflicts.

Redundant sort in judge_lesson_adoption. The closure `top3_contents` runs full sort + take(3) twice on overlapping data (existing is sorted again on the second call after being chained with the candidate). With N existing lessons this is 2·O(N log N) when a single sort of the combined vec + comparison would be O((N+1) log(N+1)). Negligible at current pool sizes, but worth flagging since the function is documented as a "static approximation" called per-proposal in build(), and the panel may grow.

The proposal_id is inserted into the 24h dedup map and `EmitReport.written` is incremented BEFORE the AppHandle is checked and BEFORE `audit_event!` is invoked. As a result, a startup-order mistake (AppHandle not yet registered) or any audit-side failure silently drops the audit row while the proposal is permanently suppressed from re-emission for 24 hours. The public API exposes no audit outcome; `EmitReport.written` reflects "claimed by dedup" not "audited". Consider either (a) inserting the dedup record only after a successful audit, (b) extending `EmitReport` with a `not_audited`/`audit_failed` counter and returning a Result, or (c) at minimum reverting the dedup claim in a catch path so retries remain possible until the audit actually succeeds.

The TTL comparison `now_ms - *ts < EMIT_DEDUP_TTL_MS` relies on non-monotonic UTC wall time, and `now_ms` is captured BEFORE the mutex is acquired. Two real correctness issues follow: (1) if the wall clock is rolled back (NTP correction, manual change, system resume from suspend) the difference shrinks, so entries can be retained well past 24h; conversely a forward jump causes all entries to expire at once and allows duplicate audit rows. (2) Under thread starvation or heavy contention, the captured `now_ms` can be stale by the time the lock is finally taken, so freshly inserted timestamps are effectively in the past and a subsequent `retain` may expire them prematurely on the very next call. Use a monotonic clock (e.g. `std::time::Instant`) sampled AFTER acquiring the lock, and store elapsed duration instead of wall time.

`emit_dedup_works_without_app_handle` asserts that `AppHandle` is unregistered, but `register_app_handle` is a public function with no test-only guard; if any other test (in this crate or an integration test) ever registers a Wry handle, this assertion silently flips to passing `written` as a real audit count instead of the intended eprintln path. `EMIT_TEST_LOCK` only serializes tests within this module, so concurrent callers in other modules invoking `emit_proposals` (e.g. via `post_consolidation` or directly) can perturb the count-delta checks (`before`, `before + 1`, `after_first > before`). To make these tests deterministic, either make the dedup map and `APP_HANDLE` injectable (so each test builds a fresh state) or expose a `#[cfg(test)]` reset hook that drains `EMITTED` and clears `APP_HANDLE`.

comments.content: `read_all` 与 `append` / `rewrite_jsonl` 之间没有任何同步。多个调用点（如 `panel::commands::load_proposals`、`precompute_human_apply_embedding`）在没有持 `EVOLUTION_STORE_LOCK` 的情况下调用 `read_all`，若与 `append`/`rewrite_jsonl` 并发执行会读到正在写入的半行 JSON，`read_jsonl` 会把这种行当作损坏并把整文件备份为 `.corrupt`，导致正在追加的条目永久丢失。请在文档中明确该函数必须在 `EVOLUTION_STORE_LOCK` 持有下调用，或把公开 API 改为内部并集中加锁。

文档中“单次 write_all 原子”的表述过强：`write_all` 可能在底层拆分为多次 `write(2)` 系统调用，且 POSIX 仅保证单次 `write(2)`（≤ PIPE_BUF）原子。若序列化结果 > 4096 字节且跨进程（无 flock）并发，多个 writer 的字节可能交错。该实现对 in‑process 锁保护安全，但需修正文档并限定写入长度或显式一次 `write(2)`。
`append` 假定文件最后一行以 `\n` 结束；若前一次写入因进程崩溃或外部编辑留下未换行结尾，新行会直接拼接在上条 JSON 末尾，产生“上一条 JSON + 当前 JSON”合并行，`read_jsonl` 会把它当成损坏行并把整文件备份，导致新条目永久丢失。请在写入前检测并补齐换行。
`append` 与 `read_all` 都把底层 `std::io::Error`、`serde_json::Error` 立即转为 `String`，丢失了错误链和结构化信息；调用方无法根据错误类型判断可重试或记录结构化日志。建议改为 `std::io::Result` 或定义专用错误类型包装源错误，在边界添加上下文。
`append` 写完后没有调用 `sync_all`/`sync_data`，进程崩溃或掉电时最近追加的条目可能仍在 OS 缓存中而未持久化，导致候选池丢失提案。建议在 `write_all` 成功后调用 `f.sync_all()` 强制刷盘（或在调用方统一保证耐久性）。

`c.to_ascii_lowercase()` only handles ASCII A-Z; non-ASCII uppercase letters (e.g. `Ä`, `É`, `Ω`, Cyrillic `М`) are returned unchanged. This silently breaks the documented "uppercase → lowercase" contract for any non-ASCII input — the same problem described with different casing/diacritics will produce different `proposal_id`s, defeating the cross-language dedup goal. The inline comment about `is_numeric` correctly switches to Unicode semantics, but the lowercasing branch did not. Either use `c.to_lowercase().next().unwrap_or(c)` (Unicode full-mapping) or apply `char::to_lowercase` and accept the iterator, and extend the test suite with cases such as `"Ä"` vs `"ä"` and `"É"` vs `"é"` to lock the behavior.

`is_reversible` is a coarse 2-rule predicate that ignores the actual mutation surface of the proposal. It returns `true` for any non-`ToolSchemaHint`/non-`High` proposal even when `Suggestion.structured_patch` is `Some(_)` (Phase 1 invariant is documented but not enforced at the type level — see `Suggestion` and its public `Option<String>`), and even when the target is `SkillDsl` or `MemoryPolicy`, which can rewrite executable DSL or persistent policy. Since shadow/activation routing "depends on it" (per the doc comment), a `true` here can authorize an irreversible action. Either include `structured_patch.is_none()` and target-kind checks in the predicate, return the patch-presence as a separate signal, or restrict the reversible branch via a newtype/constructor that statically forbids patches.

The doc comments assert a strict data-minimization contract ("**不**存原始堆栈 / 文件路径 / 用户输入" / "**不**存原始路径 / 对话内容"), but the fields are plain public `String`/`Vec<String>` with no validation, no newtype wrapping, and no constructor. Anyone constructing an `EvolutionProposal` (including a future `Deserialize` consumer if audit input is ever re-ingested) can persist absolute file paths, stack traces, or PII into the audit stream, and the type system will not complain. Either (a) wrap these fields in newtypes (`TraceId`, `ToolName`, `MemoryId`, `SanitizedSummary`) so callers cannot accidentally construct invalid values, or (b) add a validating constructor used by the audit writer that rejects/redacts the disallowed content before it ever reaches the public struct.

The test is named `proposal_id_stable_across_unicode_normalization`, but it only feeds the identical Chinese string twice and never exercises actual Unicode normalization (case folding, NFD vs NFC, or diacritic equivalence). Because the underlying `normalize_for_hash` does not fold non-ASCII uppercase (see related bug comment on `c.to_ascii_lowercase`), this test passes while the contract is broken. Add cases that compare semantically equivalent summaries differing by Unicode case (`"Ä"` vs `"ä"`, `"É"` vs `"é"`) and by canonical form (NFD `"é"` vs NFC `"é"`) and assert they produce the same id, or rename the test to reflect what it actually covers.

The comment claims this test "locks the field set — adding fields later will break audit parsing, forcing review", but it only checks that a fixed set of keys is *present* in a serialized value and never exercises deserialization. Adding a new public field passes this test (the key still appears), and serde by default silently drops extras on deserialization, so JSON containing an unrecognized field will not raise the alarm the test purports to provide. Add `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` to `EvolutionProposal` and `Evidence`, and add a deserialization round-trip (e.g. `serde_json::from_str::<EvolutionProposal>(FIXTURE)`) with a fixed JSON fixture whose shape must remain stable, so the lock is enforced both ways.

`proposal_id` is a public, freely-settable `String` with no validator. There is nothing that ensures it equals `proposal_id(p.category, &p.target, &p.evidence.summary)`. A proposal reconstructed from an audit record (Phase 2 will read them) or hand-edited can lie about its identity and bypass dedup/routing. Today this is benign because Phase 1 is write-only, but the public `Deserialize` derive already makes the value externally controllable. Either make the field private behind a constructor that always recomputes the id, or add a debug `assert_eq!` (and a runtime check in audit-ingest paths) that verifies the id matches the derived one before it is trusted.

comments.content: gather_candidates loads the entire memory table into RAM on every tick. store::load_all is unbounded, then the OR-filter (updated_at_ms>=threshold || access_count>=N) is applied in memory before the LIMIT. Over months of use this becomes O(total_memories) per 10-minute tick, both CPU and heap. Push the WHERE clause into SQL (with the OR predicate) and apply LIMIT server-side; only fall back to in-memory filtering when an explicit ORDER BY + sort is needed.

Scheduler has no shutdown/cancellation and can overlap with manual runs. The spawned loop runs forever with no cancellation token, so on app exit it is dropped mid-LLM-call or mid-transaction (the inner spawn_blocking may still complete in background, producing orphaned DB writes). Independently, while the scheduler is awaiting run_consolidation (LLM call is not under DB_WRITE_LOCK), a manual memory_consolidate_now click issues a parallel LLM call against the same candidate snapshot — only the DB write path is serialized, so you waste API quota and can produce duplicate / interleaved ops that race at id resolution. Add a CancellationToken (or watch channel) the loop selects on alongside the ticker, and an in-flight flag (or DB-level advisory) to suppress the manual run while a scheduled run is active.

last_run_at is advanced even when run_consolidation fails. The comment justifies this as anti-spam for the next tick, but for transient failures (LLM rate-limit, network blip, ApiKeyMissing after a key rotation) this means the next retry is deferred by the full configured interval (daily/weekly), so the system silently runs on stale memory until the window expires. Distinguish the two cases: only advance last_run_at on a successful Run (Ok) or on a deterministic misconfiguration; on transient Err, leave last_run_at untouched (or record a separate "last_failed_at") so the very next eligible tick retries.

Embedding batch error handling is fragile and assumed-shape. The call `contents.iter().map(|c| embed::embed_text(c)).collect()` only produces the required `Vec<Option<Vec<f32>>>` if embed_text returns `Option<Vec<f32>>`. If it actually returns `Result<Vec<f32>, _>`, a single failure will short-circuit the whole iterator (collecting into Result, aborting the batch and surfacing no per-op degradation), and apply_ops_with would then see embs.len() != ops.len() and silently mis-align embeddings to ops, or panic on unwrap downstream. Verify the signature of embed::embed_text; if it returns Result, switch to `map(|c| embed::embed_text(c).ok())` so per-op failures degrade to None as the downstream `apply_ops_with` contract assumes.

Mutex poison recovery masks state corruption: `e.into_inner()` after `eprintln!` silently continues with whatever state the panicking thread left behind in the `pending_map`. A panic while holding this lock (e.g. inside `park` after constructing `PendingExec`, or any future caller) means subsequent calls operate on a half-mutated map; the only signal is a stderr line. Consider returning `Result` (or panicking on poison) so the inconsistency surfaces instead of being silently absorbed — and do not duplicate the same recovery in three different functions.

Same `e.into_inner()` poison-recovery pattern is repeated in `park` and `take_pending_for`. Combined with the comment "（缺失时兜底实例）" on `pending_map`, a future contributor is likely to copy the pattern again. Centralize the locking into one helper (`fn with_pending_map<R, T>(app, f) -> T`) that either fails loudly on poison or returns `Result`, so the recovery decision is made in one place rather than silently masked at every lock site.

`pending_map(app)` is documented as returning a fallback instance when `AppState` is not managed. In production that means a fresh, throwaway `AppState` (and thus a throwaway pending map) is constructed on every call — `park` and `take_pending_for` end up writing/reading different maps, so pending state vanishes silently between calls. Either remove the fallback and panic/log loudly when `AppState` is missing, or have `pending_map` panic-once-and-cache so the bug is observable rather than invisible.

`mark_subtask_done` does a non-atomic load→mutate→upsert without verifying that the snapshot it loaded is still current: `expected_updated_at = t.updated_at` is set from the snapshot's own `updated_at`, not from the DB's current value, so `db_upsert` has no real baseline to check against and concurrent mutations (user toggling a different subtask during confirm) are silently overwritten. Additionally, a failed `db_upsert` only `audit_log`s and returns, so `advance_or_finish` proceeds as if the subtask was checked off and the next-step loop keeps moving. Either return `Result` so callers can react, or perform a proper compare-and-swap inside `db_upsert` using a fresh `expected_updated_at` read right before the write.

Check-then-act race in `start`: `has_pending_for` releases the pending-map mutex before `clear_for` reacquires it, so another thread can `park` a fresh `PendingExec` for the same session key in the gap and have it silently removed. Replace the two-call sequence with one atomic `take_if_present` (or `remove` followed by inspecting the value) so the "overwrite old pending with new" guarantee holds without a TOCTOU window.

`STEP_STOPS` uses `starts_with` on single-character / very short tokens, producing obvious false positives in this domain: `t.starts_with("停")` matches "停车", "停一会", "停一下检查"; `t.starts_with("别做")` matches "别做这个"; `t.starts_with("算了")` matches "算了吧"; `t.starts_with("取消执行")` matches "取消执行吧". A user typing a brief comment that merely starts with one of these characters will silently terminate stepwise execution and discard their feedback. Either require an exact match / word boundary (e.g. check that the next character is whitespace/punctuation/EOS, or use `==` against the trimmed input) or lengthen the tokens so they are unambiguous.

Adding a new variant — e.g. `ImpactLevel::Critical` or `ProposalCategory::LoggingHint` — will compile cleanly and silently reject the new variant (the `matches!` returns `false`), contradicting the doc's explicit "未来新增 impact 变体必须显式 opt-in" design intent. The type system will not flag missed updates. Consider marking both enums `#[non_exhaustive]` (forces update sites to be revisited), or — at minimum — adding a `#[test]` that asserts the patterns stay allow-lists (e.g. lock the discriminant count) so silent expansion is caught in CI.

`_ => 3` catch-all will silently map any future `ImpactLevel` variant to importance 3. Combined with the fact that `ImpactLevel` is not `#[non_exhaustive]`, adding a `Critical` or `Blocker` tier later would persist as importance 3 instead of (presumably) 5, misranking it in `mem_items.importance`. The store-layer clamp (1..=5) won't catch this misranking — it only protects against out-of-range values, not semantically-wrong-but-in-range ones. The numeric contract and current 3 variants would benefit from explicit arms so a future addition forces an explicit decision.

`EvalContext` is documented as "构造后不可变" (immutable after construction) and the module header stresses the "pure" strategy-layer contract, but the type is plain `Clone` with `pub` fields (and `KillSwitch` is itself `Clone` with `pub` bool fields — no interior mutability today). The "snapshot" invariant is purely conventional, not type-enforced; a future field addition (e.g. a `Cell<bool>` or `OnceCell`) would silently break the read-only-snapshot guarantee that orchestration relies on. Consider sealing the fields with private visibility + a constructor, or wrapping in a `&EvalContext`-only accessor API, so the invariant is encoded in the type rather than relying on convention.

Wall-clock forward jumps (NTP slew, manual clock adjustment, VM clock drift) inflate `duration_ms` and falsely trip the `> 60s` sampling rule. `saturating_sub` only neutralises negative durations; a forward jump of even a few minutes will over-record traces and distort audit signal. Consider clamping `duration_ms` to a sane upper bound before sampling, or capturing `started_at_ms` and `ended_at_ms` from a monotonic clock (`std::time::Instant`) for the duration measurement while still emitting the wall-clock timestamps in the audit record.

comments.content: `engine_status()` is documented as a "panel stats" query but the very first call triggers full OnceLock initialization — it loads `tokenizer.json` (config + truncation setup) and the ONNX session, which costs disk I/O, several hundred MB of allocator/RAM, and seconds of wall time. A UI panel that polls status before any real embed call will force eager model loading, contradicting the file's stated lazy-init design. Consider separating "is the engine slot populated?" (cheap) from "is the engine healthy?" (which has to initialize), or initializing eagerly on app startup so the side effect is intentional.

Every failure path inside `embed_text` collapses to `None` via `.ok()?` with zero logging: tokenizer encode errors, `Tensor::from_array` allocation errors, `Mutex` poisoning, `session.run` ONNX errors, `try_extract_tensor` shape/type mismatches, and the manual `data.len() != seq * EMBED_DIM` check. In production this makes silent embedding degradation completely invisible — the memory subsystem will quietly fall back to keyword-only recall with no telemetry to explain why. At minimum, gate a `log::debug!`/`eprintln!` (consistent with the existing init-time `eprintln!` style) on each path so failures are diagnosable.

Mutex poisoning recovery silently continues after a prior panic. `e.into_inner()` returns the locked guard without clearing the poison flag, so if any prior task panicked mid-transaction (e.g. inside `apply_reflection`'s tx before `commit()`), subsequent operations proceed on potentially inconsistent DB state with no integrity check. Consider treating a poisoned `DB_WRITE_LOCK` as a hard error for write paths (return Err) and only allow recovery for read paths, or at minimum require an admin-initiated reset before resuming writes.

Check-then-act race violates the documented "same key 覆盖" invariant. `find_by_key_tag` followed by either `update_by_id` or `insert_item_with` runs outside any transaction; two concurrent `remember_fact` calls with the same key can both observe `Ok(None)` and both insert, producing duplicate rows whose `tags[0]` equals the same key. `insert_item_with`'s semantic dedup is by embedding cosine, not by `tags[0]`, so two near-identical simultaneous inserts bypass it. Either wrap find+update/insert in a transaction (with `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` to serialize writers) or enforce a UNIQUE index over `tags[0]` for fact kinds and surface the conflict error.

Budget enforcement is O(items × total_block_chars) per call. `block_chars` re-traverses every section header and every line through `chars().count()` on each iteration; for a 4 000-char block with ~20 trimmable items that's ~80 000 char traversals just for the trim loop, and the hard `guard < 10_000` cap means a runaway case exits with the block still over budget. Maintain a running total once, decrement by `line.chars().count() + 1` on each pop, and treat the guard as a defensive belt-and-suspenders rather than the convergence guarantee.

`auto_extract` should be the `AutoExtract` enum, not `String`. The typed enum already exists two lines below; serde can deserialize it directly via `#[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")]` (with a `default` for the off case). As a String the helper `auto_extract_mode` is required, typos like `"auto "` / `"AUTO"` / `"auot"` silently fall through to `Off`, and the public field exposes an unconstrained value space that callers must remember to canonicalize.

Silent lesson-write failure path makes data loss invisible. `auto_lesson_on_task_failure` is fire-and-forget on every task failure: errors only land in WARN audit and there is no caller retry, no escalation, and no surfacing to the user. Unlike `injection_block` (which has a single-shot best-effort contract), lessons are durable self-improvement artifacts — a transient DB failure here is meaningful. Either (a) schedule a bounded retry with backoff inside the task failure handler, or (b) push the failed lesson into a local retry queue (file/separate table) that the consolidate pipeline drains.

Whitespace-only `value` silently triggers deletion. `validate_fact_kv` runs against the already-trimmed value (which is empty for whitespace input) and accepts it because the empty-string length check is missing, then the `if value.is_empty()` branch deletes the existing `tags[0]` row. A user passing `"   "` to update a fact will observe the record being removed with no error. Add an explicit `if value.trim().is_empty()` rejection in `validate_fact_kv` (e.g. "失败：value 不能为空"), or move the deletion check above the validation so empty values require an explicit separate parameter.

Category → kind mapping is split across two sites and silently drops the "project" branch. The local `match` in `tool_remember_fact` produces `&'static str` values `"profile" / "preference" / "project" / "general"`, but the only call sites pass them straight to `category_to_kind`, which collapses `"project"` and `"general"` (and any future added category) into `"fact"`. The intermediate `"project"` arm in the local match is dead code. Inline the mapping into one place — either produce the final kind directly from the `category` input, or remove the redundant `category` local and pass `v["category"].as_str()` to `category_to_kind`.

`save_summary` returns `Vec<(String, String)>` where the tuple is `(id, content)` — a positional pair of strings with no name at the call site. Wrap it in a small `pub struct SummaryRecord { id: String, content: String }` (or `(String, String)` newtype) so the reflection trigger can name fields instead of indexing `.0` / `.1` and so future fields (e.g. created_at, kind) don't require breaking every call site.

Data-loss bug: two extracted facts can both be judged `update` against the same existing memory, causing the first update to be silently overwritten by the second one. `plan_adjudication` runs independently per fact, so a top-1 candidate can appear for multiple facts; `parse_adjudication` only validates the per-index `existing_id` against the candidate and never checks that the same `existing_id` has already been claimed by an earlier entry. `apply_adjudications` then runs two `find_by_id` + `update_by_id` on the same id in order, clobbering the first fact's content/embedding. Track the set of update targets that have already been claimed in this batch and fall back to `New` on a duplicate (semantic dedup at insert time then either merges or inserts a new row, preserving both facts).

Atomicity gap in `mem_pending_reject`: `pending_delete` and `notif_sync_memory` run sequentially on the same auto-commit connection without an explicit `rusqlite::Connection::transaction`. If the delete statements commit and the notification sync then fails (DB busy, disk full, malformed payload etc.), the queue rows are already gone while the corresponding notification entries still reference them — exactly the kind of half-applied state `mem_pending_approve` guards against with its `tx`. Wrap both calls in a transaction so the delete and notification sync either both apply or both roll back.

`mem_pending_approve` performs O(n²) de-duplication with `Vec::contains` on an attacker-controlled `ids: Vec<i64>` from the Tauri IPC boundary, and never caps the batch size. The table itself is bounded by `PENDING_CAP=50`, but the command accepts arbitrary lists, so a malicious or buggy frontend can drive a quadratic scan plus N embeds/N inserts/N deletes in the blocking pool. Validate the batch size up front and use a `HashSet` for O(n) de-dup before any DB/embed work.

Resource leak in the rate-limit map: `LAST_EXTRACT_MS` is a process-global `HashMap<String, i64>` that is only ever `insert`-ed, never purged. Long-lived clients accumulate one entry per session_id forever (plus cloned `String` keys on every check), so memory grows unbounded with session churn. Periodically retain only recently-active entries (e.g. inside `throttle_check_set`, the same critical section already touched on every call).

`meta_upsert_model` maps every error from `upsert_model_user` into `CommandError::DomainRule`, including genuine `rusqlite::Error` values (SQLITE_BUSY, disk I/O, constraint failures) that `upsert_model_user` flattens via `.to_string()`. Downstream the frontend treats all of these as user-facing domain-rule errors, hiding infrastructure failures behind a misleading `meta: <rusqlite msg>`. Split the typed error inside `upsert_model_user` (or return `rusqlite::Error` for DB paths) so DB failures flow through `CommandError::from` and reserve `DomainRule` for the provider-missing check only.

`upsert_model_user` returns `Result<(), String>` while sibling `upsert_provider_user` / `upsert_provider_sync` / `upsert_model_sync` return `Result<(), rusqlite::Error>`. The String channel flattens both genuine DB errors (the `query_row` and `execute` paths use `.map_err(|e| e.to_string())`) and the domain check into one indistinguishable type, forcing callers like `meta_upsert_model` to either lose context or misclassify infrastructure errors as domain rules. Use a typed error (or `rusqlite::Error`) for DB paths and a separate domain signal.

The meta write-lock contract is enforced only via `debug_assert!`; in release builds the assertion compiles away, so any caller that forgets `crate::db::lock_db_write()` will not panic and concurrent writers can race (SQLITE_BUSY, torn transactions). Tighten the contract by minting a typed write-token that only the lock holder can produce and passing it into the upsert functions, or add a release-mode runtime check so the invariant is not purely a debug assertion.

comments.content: `list_providers`, `models_by_provider`, `list_models_joined`, `query_provider`, and `query_model_joined` rebuild the prepared statement string via `format!` on every invocation, but the templates only interpolate compile-time constants (`PROVIDER_COLS`, `MODEL_COLS`, `JOINED_SELECT`). Each call is on the request path (Tauri commands reachable from frontend refresh loops) and allocates a `String` for nothing. Hoist the formatted SQL into `const &str` (concatenation works because the column lists are already string literals) or use a `OnceLock`/`Lazy` prepared-statement cache.

`upsert_model_user` performs a `SELECT COUNT(*)` existence check followed by an `INSERT`/`UPSERT` without a transaction or row-level guard. Within a single SQLite connection the two statements are serialized so the command path (`meta_upsert_model`, which holds `lock_db_write`) is safe today — but any future caller that bypasses the lock (a background sync task, a migration script) will reintroduce a TOCTOU race where a concurrent provider delete between the count check and the insert leaves an orphan model. Wrap the `SELECT` + `INSERT` in `conn.transaction(...)` so the constraint is atomic, or rely on a `FOREIGN KEY` with `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON`.

Credential migration prerequisites are not enforced: the comment requires `migrate_bot_config_schema` to run before the secret-clearing migrations, but each step only logs on Err and unconditionally runs the next. If schema migration fails, the subsequent `migrate_legacy_key` / `migrate_search_keys` may rewrite an unmigrated config and lose credentials. Gate later migrations on the schema migration's success or have them refuse to operate when the schema version is missing.

Cleanup is not a global admission gate: `stop_all_executions` only flags already-registered entries, the API is stopped afterward, and `bot_py::mark_exiting()` is invoked last. New API/scheduler work accepted between snapshot and `mark_exiting` is not in the snapshot and can spawn after `wait_executions_drained` returns, then be killed mid-write. Establish a single `app_exiting` flag set at the very start of cleanup, gate every producer on it, and check it inside `wait_executions_drained`/`mark_exiting`.

Nonessential widget creation is fatal after services are already launched: `setup` registers API state, AppState, MCP, scheduler, trace sink, due notifier, DB pruning, memory, migration polling, meta sync, MCP reload, etc., before `WebviewWindowBuilder::build()?`. A widget build failure propagates out of `setup`, the later `expect` panics, and `cleanup_on_exit` never runs because `RunEvent::ExitRequested` is not emitted. Either move the widget build before background service starts, or downgrade widget failure to a logged warning like the tray/shortcut paths.

            .always_on_top(true)
            .skip_taskbar(true)
            .visible_on_all_workspaces(true)
            .resizable(false)
            .maximizable(false)
            .minimizable(false)

comments.content: Untrusted IPC path with no boundary validation: `copy_file_with_title` takes `path: String` straight from the frontend and forwards it to the native clipboard helper without canonicalization or scope checks here. Given the deliberate removal of frontend `opener:allow-open-path` (see the capability_tests comment about XSS and `$HOME/**`), the clipboard route must enforce that the path is bound to the calling task and resolve to an allowlisted root. Add a guard in this command or confirm the helper strictly rejects unbound paths.

Overlapping always-on-top timers race against each other: every call to `bring_main_to_front` spawns a new detached thread that unconditionally resets `always_on_top(false)` after 80 ms. A second activation within 80 ms of the first will see its topmost state cleared by the earlier thread. Track a generation/atomic counter per window and only let the most recent activation perform the reset, or store the handle to cancel prior resets.

16MB cap is enforced *after* the chunk is materialized. A single chunk larger than the cap (or many chunks each near-cap) is fully allocated before the check trips — OOM-by-network is still possible, defeating the comment's stated intent. Use `resp.take(MAX_BODY as u64)` (or `bytes_stream().take(...)`) so reqwest aborts reading once the cap is hit, and additionally reject any single chunk with `chunk.len() > MAX_BODY` to bound peak memory at roughly `2 * MAX_BODY`. The current `buf.len() + chunk.len() > MAX_BODY` check also can theoretically wrap on 32-bit targets if `chunk.len()` is large — `checked_add` or the `take()` approach removes that footgun.

`shared_llm_client()` is a process-wide static. Today it is constructed without default headers, but reusing the *same* client instance for unrelated third-party hosts (models.dev) couples two concerns: any future code that adds default `Authorization`/proxy/`Cookie` headers (intended for LLM providers) will silently leak them to a non-affiliated host. Construct a dedicated bare `reqwest::Client` for the models.dev fetch (or, at minimum, document the invariant that this client must remain header-free).

Cancellation-safety hole: after fetch+parse succeed the DB write is dispatched to `spawn_blocking` and only its `JoinHandle` is awaited. If the outer future is dropped (caller cancellation, manual-sync command timeout, app shutdown), the spawned thread still runs `apply_sync` to completion — the caller can no longer report success/failure, and shutdown may race with the in-flight write. Either run `apply_sync` synchronously after parse (no `spawn_blocking`), or hold the JoinHandle and ensure shutdown awaits outstanding syncs before closing the DB. Dropping a `Vec<MetaProvider>`/`Vec<MetaModel>` after parse but before commit also discards the work, so this is genuinely fire-and-forget today.

`lock_db_write()` is a process-wide `Mutex` (DB_WRITE_LOCK), confirmed in `db/mod.rs`. Holding it across every per-row upsert AND the transaction commit serializes **all** DB writes in the application (chat, history, planner state, …) for the full models.dev sync duration. With models.dev's thousands of models this can stall unrelated I/O for seconds. Consider committing in chunks (per provider or per N rows) and releasing the lock between chunks, or batch via multi-row UPSERT inside a single statement. The current design is also a test-isolation hazard: any parallel test that calls `apply_sync` (or anything that takes `lock_db_write`) will contend/serialize.

Every rusqlite error (transaction begin, per-row upsert, commit) is flattened via `e.to_string()`, dropping the error type and chain. Combined with the long-held write lock above and per-row upserts, diagnosing a mid-sync failure (e.g. constraint hit on one bad row out of thousands) becomes log spelunking. Propagate a typed error (`thiserror` enum or `anyhow::Error` with `#[source]`) that records which step and which key failed, so callers can surface actionable diagnostics.

comments.content: A raw substring match is not a safe execution trigger. Messages such as `不要执行这些任务` or `暂时别运行` contain the trigger words and will directly execute the referenced cards. It also matches unrelated words and attachment paths (`/tmp/logo.png` contains `go`, and `.docx` contains `do`) because ASCII keywords are not word-bounded. Since this result bypasses the LLM and invokes batch task execution, require an explicit command/structured trigger and reject negated or incidental matches.

This always prefers a Chinese comma even when the English comma is the actual field separator. For example, `id=abc, title=分析，汇总` is split at `，`, producing task ID `abc, title=分析` and title `汇总`; batch execution then fails to find the intended task. Select whichever separator occurs first so commas inside the title do not corrupt the ID.

The parser treats the entire remainder of the message as the selected-task block. Because titles are nested inside this line-oriented format and may themselves contain line breaks, a title such as `Review\n- id=other，标题=...` injects an additional task ID; quoted text or a second example block after the marker has the same effect. Those IDs are then executed without going through the LLM. Use an escaped/structured payload (or an explicit end delimiter) and reject unexpected trailing content instead of scanning every later `- id=` line.

The read guard remains alive while every installed regex is evaluated. A long user message or an expensive rule therefore holds the global `RwLock` for the full scan, delaying skill import/delete route rebuilds (and running CPU-bound work directly on the chat async path). Store an `Arc<Vec<CompiledRule>>` behind the lock and clone the small snapshot before dropping the guard.

comments.content: `decay_days` is a public `f64` with no validation. Zero produces `0.0/0.0 = NaN` for same-timestamp items (silently dropped by the `score > 0.0` filter); negative values invert the intended exponential decay and can overflow to `+inf`, letting a single item dominate ranking; `NaN`/`Inf` from upstream config corrupt every score. Either validate (`decay_days.is_finite() && decay_days > 0.0`) in `RankParams::of` or document and treat degenerate values explicitly (e.g. clamp the reciprocal).

`cosine(...).unwrap_or(0.0)` collapses every `None` to a legitimate zero similarity, while the later zero-match guard only checks `query_emb.is_none() || item.embedding.is_none()`. If `cosine` returns `None` for dimension mismatch, zero-norm vector, or non-finite embeddings (instead of "missing"), those items bypass the guard and can still receive positive `importance`/`recency` weights, breaking the documented "zero match → recent fallback" contract. Audit `cosine`'s `None` semantics and either widen the guard to mirror them or propagate the failure as a typed result.

comments.content: `(now_ms - base) as f64` performs a raw `i64` subtraction on two caller-supplied timestamps. Extreme or corrupted values from persistent storage can overflow: debug builds panic, release builds wrap and the subsequent `max(0.0)` cannot recover the original magnitude, yielding meaningless ages (and `exp` values). Use `checked_sub`/`saturating_sub` and decide on an explicit policy for invalid ages.

The pinned-exclusion scan is `O(items * pinned)` and every surviving candidate is `clone()`d (deep-copying `content`, `tags`, and the `Vec<f32>` `embedding`) into `scored` before top-N slicing, so embedding-heavy corpora incur large allocation/IO pressure on every retrieval. Build a `HashSet<&str>` of pinned IDs once and hold `&MemItem` references during scoring, cloning only the items that actually make it into `hits`/`recent`/`pinned`.

`hybrid_search_with` deep-clones every candidate `MemItem` (including the `Vec<f32>` embedding) before the `> 0.0` filter and `take(p.top_n)`. For large stores this is unnecessary work; hold references during scoring and clone only the items that survive into the returned `Vec`.

Module-level doc still describes injection as three stages (pinned → hits → recent), but the code (and `MemInjection`) adds a fourth `lessons` segment. Update the header to "注入四段" or otherwise reflect the actual contract so downstream formatters that build the `## 记忆` block don't omit lessons.

comments.content:
TOCTOU race: src.exists()/d.exists() is checked in the main loop, then db_load → db_upsert runs inside `tauri::async_runtime::block_on`. Between the filesystem check and the upsert, a concurrent move/delete (user action, another migration) can make the repair write a stale or now-incorrect file_path. The `file_path_untouched` guard inside recover_move_db only protects against DB changes, not on-disk state. Consider re-checking `dst.exists()` after `db_load` (or holding the path inside the same transaction window) before calling db_upsert.

(Severity is high because recovery is supposed to be the source of truth that converges inconsistent state; a stale write would silently corrupt DB-to-disk correspondence.)

`tauri::async_runtime::block_on` is used inside `recover_move_db`/`recover_delete_db`. The comment claims these are only ever called from `spawn_polling`'s std::thread so block_on is safe, but that contract is not enforced at this layer—`journal_replay_pending` is `pub` and any future caller (or refactor that moves it inside an async context, a #[tauri::command], or another spawn) will silently deadlock on the runtime thread. Either gate the call site explicitly (`#[track_caller]` + runtime assertion), split the async DB into sync variants for recovery, or restructure so the recovery runs inside a dedicated runtime.

Several recovery-branch DB writes silently swallow errors via `.ok()`: `journal_committed_inner(&conn, entry.id).ok()` and `journal_cleared_inner(&conn, entry.id).ok()`. A failure here leaves the row pending and the same entry will be re-processed on every startup. While the `file_path_untouched` guard makes move/delete replay idempotent, the failure is invisible (no log, no counter increment, no error) so it can't be diagnosed. At minimum, log a warning with the entry id and the underlying error so on-disk/journal divergence is observable.

Journal table trim uses `let _ = conn.execute(...)` which discards any rusqlite error. If this DELETE fails (lock contention, I/O, schema drift), the migration_journal table grows unbounded over time, eventually degrading startup scan performance and consuming disk. Log the error at least, and consider counting it in `errors` so callers see something is wrong.

`is_permanent_replay_error` classifies transient vs permanent failures via `e.contains("不存在")`. This is brittle: any change to the db error wording, localization, or wrapping (`anyhow!`, `thiserror` display strings) silently flips the classification and either loops forever on a permanent error or drops a recoverable pending row. Prefer a typed error variant (e.g., `MigrationError::TaskNotFound`) or an explicit error code mapped at the call site that returns it, and pattern-match on that instead of substring matching on a Chinese-language phrase.

Doc comment for `purge_orphan_pending` says `含 committed 共存的 pending 不动`, but the SQL and `purge_orphan_pending_leaves_committed_coexistence` test both show orphan pending rows ARE deleted when committed coexists (only the committed row is preserved). The doc wording suggests pending is left untouched in that case, which is misleading. Rephrase to clarify the contract: `committed rows are preserved; among multiple pending rows for the same (task_id, src), only the latest id is kept regardless of committed coexistence`.

Top-of-file doc comments start with `//! : 启动时` and `//! : 修复前必须确认任务 file_path 仍指向 src`—leading `:` with no label, looks like a stray punctuation/typo at the start of the doc line. Either remove the leading `:` or replace with the intended label/section title.

`recover_move_db` / `recover_delete_db` both call `db::db_load(app)` which loads every task, then do an O(n) `.find(|x| x.id == task_id)`. Not a hot path concern (startup only, low cardinality), but combined with the subsequent `db_upsert(vec![t])` that overwrites a single row, this is a wide hammer for a single-row fix. If `db_load` becomes expensive later, expose a `db_get(task_id)` to avoid pulling the full table on every replay entry. Worth a TODO or note.

The last assertion references `&rf` but this function defines the variable as `bad`, not `rf`. There is no `rf` in scope here — `rf` is defined only in unrelated tests (e.g., `validate_rules_accepts_delete_without_archive_dir`). This is a hard compile error: no test in `migration::tests` can run until this is fixed. Replace `&rf` with `&bad`.

This race-handling test is sequential, not concurrent. It manually simulates a race by calling `conflict_free_name`, then writing a file to occupy that name, then calling `claim_dst_name` — which only proves `claim_dst_name` increments when its target is already taken. It does not exercise the actual concurrent race window inside `claim_dst_name` (two threads select the same name before either writes). On heavily loaded CI machines the test can still pass even if `claim_dst_name`'s re-check is removed, because there is no real overlap. Use `std::thread::spawn` (or `tokio::spawn`) to run two parallel claimers against the same target name so the race window in `claim_dst_name` itself is actually exercised.

The 50ms `thread::sleep` meant to ensure the holder thread acquires the lock first is racy. Under scheduler pressure the holder can be delayed past 50ms, letting the main thread win the lock race; in that case main's three writes complete in a few ms and `waited >= 100ms` fails spuriously — or worse, the assertion would pass without ever proving that writes actually block on `db_write_lock`. Replace the sleep with explicit synchronization: have the holder signal (e.g., via a `std::sync::mpsc::Sender` or `AtomicBool` after acquiring the guard) and have the main thread block on that signal before starting its timer and writes.

comments.content: The test name `move_entry_file_conflict_names_dir` and its Chinese doc comment claim that `move_entry` applies conflict-resolution naming to directories, but the body only calls `conflict_free_name` on a directory name and never invokes `move_entry` against a pre-existing directory of the same name on the destination. As written this only verifies `conflict_free_name`'s directory-name handling, not `move_entry`'s. Either rename the test to reflect what it actually exercises (e.g., `conflict_free_name_handles_directory_name`) or extend it to call `move_entry` with a conflicting directory already on the destination and assert the resulting suffix path.

The victim DELETE runs in a separate statement before the INSERT, so an INSERT error irreversibly loses the evicted row; also removing only one row per insert never converges when the table already exceeds a lowered capacity (e.g. after tuning capacity is reduced). Wrap the count/victim selection, DELETE, and INSERT in a single transaction and trim down to capacity when needed.

Writers accept embeddings of any dimension, with NaN/Inf components, and zero vectors without validation, even though blob_to_embedding rejects malformed blobs on read. Such vectors are persisted and later returned by load_all, silently breaking semantic dedup (cosine returns None) and retrieval while the insert call reports success. Validate length == EMBED_DIM, finiteness, and non‑zero norm at the shared write boundary.

comments.content: Tags are trimmed only when loaded (see the split('.')/trim chain in item_from_row), but no normalization is performed on write. Consequently a lesson key such as " evo:x" does not start with "evo:" when checked in insert_item_with, allowing a foreign merge into a non‑evo row; after the write the persisted tag is read as "evo:x", defeating the foreign‑merge guard and breaking exact‑key identity for remember_fact. Trim/canonicalise tags at the write boundary and reject empty or whitespace‑only tags.

touch_accessed executes one UPDATE per id in a loop and returns Err on the first failure, leaving the caller's view of the table inconsistent with what was actually applied (some access_count values were incremented, some not). Retrying after a partial failure would double‑count the IDs that already succeeded. Wrap the batch in a transaction or use a single multi‑row UPDATE.

oldest_by_kind swallows per‑row SQLite/decode errors via filter_map(|r| r.ok()), so a corrupted row or schema mismatch is silently omitted from the returned list. Reflection logic will then operate on an incomplete set without surfacing the corruption. Propagate the Result so callers can react.

comments.content: JournalEntry cannot round-trip through the on-disk journal it is supposed to enable. The doc comment above explicitly states this table is replayed at startup to repair the DB after a crash, but the struct only derives `Debug, Clone` — no `Serialize`/`Deserialize`. Without these derives the journal rows cannot be persisted by `serde_json`/`bincode`/`rmp_serde` (whichever the migration layer uses), so the very lost-update/孤儿-file scenario this struct exists to prevent is the one that cannot be recovered. Add `Serialize, Deserialize` (and a `#[serde(rename_all = ...)]` if a stable on-disk schema matters).

comments.content: Two parallel `String` "enum" fields at critical data-integrity boundaries. `JournalEntry.op` and `MigrationRule.action` are both `String` with the allowed variants spelled out only in a comment (`'move' | 'delete'` / `"move" | "delete"`). This makes invalid states representable and forces every consumer (replay, apply, reporting) to re-parse and re-validate the same string. Model them as `enum JournalOp { Move, Delete }` and `enum RuleAction { Move, Delete }` (with `#[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")]`) so an unknown variant fails fast at the (de)serialize boundary and the rest of the code can exhaustively `match` without `unwrap`/default branches.

comments.content: Stray/garbled punctuation in the `cancelled` field doc comment: `（；仅 Serialize` opens with a fullwidth parenthesis `（` immediately followed by a Chinese semicolon `；`. This is a leftover from editing and obscures the documented invariant about the field always being serialized. Replace with normal punctuation, e.g. `(仅 Serialize; ...)`, so the contract that the field is always emitted in the JSON payload is unambiguous to future readers and to any frontend tooling that depends on it.

TOCTOU between resolve and create/verify: resolve_archive_dir_checked only canonicalizes the deepest *existing* ancestor; the residual window between this return and the subsequent create_dir_all (or verify_archive_dir_created) allows a concurrent symlink swap to redirect the archive outside the desktop base. The inline comment defers this to a Phase-6 follow-up, but in the meantime any caller that creates the resolved dir before the verify is exposed to a real path-escape. Consider performing create_dir_all *before* the verify (and re-checking), or hard-link the verify back into resolve so the caller cannot act on a stale result.

claim_dst_name → move_entry TOCTOU with cross-platform overwrite risk: claim_dst_name picks a non-existing name, but the actual fs::rename/fs::copy inside move_entry can race another worker that wins the same slot; fs::copy silently overwrites on Unix when the dst was created in the window, so the documented 99-iteration protection does not prevent data loss — only prevents a livelock. Either open dst with O_EXCL|O_CREAT (Unix) and treat AlreadyExists as retry, or place each move under a staging sibling like copy_dir_recursive does, so the final commit is an atomic rename.

MOVE_REMOVE_FAILS HashMap grows without bound: record_move_remove_failure inserts a String key per failed src and never evicts. Over a long-running app, the map accumulates one entry per unique src that hits the cap, contradicting the documented "restart clears count" expectation and leaking memory proportional to total distinct failed sources. Add a bounded LRU/TTL (or at least remove the entry once a copy-then-remove finally succeeds) and consider keying by a normalized hash when paths are long.

Staging sibling reused without pre-check in copy_dir_recursive: '{name}.copying' is not inspected or cleared before copy_dir_recursive_into runs, so a leftover from a prior aborted run is reused; cross-platform differences then matter — fs::rename atomically replaces an existing dst on Unix but errors on Windows, and fs::copy overwrites existing files on Unix but fails on Windows. Combined with create_dir_all being idempotent, this can produce inconsistent partial-copy behavior across platforms and silently clobber a leftover .copying directory. Probe for an existing staging (refuse or fs::remove_dir_all first) before writing, and use an OpenOptions/create_new pattern for individual files to make behavior portable.

Silent error swallowing in log_line and emit_upserts hides the migration audit trail: both use `let _ = ...` to discard fs::OpenOptions/writeln and app.emit_to results. When the log directory is unwritable or the main window is gone, every migration entry simply disappears and operators have no signal — directly defeating the journal that the surrounding code is built around. At minimum log to eprintln on failure, and consider returning Result from these helpers so the caller (the migration engine) can record the failure in the journal.

The derived `Deserialize` only accepts the exact lowercase variants, but the doc comment at the top describes a `Widget/未标记` fallback — i.e. missing or unrecognized source values should be classified as `Widget`. With this derive, any incoming event whose `source` is absent or contains an unknown string will fail to deserialize into `MutationOrigin`, so the documented fallback must be implemented at the call site (e.g. `Option<MutationOrigin>` with a custom mapping). That contract is not enforced by the type system; consider `#[serde(other)]` on `Widget`, or a separate wrapper enum, to make the fallback explicit and impossible to forget.

comments.content: The hand-written `as_str` duplicates the lowercase mapping already declared via `#[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")]`. Adding a new variant now requires touching three places — the enum, this match, and `src/lib/mutationOrigin.ts` — and only the compile error on the missing match arm protects against drift on the Rust side. The test mitigates this, but consider deriving `Display` (or just using `serde_plain` / a single source of truth) so the protocol string is defined once.

The test verifies that `as_str` matches `serde_json::to_value` for each variant, but it does not exercise deserialization at all. Given that this enum gates persistence routing (`Bot/Api/Migration` skip the SQLite write, everything else writes), a malformed or unexpected `source` value silently mis-routing data is a high-impact risk. Add a deserialization round-trip (each lowercase string → correct variant) and, once the missing/unknown fallback discussed above is settled, an explicit test for that fallback so the contract can't regress.

Each `tauri::async_runtime::block_on` creates a brand-new tokio runtime and tears it down on return; the comment above promises every caller goes through `spawn_blocking` or `std::thread`, but that invariant lives entirely in call-site discipline. The moment a future maintainer wires a UI command as `async fn` and awaits `run_migration` directly on a tokio worker thread, `block_on` will deadlock that worker and starve the runtime. Prefer making `run_migration_inner` `async` (and letting callers `.await` it) or move all DB I/O onto a dedicated blocking thread that owns its own runtime, instead of relying on a fragile "never call me from a tokio thread" contract.

comments.content: `journal_cleared` and `journal_committed` are the only thing closing the loop between filesystem state and DB state — discarding their errors with `.ok()` means a wedged journal row is silently ignored. On the next start, `journal_replay_pending` will re-attempt the move/delete: if the original move actually succeeded, replay will see src gone + dst present and re-issue the DB fix (wasted work); if the original move/delete failed and `journal_cleared` was the cleanup that didn't happen, every subsequent run repeats the same failing operation and can stack up duplicate copies in the archive dir. Log the failure (and/or surface a counter on `report`) so an operator can see "5 journal commits failed this run" instead of a forever-spinning recovery.

comments.content: `AssertUnwindSafe(|| run_migration(&app))` asserts the closure is unwind-safe, but `run_migration` opens a DB connection, writes journal rows, performs filesystem I/O, and holds a `MigrationGuard`/`CancelGuard`. Drop of those guards will run during unwinding (and that's the point), but the partial filesystem/DB/journal mutations are not transactional: e.g. a panic between `move_entry` succeeding and `db_upsert` leaving the journal pending is fine, but a panic inside `tauri::async_runtime::block_on` after the `db_upsert` future has begun executing leaves the connection state and runtime in an unspecified condition. The intent ("single round crash only kills this round") is reasonable, but it should be documented in terms of concrete invariants (which invariants the journal *does* and *does not* protect against unwinding), or the loop should propagate `Result` and restart on transient errors instead of catching panics.

comments.content: Classic TOCTOU: `src.exists()` gates the journal-recovery branch and the subsequent `journal_pending` + `move_entry`/`fs::remove_*`. The file can vanish between the check and the operation, causing the move to fail and the `move_remove_permanently_failed` counter to increment for what is actually a benign race (the file was just deleted by the user/cleanup tool between the snapshot read and the loop reaching this task). Once that counter reaches `MAX_MOVE_REMOVE_FAILURES`, the task is permanently skipped — silently losing the user's data because of a transient race. Re-check `src.exists()` immediately before `move_entry`/`remove_*` and treat "vanished between check and act" as a benign Unbind rather than a remove-failure.

comments.content: Every async DB and journal call converts a structured error to a bare string with `.map_err(|e| e.to_string())`, then `?` propagates the string. At minimum attach `context` (e.g. `format!("db_load failed: {e:#}")` with `{:#}` to render the chain) before downcasting; ideally propagate `CommandError` variants so the UI can render structured diagnostics instead of opaque strings.

comments.content: Privacy invariant is "识别绝不上传外网" but the prefix check covers only `http://`, `https://`, and `data:`. `file://` URLs and Windows UNC paths (`\\server\share\file.png`) pass through to `resolve_with_perm`, whose `canonicalize` on Windows will attempt an SMB resolution of the UNC host — silently contradicting the no-network guarantee. Either block UNC/`file:` explicitly (e.g., also reject `\\` prefixes and `file:`/`ftp:`/etc. schemes) or document that UNC is in scope and gate it via the permission prompt path.

Both `audit_log` calls discard the return value with no `?`, `.ok()`, or match. If `audit_log` returns `Result`, logging failures (disk full, log file locked, audit subsystem down) are silently dropped, which can defeat the very audit guarantee the module relies on. Either propagate / log+ignore explicitly, or assert/document that `audit_log` is infallible.

Tautological test: the assertions only check that the hard-coded input strings match the same prefix predicates used in the production check — a regression that removes the network-rejection branch, expands the accepted scheme list, or moves the logic elsewhere would still pass. Extract the predicate (e.g., `fn is_network_uri(s: &str) -> bool`) and assert against it, or build a thin wrapper that doesn't require `AppHandle` and call `tool_ocr_image`-equivalent logic end-to-end.

SAFETY comment is hand-wavy: it asserts that `NSPasteboardTypeString` is a stable Foundation global with no aliasing risk, but does not verify the actual `objc2_app_kit` declaration's lifetime. If that constant is exposed as `*const NSString` without an explicit `'static` lifetime (which is how several objc2_app_kit string constants are declared), the reborrow inside the `unsafe { ... }` extends a borrow past the actual lifetime of the static storage, which is unsound. comments.content: Result type asymmetry between the two platform helpers is a real API-design hazard, not just a documentation note: `copy_file_macos` returns `Result<(), String>` while `copy_file_windows` returns `Result<(), CommandError>`. This forces the caller (`copy_file_with_title`, presumably) to bridge macOS errors via `From<String>`, lose the `DomainRule { domain: "clipboard", ... }` shape on macOS, and to maintain a hand-written conversion that is exactly the kind of place where a future upgrade to typed errors will silently regress. Either promote macOS to return `CommandError` directly (and update the test referenced in the doc comment) or introduce a small shared `enum ClipboardError { Domain(...), AppleScript(...), Other(String) }` that both helpers return.

The three failure branches after `SetClipboardData(CF_HDROP, ...)` has committed (title `GlobalAlloc` failure, title `GlobalLock` null, title `SetClipboardData` failure) each independently have to remember to (a) `GlobalFree` the title handle on the title-handle paths, (b) `EmptyClipboard` so the clipboard does not silently retain a stale file, and (c) `CloseClipboard` so subsequent `OpenClipboard` calls do not stall. Today all three paths do this correctly, but the invariants are spread across three near-identical match arms with no shared helper — one missed `EmptyClipboard` would re-introduce the "user sees 'copy failed' yet paste still delivers the file" bug that the surrounding `//  #4` and `//  #119` comments specifically call out as historical regressions. Extracting a small `fn finalize_post_hdrop(th: Option<HGLOBAL>)` would localize the invariant and make regressions much harder.

The `+2` bytes in `total` and the trailing `*dst.add(file_wide.len()) = 0` write below are a tightly coupled pair: `file_wide` already contains its own NUL terminator (from `encode_wide().chain(Some(0))`), so the extra `+2` exists solely to hold the *second* NUL that DROPFILES requires (`pFiles` points at a double-NUL-terminated list). The two sites are not commented together and look unrelated — a future edit that, say, drops the `+2` to "match file_wide exactly" would silently produce an unterminated file list (Explorer / drag-receivers may treat it as a single truncated filename) or, conversely, removes the trailing `= 0` line would create a 2-byte heap overrun past the GMEM_MOVEABLE buffer. Add a one-line comment next to `total` explaining "the +2 reserves the second NUL written at `dst.add(file_wide.len())` below", or compute `total` as `size_of::<DROPFILES>() + (file_wide.len() + 1) * 2` to make the second NUL explicit.

comments.content: Cross-key semantic merge overwrites `content` and the full `tags` list, destroying the original key reference (only surfaced via `orig_key`). A semantically-similar write with a different key can silently replace a distinct fact without any source/trust guard. Consider adding a same-key requirement (or stricter source/kind checks) before merge, or at minimum asserting that the target's key can still be looked up after merge.

Near-threshold refusal test only asserts `len == 1` and the outcome variant. It does NOT verify the target row's `content`/`tags` are unchanged. If the implementation performed the merge UPDATE before refusing, the row count stays 1 but the target is silently corrupted and the test would still pass. Add `content` and `tags` assertions on the surviving row.

Test named `degraded_full_flow_keyword_only_no_panic` claims to exercise the keyword-only flow, but the query `"晚餐吃什么"` shares no CJK bigrams with either stored item, so `hit_ids` is always empty and `touch_accessed` is a no-op. The keyword-search branch in degraded mode is therefore never actually exercised. Use a query that shares bigrams with at least one item and assert that `hit_ids` is non-empty and that `touch_accessed` increments `access_count` for the hit.

`capacity_eviction_order_and_protection` picks an arbitrary `load_all()[0].id` to promote to protected, then only asserts row count and that this ID survives. It never asserts (a) the newly inserted memory is actually persisted, (b) which specific row was evicted, or (c) that no other row was mutated. Use a deterministic identifier (e.g. capture id via the `InsertOutcome::Inserted` arm), assert the new row is present after eviction, and assert the expected victim (e.g. oldest non-protected) is gone.

`hybrid_score_mixed_mode_guards_vectorless_items` locks in behavior where a vector-backed item with cosine 0 to the query scores above zero purely from importance/recency constants. This means an unrelated memory with high importance/recency can still occupy top-N results whenever the query has an embedding. The test explicitly says the guard does not apply when `embedding.is_some()`; this is a design decision worth re-examining — enforce a relevance floor for vector-present queries or document this as intentional.

FAIL-OPEN after deserialization: load_rules_from returns the deserialized RulesFile without calling validate_rules, so a persisted rule with action == "move" and an empty archiveDir passes load but `resolve_archive_dir` at runtime resolves the empty string to the desktop base directory — destructive files move to the wrong place. Additionally, RulesFile.version is read from the file but never compared against the supported version (currently 1); a future format with incompatible semantics would be silently accepted and acted on. Call validate_rules(&r)? after deserialization (mapping the validation error to CommandError::DomainRule) and reject unsupported versions before returning.

Concurrent save race: there is no locking around the load → mutate → save cycle, and db::atomic_write writes to a fixed sibling tmp path (`<name>.tmp`). Two concurrent save_rules calls can interleave so that one writer's rename succeeds with the other writer's bytes (false Ok response) while the loser fails because its tmp is gone (false Err); user-authored rules can be silently overwritten. Wrap the RMW pair in a process-level mutex or OS file lock so that the read–modify–write cycle is serialized; pairing this with the load-side fix in load_rules_from closes the integrity gap end-to-end.

Change the signature to Result<(), CommandError> and build CommandError::DomainRule { domain: "migration".to_string(), reason: ... } at each return Err site.

comments.content: Misleading IO error hint: the message hard-codes "请检查文件权限" for every non-NotFound IO error, but the error could be InvalidData (encoding/UTF-8 corruption), IsADirectory, file locked by another process, etc. Tailor the hint to the actual std::io::ErrorKind (e.g., InvalidData → "文件编码损坏"; IsADirectory → "目标路径是目录"; PermissionDenied → keep the permission hint) so users aren't sent to fix the wrong thing.

Asymmetric contract for delete actions: validate_rules only requires non-empty archive_dir for action == "move", so a delete rule with a relative archive_dir (e.g., "归档/旧文件") passes validation — but parse_rules_csv explicitly rejects the same shape (see the "第 N 行动作是「删除文件」，归档目录列必须留空" branch). Defense-in-depth: save_rules_to is pub(crate) and trusts the caller to have validated. The current call site in commands.rs does validate first, but any future internal use that forgets to call validate_rules will persist unchecked rules — and the function's Result<(), String> return type gives no opportunity to surface a structured error. Re-run validate_rules here (returning CommandError::DomainRule) so the persistence boundary is self-defending and the error type matches the rest of the module.

`OpenOptions::create(true).append(true)` on Unix does NOT set 0600 — the new file is created with mode `0666 & ~umask` (typically 0644), directly contradicting the comment "创建即 0600（与 audit::open_log_append 一致）" and `audit::open_log_append` (which explicitly chmods the freshly-created file to 0o600, per src-tauri/src/audit.rs:343). Concrete impact: the fallback `bot.log` here ends up world-readable while audit-created `bot.log` is owner-only; if both writers ever race (this file is opened without `BOT_LOG_LOCK` from a detached thread, while audit opens under the lock), the file ends up owned by this function's process but readable by all users, leaking `exe_dir`/`resolved` path info. Either set the mode explicitly (`OpenOptions::new().create(true).append(true).mode(0o600)` on Unix, or call `set_permissions(0o600)` after open — matching audit's pattern), or drop the comment claim. Also consider whether existing pre-existing files should be chmod'd on each write (audit does this on first open); at minimum, also chmod if `metadata().mode() != 0o600` so existing files from older, non-0600-aware runs get tightened.

`break` on `create_dir_all(flags)` failure abandons every remaining `LEGACY_ROOT_RUNTIME_FILES` entry for this run, contradicting the documented intent "单文件失败 → 保留原位下次启动再试，不影响其余文件" (read as: each file is independent, other files should still be processed this run if their preconditions hold). Today, a transient permission flake on `flags` directory creation on the first iteration skips all later legacy files — they only get a chance next launch. `continue` would at least let independent files still be attempted (and the `create_dir_all` re-attempt is essentially free once the directory exists). Even better: factor the dir-creation out so a one-time failure doesn't gate per-file work.

The canonicalize fallback is asymmetric and can silently break the documented "safe side (over-detect temp)" guarantee. The doc claims that if either side fails to canonicalize, comparing the two raw paths errs on the side of "in temp" — but that's only true when both fall back to raw-vs-raw. If `tmp` canonicalizes but `dir` does not, `tmp_canon` is the resolved path (e.g. `/private/var/folders/...`) and `dir` is the unresolved input (e.g. `/var/folders/...`); `dir_canon.starts_with(&tmp_canon)` becomes false (raw `/var/...` does not start with canonical `/private/var/...`), and the second clause `dir.starts_with(&tmp)` is also false because `tmp` was canonicalized. Net: an exe genuinely under temp gets classified as NOT in temp and the probe-write branch is entered against a possibly non-writable temp location. To preserve the "safe side" invariant, fall back to comparing BOTH raw vs BOTH canonical, never mixed: e.g. always canonicalize both, and on any canonicalize failure use `dir.to_path_buf().starts_with(&tmp)` (raw-vs-raw only) so the safe-side comparison is uniform.

`escape_for_log_inline` is a hand-duplicated copy of `audit::escape_for_log` whose only in-file test is `escape_for_log_inline_strips_newline_and_pipe` (three trivial inputs: `"a\nb"`, `"a| b"`, `"clean"`). The contract claims byte-level parity with `audit::escape_for_log` — covering `\n`, `\r`, `|`, `| `, U+2028/2029, and `is_control()` via `escape_default()` — but the parity lock is one-sided: changes to `audit::escape_for_log` (e.g. truncating by `chars().take(max)` first, or adding U+0000/NUL handling) will silently desync this copy, and the only safety net is a downstream log-viewer noticing broken rows. Add (a) a parity test that feeds a representative matrix of inputs (control chars, U+2028/2029, mixed pipe/space, empty, very long) to both functions and asserts `==`, and (b) at minimum a quick sanity test covering `\r` and U+2028/2029 here, since the inline escape is the only thing standing between a malicious or weird `exe_dir` / `resolved` / `reason` and a corrupted `bot.log` row.

`is_macos_app_bundle_dir` uses `ends_with(".app")` (case-sensitive ASCII) on `to_string_lossy()` of a single path component. Two failure modes: (1) a bundle named `Foo.APP` (uppercase suffix, legal on case-insensitive APFS) is not detected as a `.app` bundle, so the portable branch is wrongly entered for a writable app-bundle interior — DB / log / AI_Gen_Files land inside the app and are wiped when the user deletes the app; (2) on a path with non-UTF8 bytes the `to_string_lossy()` conversion can produce a `…` placeholder in the bundle-name component, so `ends_with(".app")` returns false for a legitimate bundle whose name happens to contain invalid UTF-8 (rare but real). Both edges are silently mishandled because the fallback for "not a bundle" is "use this dir as portable data root", which is exactly the destructive case the function exists to prevent. Use `c.as_os_str().eq_ignore_ascii_case(".app")` (or a manual suffix check against the raw `OsStr` bytes) so case doesn't matter and lossy conversion isn't involved.

The fallback-WARN thread spawned in `probe_log_dir` is detached: `std::thread::spawn(move || …)` discards the `JoinHandle`, and the surrounding code does not join it. The whole reason for offloading to a thread (per the comment) is to avoid holding `BOT_LOG_LOCK` while writing — but the trade-off is that `write_fallback_warn` runs unsupervised. Two real consequences: (1) if the process exits within milliseconds of the first probe (the very scenario most likely to produce this WARN — Tauri startup failure, panic during init, immediate shutdown due to data-dir permission denied), the thread is terminated mid-write and the WARN is lost — which is the diagnostic event operators most want to see; (2) the in-flight open()/writeln! is unbounded I/O against the user FS with no timeout. Either hold the JoinHandle and `.join()` near process shutdown (e.g. register with a global registry, or use a `Drop` on a static that joins), or at minimum document the accepted loss in the function's public contract so it doesn't pretend to be reliable telemetry.

Schema example is inconsistent between the two prompts and leaves step element shape implicit. PLANNER_PROMPT shows concrete string array elements (`"步骤1", "步骤2"`), but REPLANNER_PROMPT only shows bare `[...]` ellipsis. This asymmetry makes it easy for the model to drift between the first-plan and replan calls (e.g. emit objects in one and strings in the other), forcing the downstream JSON parser to handle multiple shapes. Tighten REPLANNER_PROMPT to mirror the concrete example and explicitly state the element type.

Storing src/dst via `Path::to_string_lossy()` collapses any non‑UTF‑8 byte sequence to U+FFFD, so two distinct filesystem paths that only differ by invalid UTF‑8 bytes map to the same SQLite TEXT value. The journal is later queried by (task_id, src) during replay, so colliding entries will silently overwrite each other and recovery may operate on the wrong file. Validate that paths are valid UTF‑8 before writing, or store a lossless representation (e.g. escaped OsString) and reject non‑UTF‑8 paths outright.

The INSERT into migration_journal reuses `src.to_string_lossy()` for the src column; the same lossy conversion issue applies here. Combined with the SELECT above, a non‑UTF‑8 src path is silently mangled both when written and when read, masking duplicate entries. Use the validated UTF‑8 string from above (`src_s`) instead of calling `to_string_lossy()` again.

`journal_committed_inner` updates the state without checking that the row is currently `pending`, so a stale id (or a row that was already cleared) is silently flipped to `committed`. This breaks the pending→committed/cleared state machine and can resurrect rows whose underlying file operation never happened, causing replay to act on a ghost entry. Add the `state = 'pending'` predicate and verify rows_affected so callers see a hard error on stale ids.

`journal_cleared_inner` has the same state‑machine gap as `journal_committed_inner`: the UPDATE accepts any id and silently flips a row that may already be `committed` (or another non‑pending state) back to `cleared`, destroying evidence of a completed operation. Restrict the transition to pending and surface a typed error when no row was updated.

Every call to `journal_pending_inner` and `journal_find_pending_inner` performs a full scan of `migration_journal` because there is no index covering `(task_id, src, state)`. Cleared/committed rows are never deleted, so the table grows monotonically and the `ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1` plan still has to visit the whole result set. Add an index in the schema migration (e.g. `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_migration_journal_task_src_state ON migration_journal(task_id, src, state);`) so the SELECT can stop at the first matching row.
