The rest of the crate uses that marker as a debug_assert that the global lock is held; `journal_*_inner` relies on the documented contract that the caller holds the lock, but nothing enforces it at runtime and the poison‑recovery log here lives outside the central audit path. Delegate to `crate::db::lock_db_write()` (it returns the same non‑reentrant guard, so the anti‑deadlock comment still applies) or add a `debug_assert!(crate::db::holding_db_write())` here to keep the contract honest.

The MI‑04a dedup relies on `journal_pending` holding `db_write_lock`, but `journal_pending_inner` is `pub(crate)` and is also called directly from unit tests (which do not acquire the lock). A future caller that forgets the lock will reintroduce the orphan‑entry bug the fix was meant to prevent. Either enforce the invariant at the database level with a partial unique index (e.g. `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_migration_journal_pending_task_src ON migration_journal(task_id, src) WHERE state = 'pending';`) and wrap the SELECT+INSERT/UPDATE in a single SQLite transaction, so the engine — not the caller's lock discipline — guarantees at most one pending row per (task_id, src).

comments.content: `migration_cancel() -> bool` 永远返回 `true`，但上方 doc comment 明确区分了三种状态：『命中当前 run 检查点（已取消在跑的迁移）』/『无 run 时置位留存给下一轮』/『标志已置位（重复请求）』。返回 bool 把这层状态抹平了，未来接线的取消 UI 无法区分『已中断在跑任务』与『无任务被取消、只置了标志』。建议改成 `enum MigrationCancelOutcome { InterruptActiveRun, LatchedForNextRun, AlreadyPending }`，并更新 doc comment；同步保留 `#[tauri::command]` 序列化兼容（serde 标签化即可）。

The two constants duplicate the entire instruction body and differ only in the hardcoded character cap (200 vs 300). The module doc warns that edits must be kept in sync, but the structure itself invites silent drift: any wording change to SUMMARY_SYSTEM_PROMPT (e.g. rephrasing "保留：任务相关决定、用户偏好、…") that is not mirrored in COMPACT_SYSTEM_PROMPT will change one prompt's behavior without any compiler signal. Consider deriving both from a single shared template (e.g. a `format!("…{limit}…", limit = N)` or a `const fn build_summary_prompt(limit: u16)` helper) and exposing only the two length-specific `pub(crate) const`s, so the instruction body lives in exactly one place.

The literal `17` in `assert_eq!(ALL.len(), 17, ...)` is a manual sync point that must be incremented whenever a new prompt constant is added to `ALL`. The test catches drift only after the fact; a developer who adds to `ALL` without updating `17` (or vice versa) gets a test failure rather than a compile-time signal. Consider deriving the count from `pub(crate) use` re-exports or making the count assertion a no-op (the `for` loop already enforces the per-entry invariants; the explicit length check is redundant for catching missing registrations since each test that references a missing name fails to compile).

Severity: low — this is the intended belt-and-suspenders pattern, but the magic number duplicates information already encoded in the `ALL` array and the `pub(crate) use` lines.

comments.content:
The hardcoded tool-name anchors (`create_task`, `query_tasks`, `complete_task`, `link_file_to_task`, `web_search`, `AI_Gen_Files`) create a brittle string-level coupling to the tool registry that has no compile-time link. If the tool registry renames any of these (e.g., `complete_task` → `finish_task`), the test fails with an opaque "缺锚点" message rather than pointing to the registry definition. Consider factoring tool names into `pub(crate) const`s in a shared module (e.g., `crate::tools::NAMES`) and asserting `SYSTEM_PROMPT.contains(crate::tools::COMPLETE_TASK)` so a rename on one side produces a compile error referencing the other side. Same pattern applies to `execute_prompt_keeps_task_card_contract`.

Severity: medium — this is the only mechanism preventing silent prompt/registry divergence, but a rename produces a low-signal test failure.

Word-budget thresholds `"200 字"` and `"300 字"` are design contracts encoded as raw Chinese substring literals. A trivial formatting change in either the prompt or the assertion (e.g., `200字` vs `200 字`, `≤200 字`, `~200 字`, full-width `２００`) breaks the contract with an opaque message. Since both halves are owned by this crate, extract the budgets to named constants (e.g., `const SUMMARY_BUDGET: usize = 200;`) and assert `SUMMARY_SYSTEM_PROMPT.contains(&format!("{SUMMARY_BUDGET} 字"))` so the threshold is single-sourced and a unit change ripples correctly. The `p.chars().count() >= 30` heuristic in `all_prompts_are_registered_and_non_empty` has the same shape — it is a magic threshold without a named constant.

Severity: low — these are intentional substring checks, but the magic numbers and string formats are duplicated between prompt content and assertion.

The `STEPWISE_ADDENDUM` priority rule is enforced only by a substring check for `"以本段为准"`, while the actual concatenation order (STEPWISE is appended after EXECUTE) lives in a caller outside this file. There is no type-level or structural guarantee that (a) STEPWISE is concatenated *after* EXECUTE rather than before, or (b) the priority sentence survives a translation/rewrite. If the call site reorders the concatenation, the test here still passes. Consider either (a) co-locating the concatenation logic in this module behind a single `pub(crate) fn execute_full_prompt() -> &'static str` so ordering is structural, or (b) adding a test that exercises the real concatenation path used at the call site.

Severity: low — the doc-comment on the test makes the intent clear, but the contract is enforced at two different layers (content here, order elsewhere) with no link between them.

Mutex poison is swallowed and the lock is salvaged via `e.into_inner()`, then execution continues as if nothing happened. If a previous thread panicked mid-write, the log file can be in an inconsistent state (partial line, missing flush, half-rotated file) yet subsequent audit entries will be appended on top of that corruption. For an audit/security log this is a data-integrity hazard — at minimum, log the poisoning to the audit log itself (or to a fallback sink) before recovering, and consider failing the write so the caller knows the audit line was not durably recorded.

Both filesystem failures are silently dropped: `if let Ok(mut f) = open_log_append(path)` discards the open error, and `let _ = writeln!(f, "[{ts}] {safe}")` discards the write/flush error. For a security/audit trail this is a real data-loss bug — an audit line that fails to open or fails to flush vanishes with no signal to the caller and no fallback record. Surface the error (at least propagate a `Result`, or write a fallback entry to a secondary sink / `eprintln!` with structured context) instead of unconditionally returning `()`.

`BOT_LOG_LOCK` is held across `rotate_log_if_large` (which may copy up to 5 MB), the file open, `chrono::Local::now().format(...)` formatting, sanitization, and the write. Any blocking step in this sequence — especially rotation I/O — blocks every other audit-logging thread in the process and widens the window where a panic can poison the lock. Consider scoping the guard tightly around just the open+write critical section, performing rotation either before taking the lock (with its own file lock) or under a separate `rotate_lock`, so unrelated loggers are not serialized behind a worst-case 5 MB copy.

Audit-log sanitization is borrowed from `crate::api_handlers::ratelimit::sanitize_log_line`, coupling a security-critical audit invariant to an unrelated rate-limit helper. A future change to that module (relaxed escaping, different default, removal) would silently weaken or remove log-injection defense for the audit trail. Move `sanitize_log_line` into a shared `audit` / `log_sanitize` module (or duplicate the function here) so the audit path owns its own escaping policy independent of HTTP access logging.

comments.content: Tests assert semantic anchors as exact Chinese-language substrings (`"剩余 3 轮或工具调用达 80%"`, `"结构化 JSON"`, `"acceptance_criteria 必填"`, `"不得让子 agent 再派发"`). Rephrasing the prompts for clarity — even while preserving intent — will break these checks. If the strings are treated as a stable contract, hoist them into named `&str` constants shared between prompt and test; otherwise accept that this test file is the contract and consider tagging it accordingly so future prompt edits don't trip over it.

`profiles_list_their_whitelisted_tools` reaches into `crate::bot::registry::{CODER_TOOLS, GENERAL_TOOLS, RESEARCH_TOOLS}`. This test is the only link tying the profile prompts to the live tool whitelist — if any tool is added to a registry list but the corresponding profile prompt is forgotten, the test fails (good); but if a profile prompt is later refactored to share a constant with another profile, the test will still pass and won't catch a divergent whitelist. Consider also asserting that each whitelist's tool set is a strict subset of the union (or the documented registry root list) so prompt drift away from the registry surfaces here too.

notif_sync_memory rewrites the JSON payload with only `{"ids": remaining}`, discarding every other key that may have been stored. If the payload ever carries additional metadata (e.g. session id, timestamps, summaries), this UPDATE will silently delete that information. Preserve the original payload by merging `remaining` into the existing object instead of replacing it.

`notifications_resolve` always emits `notifications-changed`, even when the underlying UPDATE touched zero rows (id missing or already resolved). This both produces needless UI churn and masks caller mistakes because the command reports success regardless of effect. Return the number of rows updated from `notif_resolve` and only emit when >0.

`notif_resolve_artifact` loads every pending artifact notification, parses each payload in Rust, and only then filters by `taskId`. With many pending rows this is O(N) memory + JSON parsing per call. Use SQLite's `json_extract` (or a dedicated indexed column) so the filter runs in SQL, and wrap the updates in a transaction so a failure leaves the table consistent.

`notif_sync_memory` issues one `SELECT COUNT(*)` per id (N+1 queries) and `unwrap_or(false)` swallows any DB error as "not present". If a transient error occurs or the payload contains non‑integer ids, `remaining` can become empty and the notification will be prematurely resolved. Fetch the pending ids in a single query, build a `HashSet`, and treat unknown/parse‑error IDs as fatal for that notification rather than silently discarding them.

Per-call working directory is created under `py_runs_root` and never removed. Every successful or failed invocation of `run_dotnet_revisions` permanently leaks a UUID-named directory (plus `params.json`), so disk usage grows unboundedly for any user who triggers the .NET revisions path more than once. Use `tempfile::TempDir` (auto-cleans on drop), or explicitly `std::fs::remove_dir_all(&dir)` in both the success and error arms before returning, so cleanup happens even when `run_python_at` returns `Err`.

TOCTOU: `is_file()` is used as the only gate before later passing the path to `run_python_at` / `cached_dotnet`. Between this check and the spawn, a symlink swap or write into the `exe_dir/dotnet/` folder can substitute a different file. Resolve + open with `File::open` (which fails atomically on the actual file contents) and use the resulting handle/path, or canonicalize the candidate before the existence check. Low practical risk because the exe directory is normally not user-writable, but worth tightening.

`PY_PROBE_COUNT` is a diagnostic counter with no cross-variable synchronization contract — `Ordering::SeqCst` is overkill and forces a full memory fence on every cache-miss path. `Ordering::Relaxed` is the correct ordering for a monotonic counter; no other state in this file needs to observe this increment synchronously.

comments.content: `drain_output` uses stringly-typed dispatch (`if kind == "out"`) and returns a 4-tuple `(String, String, bool, bool)` of anonymous values. A typo or new variant on the producer side silently misroutes stdout into stderr, and the call sites must remember which bool is "got==2" vs "truncated". Replace the `&'static str` channel tag with a shared enum (e.g. `enum Stream { Stdout, Stderr }`) and return a small named struct so the contract is self-evident and type-checked.

`read_capped_drain` swallows the read error: when `read_to_end` fails mid-stream, `buf` is returned with `truncated == false`, so callers cannot distinguish a complete-but-truncated read from an interrupted read that left output incomplete (the comment explicitly warns about "假完整" output). Surface the failure — e.g. return `(Vec<u8>, TruncationStatus)` with a `Complete | Truncated | Interrupted` enum, or return `io::Result<(Vec<u8>, bool)>` — so the caller is forced to handle it instead of silently shipping partial output to the user.

`drain_output` silently assumes the producer emits exactly one stdout and one stderr message: `got` is incremented per message and each arrival overwrites the corresponding buffer (last write wins), so a producer that sends two stdout chunks (or interleaves stderr/out before the loop reaches `got == 2`) will drop earlier payloads. The function's name promises draining, but it can lose data. Either change the protocol to send exactly one chunk per stream (enforce/document it), or accumulate with `+=` instead of `=` and stop only after both kinds have been observed.

`truncate_output` walks the entire string twice for large inputs: `s.chars().count()` is O(n), and the truncated branch then does another O(n) `chars().take(OUTPUT_CAP).collect()`. For a string near or above the cap this is 2·n char traversals plus the second allocation. Do it in one pass with `s.char_indices().nth(OUTPUT_CAP)` to find the byte boundary and slice `&s[..idx]` (which is also `O(1)` and avoids re-allocating the kept prefix), or pre-check `s.len()` in bytes as a cheap upper bound before paying for `chars().count()`.

`join_reader_threads` silently detaches the reader thread on timeout: after logging the leak it drops the `JoinHandle` via the `for` loop iteration end, leaving the OS thread running. Because the reader typically owns the `Sender` end of an `mpsc::channel` (and the child's stdout/stderr pipes), a still-running reader will block forever on its next `send` once the receiver is dropped, and the child's pipe FDs / handles stay live in the kernel — producing exactly the kind of "reader_leaked" accumulation this function tries to surface. Either close the receiver-side explicitly before/after the timeout (so the sender errors out and the reader exits), or have the reader thread observe a shared shutdown signal so it actually terminates.

TOCTOU between the symlink check and the subsequent `rename`/`copy_rec`: `symlink_metadata(&src)` is consulted, then later `std::fs::rename(&src, &dest)` (or `copy_rec`) acts on the same path with no atomic guarantee. A concurrent writer can swap a regular file for a symlink inside that window — and the very comment above the check explicitly acknowledges that `rename` would then move the symlink itself into `AI_Gen_Files` while its target stays outside `dir`, defeating the defence. Resolve once and operate on the same handle (e.g. `DirEntry` + `renameat`/`renameat2` with `RENAME_NOREPLACE`, or open with `O_NOFOLLOW` and use `renameat` on the fd) instead of re-stat'ing the path.

`copy_rec` aborts via `?` on the first failing child, but the just-created `dest` directory plus any successfully-copied siblings stay on disk. That contradicts the harvest-rollback path's whole rationale of "no orphan copies". Track whether `create_dir_all(dest)` ran and, on any recursion error, `remove_dir_all(dest)` before propagating the error so callers see a clean all-or-nothing copy.

`sweep_stale_py_runs_in` reports a misleading count: `removed += 1` runs whether or not `std::fs::remove_dir_all(&p)` actually succeeded (the error is discarded by `let _`). Permission errors, locked files on Windows, or transient I/O issues are silently counted as successes and never reach `py_audit`. Increment only on `Ok`, and surface failures — either a second counter for `failed` or per-entry audit lines — so operators can see when stale dirs can't be reaped.

`dedup_dest` has two problems: (1) `candidate.exists()` followed by an external rename/copy is a classic TOCTOU — two concurrent harvesters can pick the same destination and one will silently overwrite the other; (2) `n` is unbounded, so a process continuously minting collisions (`a`, `a (1)`, `a (2)`, …) spins forever doing syscalls. Use exclusive create (`create_new` / `O_EXCL` / `RENAME_NOREPLACE`) to claim the path, snapshot the directory listing once, or put a sane upper bound on `n` and bail out with an error instead of looping.

The harvest path emits rich audit messages for the symlink skip and the rollback case, but the failure branches where work was actually lost — `rename` fails AND `copy_rec` fails (the outer `else { false }`) — return silently and the `copy_rec` `Err` is thrown away. Users see `harvested=N` for one run and zero the next with no diagnostic explaining why a file vanished (or didn't). Add an audit in that branch too, including `src.display()` and the underlying `copy_rec` error so it's actionable.

`{src:?}` uses `Debug` formatting on a `PathBuf`, producing a quoted/escaped path string in the audit log. Every other audit line in this file uses `src.display()` (e.g. line 30); switch to `{src}` or `src.display()` here for consistency and readability.

Excel formula-injection guard is incomplete: the comment itself names the threat (WEBSERVICE/DDE on open), but the runtime check only catches cells whose openpyxl data_type is `'f'`. (1) When the model emits values like `'+1+1'`, `'-2+3'`, `'@SUM(...)'` Excel/Calc still evaluate them on open, and openpyxl may persist them as string `'s'` (or worse, as `'f'`) depending on value origin. (2) The guard inspects only the last appended row (`ws[ws.max_row]`); cells added via direct assignment, merges, or later `ws.append` calls later in the iteration are not re-scanned. Recommend sanitizing any string cell value whose first char is in `=+-@` (or its trimmed form starts with one) at write time, and applying the guard to every cell of the appended row (e.g. iterate `ws[ws.max_row]` after each append AND a final sweep over all populated cells).

`file_path_to_string` returns the raw URL for the `Url` variant (e.g. `file:///home/u/a.docx`). That string is then handed to `EXTRACT_SCRIPT` and `MAKE_DOCX_REVISIONS_SCRIPT`, both of which call `os.path.exists(p)` / `docx.Document(p)` / `shutil.copyfile(path, out)`. On POSIX `os.path.exists("file:///...")` is always False, so the script falls through to the "缺少原文" error path even when the user selected a real file via a system dialog that returns the URL form. Convert to a filesystem path (e.g. `url.to_file_path()` / strip the `file://` scheme) before returning, or only return `Some` for the `Path` variant.

Public API surface in this module collapses typed errors into `Result<_, String>` at every layer: `run_doc_script`, `run_doc_revisions`, `spawn_blocking_map`, `py_exec_sync`, `py_exec_sync_async`, `pdf_render_pages`, plus inline `.map_err(|e| e.to_string())` chains. By the time errors reach the `command!` boundary (or the audit log), the underlying runtime/runtime-gate/script-error kind is gone — only a free-form string remains, and callers cannot match on error category. Recommend carrying a typed error (the crate already has `CommandError`; consider a `DocError` enum or `thiserror`) through the call chain and only converting to a display string at the very edge.

TOCTOU + race in `gen_out_path_in`: the existence loop returns a path that the caller will hand to a Python script which later calls `wb.save(out)` / `d.save(out)`. Two concurrent `doc_make_*` invocations resolving in the same second can both see `candidate.exists() == false` and both write to the same path (last writer wins, clobbering). Also, an attacker (or stale file deletion) can remove the chosen path between the check and the actual write. Either (a) create an empty sentinel atomically (e.g. `OpenOptions::new().write(true).create_new(true).open(...)`) before returning, or (b) let the Python script append to a `.tmp` suffix and rename atomically; in any case, don't trust a pre-check done in Rust.

`py_exec_sync` writes the entire user-submitted Python source to the audit log. `escape_for_log` only neutralizes control characters for log-injection; it does not redact. Any secret/credential/token embedded in user code (which this entry point is explicitly designed to accept) ends up persisted in the audit trail — and the audit pipeline elsewhere likely ships to a centralized store. Either drop the script body from the audit record entirely, store a short content hash for correlation, or require an explicit `redact=true` flag from the caller.

`resolve_doc_path` classifies a normal user-cancel as `CommandError::Internal`. "用户取消了选择" is not an internal/server fault — it is a routine, expected branch where the user simply didn't pick a file. Use a dedicated `CommandError` variant (e.g. `UserCancelled` / `Aborted`) so the UI can distinguish "abort" from "internal failure" and so the audit / metrics layer doesn't flag benign cancellations as server errors.

`Err("...".into())` here is a needless `&str → String` conversion inside the error path of `py_exec_sync`; the surrounding error returns in the same function use `format!(...)` and `Err("...")` patterns inconsistently. More importantly, the string itself mixes an actionable message, a settings page location, and a permission-mode hint into one literal — callers (UI toast, audit, log) cannot split "why" from "how to fix". Consider a typed error variant carrying `(reason, hint)` so each surface (UI/audit/log) can render the relevant part.

`doc_make_word_revisions` calls `original_path.clone().unwrap_or_default()` solely to preserve the value for the trailing audit log, then `original_path.unwrap_or_default()` to move into the JSON. That clone is redundant: take `let src = original_path.as_deref().unwrap_or("").to_string();` (or `original_path.clone()` and then `mem::take(&mut original_path).unwrap_or_default()`) so the JSON path moves cleanly. As written, every call allocates an extra `String` of an arbitrary user-controlled file path just for one log line.

`profile_remove_avatar` deletes whatever path `profile_dir(&app).join(f)` resolves to without re‑validating `f` via `avatar_filename_only`. A hand‑edited / imported / corrupt `profile.json` can put values such as `"../../wmessage.db"`, `"/etc/passwd"`, `"a\\b.png"` or even an absolute path into `avatar`; after the function successfully clears the JSON reference (which only requires the read‑modify‑write lock) the next line will unlink that arbitrary file with the privileges of the Tauri process. Because the field is also accepted from the IPC layer, this is reachable from any compromised renderer as well. Validate the stored name through `avatar_filename_only` (rejecting `None`) and, on rejection, audit the event instead of deleting. Optionally also verify the resolved path is a child of `profile_dir` (canonicalize both) before `remove_file`.

`profile_set_avatar` deletes *all* prior avatars for this `kind` **before** the new avatar is committed. If `std::fs::copy`, `save_data`, or the final `rename` later fails, `profile.json` is left pointing at the old filename (or at the new filename when the save succeeded but the rename did not) while the old file is already gone — the user's previous avatar is silently lost with no rollback path. Defer deletion of the previously stored avatar (and any other‑extension siblings) until **after** `rename(&dest_tmp, &dest)` succeeds; only then look up the prior `entry.avatar` recorded before the overwrite and remove it. The cleanup loop should keep `dest` (or the old extension's file) untouched until the new file is on disk.

The new avatar is committed in the order `save_data(&profile.json)` → `rename(&dest_tmp, &dest)`. Because `profile.json` is updated *before* the on‑disk file is in place, a failure of `rename` (cross‑device move, AV/EBUSY, Windows sharing violation, quota, etc.) leaves `profile.json` pointing at a filename that does not exist (or, after the old file was removed by the earlier cleanup loop, pointing at a file that was never created). The function then returns `Err`, but the persisted state is already inconsistent — the next `profile_get` will return `avatar_data_url=None`. Reverse the ordering: perform `rename(&dest_tmp, &dest)` first while the old entry is still in the JSON, then call `save_data`. If `save_data` fails after the rename, `cleanup_set_avatar_failure` can be extended to revert the rename using `rename(&dest, &dest_tmp)` (or, on platforms where rename‑over‑existing isn’t atomic, remove the new file).

`ensure_person_id` has a classic RMW race: both `pid` (generated before the lock) and `data.person_id` (read inside the lock) are used independently. When two first‑run callers race, each persists *its own* `pid` to `profile.json` via the double‑check (only the second sees the first's write, the first has already finished), and then both still call `people_upsert_entry(&pid, …, is_self=true)` using their *local* `pid`. Result: two self rows in `people` with different ids while only one of them ends up in `profile.json`; every subsequent export uses the surviving id and the orphan self row leaks. On `save_data` failure the function still upserts `pid` and returns it as if persisted, breaking the documented "固化 idempotent" contract and producing a fresh self row on the next call. Fix: under the lock load `profile.json`, compute the canonical pid (`existing or newly generated`), write it, capture it from the locked `data`, and use that canonical value for the `people_upsert_entry` and the return tuple; also propagate the `save_data` error (change the signature to `CommandResult`) so the caller does not get a non‑persistent pid.

`entry_view` blindly `metadata()`/`read()`s whatever file sits at `profile_dir(app).join(f)`. The filename validation only rejects literal `/`, `\` and `..`; it does **not** inspect the file itself. If an attacker (or a hostile dropper in a portable install on a shared drive) can plant a symlink at `profile/avatar-user.png` pointing at e.g. `~/.ssh/id_rsa`, the next `profile_get` will read that file, base64‑encode it, and emit it to every window via the `profile-changed` IPC event. Use `std::fs::symlink_metadata` and reject (audit + `None`) when the entry's `file_type().is_symlink()` is true, or open with `OpenOptions::new().read(true).custom_flags(libc::O_NOFOLLOW)` on platforms that support it.

The corrupt‑JSON backup filename uses `chrono` format `%Y%m%d-%H%M%S%.3f`, which has only millisecond precision. Two independent corruption events that arrive within the same millisecond (e.g. two `load_data` calls from a periodic watchdog and an IPC handler) will both compute the same `bak` path; the second `std::fs::rename` will silently overwrite the first backup, destroying the earlier evidence of corruption. Append a high‑resolution suffix or a per‑process counter (or PID + atomic counter) so every backup target is unique. This also makes it possible to diagnose correlated corruptions instead of seeing only the latest snapshot.

comments.content: Prompt instructs `run_python` for bulk cross-file edits and data processing, but the underlying tool (`SCHEMA_RUN_PYTHON`, `run_python_ungated` in `py/runtime.rs`) explicitly provides "无文件系统隔离" — only CPU/memory/time limits are enforced, no chroot/path restriction, so arbitrary Python can read/write anywhere on the user's filesystem, spawn subprocesses, and access the network. The "安全红线" at the end ("绝不执行系统命令、修改系统设置、访问系统目录"; write-tool whitelist "白名单外弹确认") is purely prompt-level and is actively defeated by rule 12 ("用户要写代码/跑数据处理时用 run_python") and rule 19 ("同一处改动散布多个文件或多处重复出现时，用 run_python 批量替换比逐个 edit_file 更高效可靠"). Either tighten the prompt to forbid run_python from touching whitelisted paths / launching subprocesses (relying on prompt adherence is fragile), or back the tool with a real sandbox (chroot, macOS sandbox-exec, Windows Job Object + restricted token, container) so the security red lines become enforced invariants instead of advisory text.

comments.content: `Path::exists()` does not distinguish a missing flag from any I/O error (permission denied, stale handle, network data dir, …); it simply returns `false`. The Tauri command thus silently swallows real filesystem failures and reports the feature as disabled, which can hide a corrupted state from both the UI and `py_exec_sync`. Replace with an explicit metadata/try_exists probe that maps non‑NotFound errors to `CommandError::IoError` so callers can react.

The "enable" branch uses `std::fs::write` which opens with create/truncate before writing. If the process is killed, the disk is full, or any other error occurs after the file is created but before the byte is written, the flag file remains on disk and `py_get_enabled` will return `true` even though the command returned an `Err`. Because the flag's semantics are presence‑based, the write should be atomic – either the file is created in a fully‑visible state or nothing is created at all.

`py_get_enabled` and `py_set_enabled` are declared as synchronous `#[tauri::command]` handlers but perform blocking `std::fs` calls (metadata, `create_dir_all`, write, remove). Tauri invokes sync commands on the IPC dispatcher thread (effectively the main UI thread), so any slow filesystem (network mount, AV scan, locked file) will freeze the UI while the command runs. Wrap the bodies in `tauri::async_runtime::spawn_blocking` and make the commands `async` so the work runs on the blocking pool and never stalls IPC.

comments.content: VECTOR_CACHE is held across the synchronous `embed_text` call, so a single slow ONNX inference serializes every concurrent caller — including pure cache hits from unrelated commands — for the full inference latency. The inline comment justifies the trade-off, but `tag_similar_pairs` is not the only path that touches this global; any future reader/writer of `VECTOR_CACHE` will block. Drop the lock before the blocking call and re-acquire it just for the insert; the brief race window on a cache miss is acceptable for this workload and can be tightened later with a single-flight guard (e.g. `DashMap` entry API) if duplicate ONNX calls actually show up in profiling.

`VECTOR_CACHE.lock().ok()?` silently maps a poisoned Mutex to `None` for the rest of the process — no recovery, no log, no audit. Combined with the surrounding `filter_map` (see next comment), this becomes indistinguishable from a per-tag embedding failure and can permanently disable the cache after any panic in another thread that ever touched it. Either recover explicitly via `PoisonError::into_inner()` or surface the poison as a typed error so it can be audited/re-initialised.

comments.content: `filter_map(|t| cache_get_or_embed(t).map(|v| (t.clone(), v)))` silently drops every tag whose embedding returns `None` — poisoned cache, transient engine hiccup, or a tag the embedder rejects. The audit event only reports the surviving aggregate (`embedded`), so the front-end receives a synonym set that may be partially empty with no signal. Track failures separately and surface them via the audit `skipped` field (and ideally return them so the caller can warn the user instead of silently shrinking coverage).

The `spawn_blocking` `JoinError` is flattened via `format!` into `CommandError::from(String)`, which throws away the original error type — panic vs cancellation vs timeout — and any panic payload from the worker. The same pattern should use a dedicated `CommandError::WorkerJoin` (or similar) variant that preserves the `JoinError` (or its `Debug` representation) so logs/audit can distinguish a real worker panic from graceful cancellation, and so call sites don't have to grep for the Chinese string.

comments.content: Guard's ownership check is only `subagent_id` equality, so an ABA scenario — same `session_id` + same `subagent_id` reused by a retry/resume — causes the old guard's Drop to delete the newer runner's registration. This silently disables the recursion gate (`is_subagent_session` returns false) for the live subagent, allowing it to spawn further subagents. The ownership identity should be unique (e.g. an `Arc<()>` weak token, generation counter, or guard-issued nonce) not just a string field that is expected to repeat.

`register_subagent_session` blindly overwrites an existing entry, replacing the `Arc<AtomicUsize>` budget counter. A duplicate registration (retry/reuse of the same session_id, or a buggy double-spawn) resets `used_tool_calls` to whatever the new caller supplies — a second runner can effectively nullify `max_tool_calls` enforcement. Callers that already hold a clone of the old context can still increment the *detached* old counter, bypassing any future re-check. Either reject duplicate keys, or require the new context to carry the *same* `Arc<AtomicUsize>` (carry-and-check) so the counter is preserved across retries.

The task-execution-flow registry has no RAII guard, no ownership check, and no idempotency token. A panic between `register_exec_session` and `unregister_exec_session` permanently leaks the entry (making `is_task_execution_flow` always true). Conversely, session-ID reuse causes the new registration to be silently overwritten, and a late `unregister_exec_session` from the previous (stale) runner removes the new entry — misclassifying a live task execution as a plain conversation. Both `register_exec_session` and `unregister_exec_session` should be wrapped in a guard analogous to `SubagentSessionGuard`, or at minimum check that the current entry's origin matches the one the caller originally registered.

`eprintln!` writes to stderr synchronously while the registry mutex is held. If stderr is redirected to a slow/blocked sink (broken pipe, full pipe, NFS-backed terminal in some setups), every concurrent caller of `register_subagent_session`, `register_exec_session`, or the lock helpers themselves will block on this write. In an async runtime, this is a direct way to stall the reactor or deadlock workers waiting for the registry. The log message is purely diagnostic — move it outside the critical section (capture the message first under lock, print after releasing).

The guard-drop test deliberately uses *different* subagent IDs (`sa_old` vs `sa_new`), so it only validates the easy half of the invariant. The actual bug — same `session_id` + same `subagent_id` reused by a retry/resume, where the old guard's Drop should NOT remove the newer entry — has no regression coverage. Add a test with `sample_ctx("sa_same")` for both guards to catch the ABA race once it's fixed.

total_used is incremented by the pre-truncation text length (line 472) before the TOTAL_CAP check, but never decremented when the text is truncated on line 475 — so total_used stays inflated at prev + PER_FILE_CAP instead of reflecting the bytes actually injected. With the current caps the next iteration's `if total_used >= TOTAL_CAP` guard at line 444 still masks the bug for file inclusion (it correctly skips), but the counter is a latent defect: any tweak of PER_FILE_CAP / TOTAL_CAP (e.g. raising PER_FILE_CAP or lowering TOTAL_CAP) will cause files that still fit under the budget to be wrongly skipped, and any future audit/log that reads total_used will report wrong numbers. Fix by computing `remain = TOTAL_CAP.saturating_sub(prev_total)` first, capping the take by min(remain, PER_FILE_CAP), and assigning `total_used = TOTAL_CAP` (or `prev_total + final_len`) after truncation.

The retry loop (lines 586-632) immediately re-invokes summarize_messages on any parse failure with no backoff or jitter, and the bound `attempts >= 2` is checked only after the second failure has already been paid for. Combined with the contract-violation that only the latest `last_err` is retained while audit only fires on final failure (line 633's `fail!`), transient API hiccups get no breathing room and intermittent parse errors can ping-pong at full token cost — and you lose the first failure signal in telemetry. Consider adding a small backoff (e.g. 200–500ms) between attempts and emitting an Info-level audit on the first failed attempt with the parse error so flapping is visible without leaking into the user-facing error.

`parse_and_validate(&raw)` (line 601) already runs a full `serde_json::from_str` on the LLM output, then `parse_assumptions(&raw)` (line 603) does another `serde_json::from_str` on the same string — the previously parsed `serde_json::Value` is dropped on the floor. For large LLM outputs this is duplicated work (allocations + JSON parse). Refactor `parse_and_validate` to return the parsed `serde_json::Value` alongside the validated subtasks (or run `parse_assumptions` inside `parse_and_validate` on the already-parsed Value) so the second parse goes away.

`validate_attach_path` (lines 409-428) canonicalizes the user-supplied path and inspects only the resolved extension — it does not verify that the canonical path lives under any allow-listed directory (e.g. user's home, app data dir, or a project root). The accompanying comment claims "用户在对话框亲手选的文件 = 明确授权", so the design trusts the caller; this assumption is fine for the chat-dialog picker, but the function is `fn` (no `pub`/`pub(crate)`) and is only invoked from `build_attachment_blocks`, whose input comes straight from the `attachments: Option<Vec<String>>` invoke parameter — which an attacker (or a malicious frontend module) can fabricate. The current behavior will happily open any readable .docx/.xlsx/.pptx/.pdf on the host (e.g. `/etc/shadow.docx`, `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pdf`, browser cookies exports). At minimum, add a directory-containment check (e.g. `canon.starts_with(allowed_root)`) or take the allowed-root list as an argument from the trusted caller.

Contract/code mismatch on per-card subtasks: the hard-coded CONTRACT_SEGMENT on line 33 tells the model `subtasks: 2~8 条子任务文本`, but `validate_decompose` (lines 257-283) only rejects `list.len() > 8` and silently accepts 0 or 1 items — collapsing an empty list to `None` (lines 279-282). A model that emits a single sub-task per card will pass validation and silently contradict the contract the model was told to follow; downstream consumers (UI heuristics, QA passes) that assume ≥2 items will then see inconsistent shapes with no warning. Either reject `< 2` items (or coerce to None like today, but only when contract says "optional"), or update the contract text to say "0~8 条" so the contract and the validator agree.

comments.content: Re-including `tests/mock_llm.rs` via `include!` re-registers every `#[tokio::test]` defined there inside the bot_test_connection binary, so mock_llm's own tests will run twice across the suite (and any shared mutable state across runs could interact). Prefer placing the shared mock under `tests/common/` (a non-test module) and importing from both test binaries, or guard the duplicated tests with `#[cfg(...)]` so they only register in one binary.

`paths[0]` is indexed without first asserting `!paths.is_empty()` (or that `server.request_count() > 0`). If `probe_connection` ever short-circuits (URL validation failure, early return on a future code path, redirect-loop change) the index panic surfaces a less informative failure than the surrounding assertion. Either check `server.request_count()` first or use `.first().expect("probe made one request")` so the failure message is actionable.

The unreachable-host assertion relies on `127.0.0.1:1` always producing `connection refused`, but this is OS-/network-stack-dependent: some BSDs, older macOS, hosts with a firewall that drops rather than rejects, or systems where tcpmux/inetd is enabled can produce a hang, timeout, or different error category. If the contract under test requires a specific "network error with message" mapping, pin the assumption by also asserting on the error text contains a stable substring (e.g., "connection" / "refused") or pick an address guaranteed to fail (e.g., a TEST-NET-1 IP).

`paths[0].contains("GET /v1/models")` couples test correctness to the exact log-line format produced by `MockLlmServer::request_paths()`. Any change in the mock's log format (separator, trailing slash, query string, method ordering) silently degrades the assertion to a no-op. Expose a typed accessor from the mock (e.g., `request_methods()`/`request_paths_only()`) and assert on those, or at least assert `server.request_count() == 1` immediately before the path indexing.

Latent bug in `py_gate_acquire_inner`: the second EXITING branch (`*avail += 1`) increments the permit count without a preceding decrement. The comment claims "归还许可" (return permit) but no permit was taken, so if this branch were ever reached under different locking semantics it would leak a phantom permit and let an extra task past the gate. Currently unreachable because both EXITING checks run under the same `PY_PERMITS` mutex guard (the atomic value cannot change between them), but the code does not match its documented intent and is a maintenance hazard.

`SETRLIMIT_PROBE` OnceLock verdict is never invalidated. When `run_python` retries on `spawn_not_found` it calls `invalidate_python_cache()` and may swap to a different interpreter (e.g. system python vs. venv, or a freshly installed interpreter), but the once-per-process `rlimit_as`/`rlimit_cpu` verdict is reused for the new interpreter. A different sandbox/environment may have different setrlimit support, leading to pre_exec setting limits that the kernel will now reject, or to silently skipping limits where the new environment supports them.

`kill_tree` reads `child.id()` after `try_wait()` returned `Some(status)`. Per `std::process::Child` documentation, the PID is no longer guaranteed unique after the child has been reaped — the OS may have reassigned it to an unrelated process. In the `if !drained` path, draining the remaining stdout/stderr after wait can take up to 2s, giving the kernel a real window to recycle the PID. Sending `kill -9 --<pid>` to a recycled PID's group can terminate an unrelated process tree.

`kill_tree` casts `child.id() as i32` and `format!`s `-{pid}` without the `pid > i32::MAX as u32` defensive guard that `is_live_group_leader` documents as required. On wraparound the formatted string would target a wrong process group (potentially the caller's own), exactly the hazard the guard in `is_live_group_leader` was added to prevent. Practical pids stay below `2^22` so impact is low today, but the kill path is explicitly marked 安全关键 and the two should use the same guard.

`kill_py_children` silently drops any PID that `is_live_group_leader` rejects (returning `false`), with no audit/log and no fallback. Today the only registration path is `ChildRegGuard::register(child)` which captures `child.id()`, and that PID is always the group leader because `cmd.process_group(0)` is called at spawn — but this invariant is undocumented and unenforced. Any future spawn path that records a non-leader PID (or a PID from a forked helper that has since left the group) will be silently skipped by `kill_all_py_children`, leaving orphan Python processes.

cleanup() removes the three shared evolution jsonl without holding any lock, while only the subsequent DB deletes are serialized by DB_WRITE_LOCK. Per the file header, the deps directory is shared across nextest processes that can stomp on these files; a parallel writer (e.g. another test mid-write) racing with the unguarded remove_file can corrupt or remove a half-written jsonl. Either gate these removals behind the same DB_WRITE_LOCK, or rename them to a per-process suffix so they can't collide with parallel runs.

TOCTOU window between db::open_db(app) and DB_WRITE_LOCK acquisition: the DB connection is opened before the lock is taken, so any concurrent writer (another test process sharing deps) can insert u20-gov-marked rows between open_db and lock that the subsequent delete_by_key_tag loop will silently miss, leaving pollution across runs. Open the DB inside the lock scope or perform the deletes through a helper that owns the connection together with the guard.

Box::leak of the MockRuntime app to obtain a 'static AppHandle is documented as intentional, but GovGuard::drop then calls cleanup(&self.app, ...) and restore_cfg(self.original_cfg.clone(), &self.cfg) against that leaked handle and the leaked original_cfg read. Cleanup correctness is therefore coupled to intentional memory leakage surviving until process teardown; if any future change ever drops the leaked app or shortens its lifetime, panic-path cleanup will silently start using a dangling handle. Consider documenting this invariant inline on GovGuard or holding the AppHandle inside an Arc that the guard can release explicitly.

The hijack-prevention assertion err.contains("拒绝") binds the test to a localized substring of the production error message. If the error string is reworded (even an unrelated copy edit), this assertion will fail with a misleading diff instead of flagging the real semantic change. Prefer asserting on a stable error variant/code (e.g. an enum like ConflictRefused mapped to a typed error) rather than the human-readable substring.

`store::load_all(&conn)` is called inside the per-corpus loop and then linearly filtered for `content == old` — that's an O(n·m) full-table scan repeated 10 times. Hoist the table load (or a `HashSet<String>` of every observed `content`) outside the loop so the "no stale row for old content" check is O(1) per group and the invariant is explicit.

Test builds JSON for the mock LLM by interpolating `new` / `orig_id` directly into a JSON string literal via `format!`. Safe for the current Chinese-only corpus, but if any future entry contains `"`, `\`, control characters, or non-BMP code points, the mock will receive malformed JSON and the test will fail with a confusing parser error rather than a clear assertion. `mock_handle()` permanently leaks a `tauri::test::mock_app()` per test invocation via `Box::leak`. In a long test session (or with repeated runs from a watcher) this accumulates — each leaked `App` retains its full state graph. If the leaked handle is only used as a constructor for `AppHandle`, hoist the `MockRuntime` app into a `OnceLock`/`OnceCell` so the mock app is built exactly once and the handle is just cloned.

Either mark this test `#[serial]` (e.g. `serial_test`) or open a per-test SQLite file via a tempfile path so the assertion is deterministic regardless of suite order.

Wrap the call in `tauri::async_runtime::spawn_blocking` (or change `write_event` itself to async) so the async request path stays non-blocking.

If a task panics while holding this lock (e.g. mid-update of the attempt counter), subsequent operations silently use the torn state, potentially writing inconsistent attempt counts (rework loop at line ~749 has the same pattern). Prefer `.unwrap_or_else(|e| { eprintln!("[workflow_runner] attempts mutex poisoned: {e:?}"); e.into_inner() })` or propagate the poison to the controller's error path.

Per the design §8.1 stop semantics, this delays user-visible stop response. comments.content:
Best-effort DB writes silently dropped, leaving engine state inconsistent with DB. `write_node_result` only broadcasts on `db_upsert.is_ok()`; on failure the new `node_result` (with `status`, `acceptanceVerdict`, `attempt`, `ms`) is lost. But the controller then computes `let ok = column_done && !fused && result.is_ok() && !acceptance_failed;` from the pre-write in-memory state and emits a `NodeOutcome{ ok, .. }`. So the engine may report `ok=true` while the DB still shows `status=success` for an acceptance-failed node (or vice versa). The same TOCTOU pattern appears in `mark_note_prefix` (skip/熔断 notes can be lost) and `reset_node_for_rework` (column reset to Todo can be lost, causing rework loop to skip a node that is still Done and refused by `run_task_in_chat`). Document the invariant or surface write failures to the controller.

Severity: high — produces wrong audit/rework behavior.

Per-spawn deep clones of shared maps cause O(N²) allocations. `spawn_node` is called once per node and inside its body clones `model_by_id: HashMap<String, Option<String>>`, `upstream_of: HashMap<String, Vec<String>>`, `goal: Option<String>`, and `workflow_id: String` on every invocation. For a workflow with N nodes this allocates ~N full HashMaps plus N strings per spawn. Wrap these shared maps in `Arc` once at the controller scope (e.g. `let model_by_id = Arc::new(model_by_id);`) and clone the `Arc` (cheap) inside the closure; `goal` can be `Arc<Option<String>>` or `Arc<str>` likewise.

Severity: medium — measurable on large workflows (50+ nodes).

`OutcomeFallback::drop` relies on the unbounded `tx` still being alive and uses `std::mem::take(&mut self.id)`. Two concerns: (1) if the controller has already exited and dropped the receiver (e.g. workflow finished normally while this task was still in `run_task_in_chat_ctx`), `tx.send` silently fails and a panicked task is never accounted for — the `running` set may have a stale entry until the `Arc` is dropped. (2) `mem::take(&mut self.id)` requires `String: Default`; while true, this is a subtle invariant — a comment explaining "`sent` is the single source of truth; `mem::take` is defensive in case the panic happens before `sent` is initialized" would harden it. Consider using `ManuallyDrop` or simply `self.id.clone()` since the Drop impl consumes the borrow anyway.

Severity: medium — only triggers on panic, but panics in async tasks are not rare during model loop failures.

Check-then-act on `running` set silently treats poison as "not running", risking double-spawn. `running.lock().map(|r| !r.contains(&d)).unwrap_or(false)` and `running.lock().map(|r| r.contains(&skipped)).unwrap_or(false)` (also in the rework loop) silently default to `false`/`true` on poison. If the lock is poisoned (a panic while another task held it), the controller may decide `d_free = true` and spawn `d` again, while `d` is in fact still running. Combined with the poison-recovery on `attempts`, this can produce two concurrent `run_task_in_chat_ctx` calls for the same node. Prefer surfacing the poison (at minimum via `eprintln!`) and skipping the spawn on failure.

Severity: medium — corner case but produces real concurrency violation.

comments.content:
`build_dag` cycle detection uses Kahn's algorithm but `processed = queue.len()` initializes the count to the size of `ready`, not zero. This is correct only because every node in `ready` was already added to `processed` without being "popped", which conflates "was placed in ready" with "was processed". The algorithm still produces the right answer (cycle iff processed < total_active), but the invariant is non-obvious — a reader could easily mis-edit this. Add a one-line comment or rewrite as `let mut processed = 0usize; ... processed += 1;` inside the loop after popping.

Severity: low — correctness is fine, but the off-by-one initialization is a maintenance hazard.

`retries_left` initial budget of 1 is shared across the C1 (execution-failure retry) and the acceptance rework budget but is not reset for nodes entering the rework loop. In `review_and_rework`, the rework spawn path calls `spawn_node` with the same closure that uses `retries_left` from the *main* controller scope (not reinitialized). For a node that already exhausted its C1 retry in the main run and then was scheduled for rework, `retries_left` is 0, so a failure during rework will not be auto-retried — and the rework loop has no retry of its own. If a rework execution fails, it propagates immediately to "failed" + downstream skipped, even though the user might expect one more attempt. Consider reinitializing `retries_left` to 1 for nodes in `rework_set` at the start of `review_and_rework`.

Severity: medium — violates the documented "有界返工环" expectation that rework nodes get a fresh execution budget.

comments.content: `end_trace` collapses every non-Ok path into `TRACE_STATUS_FAILED` and represents user-/system-initiated stops as `TRACE_STATUS_DONE` because `run_model_loop` returns `Ok` on stop (`bot_model_loop.rs:1267-1270, 1371-1373`) and `run_task_in_chat_with` then calls `end_trace(.., outcome.is_ok(), ..)` (`bot_chat.rs:1863-1870`). The schema defines `TRACE_STATUS_STOPPED` and `TRACE_STATUS_TIMEOUT` (`db/trace.rs:30, 1477`) but they are never produced here, so trace analytics mis-classify cancelled runs as successful. The signature needs an explicit outcome (or status + stop flag) so stopped/timeout paths can be persisted accurately.

`end_trace` removes the `session_id -> trace_id` registry entry and then runs `trace_finish` without waiting for the background writer to drain queued spans/file_changes for this trace. `trace_finish` derives `files_changed` from `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM file_changes WHERE trace_id=?` (`db/trace.rs:286`); if the writer is still holding rows for this trace, the count is permanently under-reported. After commit, late inserts become orphans (no FK). Either drain the channel first (and wait for the writer to ack), or move the registry removal until after `trace_finish` succeeds.

`begin_trace` and `end_trace` run `trace_start` / `trace_finish` on a fresh `Connection` inside `spawn_blocking`, but the module doc explicitly states "与主写者共用 `DB_WRITE_LOCK` 纪律" and the writer carefully takes `crate::db::lock_db_write()` around every batch. Lifecycle writes therefore run concurrently with the writer and any other DB writer, opening the door to `SQLITE_BUSY`, lost updates, and the count race described in the previous finding. Wrap each lifecycle write in the same `lock_db_write()` guard.

The `writer` task is `spawn`ed on the async runtime but performs synchronous `rusqlite` work and holds `crate::db::lock_db_write()` (a `std::sync::Mutex`) across each batch. Under contention or slow disk this blocks an async worker thread and serialises every DB writer on the critical section. Drain the batch into a `Vec` on the async runtime, then perform the actual insert via `tauri::async_runtime::spawn_blocking` so the blocking work does not stall the runtime (and the lock is held off the async task).

`record_span` / `record_file_change` use `try_send` on a 2048-cap channel and silently drop on `Full`, in contrast to DB-side losses which are audited (`trace.batch_dropped`) and text overflow which is audited (`trace.span_overflow`). Channel saturation now looks like zero coverage with no external signal. Add a counter or rate-limited `trace.queue_overflow` audit so observability regressions are detectable.

`init` discards the `JoinHandle` returned by `tauri::async_runtime::spawn(writer(...))`. Any panic inside `writer` (e.g. the `expect("上方保证已建连")`, mutex poisoning, audit panic, SQL panic) kills the trace pipeline permanently while `SINK` keeps the dead sender, so callers silently lose every subsequent span until the app restarts. Retain the handle (or use a supervised task) and at minimum log + try to restart on join-error.

Emit a `trace.batch_dropped` (or equivalent) audit event here so observability loss is recorded consistently.

`end_trace` returns silently when the `TraceCapture` mutex is poisoned (`let Ok(mut c) = hook.lock() else { return };`), with no log and no audit. Compare with `app_state::trace_id_for_session` which explicitly `eprintln!`s and recovers from poisoning. Apply the same pattern so a poisoned hook doesn't quietly leak `running` trace rows.

respond_core 的 notif_get 仅校验存在性、不检查当前 status。即便通知已被前一次应答置为 DONE、或被 invalidate_workflow_questions 置为 DISMISSED 后再次应答，仍会无条件 notif_resolve 并调用 brief_insert（卡级 + 全局级各一条）。这意味着：用户对同一问题双重点击 / 重试时会产生重复 brief 记录（一次应答多出 4 条 brief），与函数注释里「幂等 Ok(None)」的承诺不一致；亦会让「重跑生效」场景出现误写的担忧。建议把 notif_resolve 改为条件 UPDATE（`UPDATE ... WHERE id=? AND status='pending'` 并检查受影响行数），受影响为 0 时直接 Ok(None)，并相应把 brief_insert 也包进同一个事务。

测试覆盖同样缺失：现有测试只对同一 qid 调用一次 respond_core，没有验证「重复应答」或「DISMISSED 之后应答」两条分支的幂等行为，建议补一个连答两次后断言 brief 计数为 1 的回归用例。

invalidate_workflow_questions 的循环对每条 id 单独调用 notif_resolve，没有用事务包裹。一旦 rusqlite 在中间某次调用失败（例如锁等待超时、IO 错误），部分 notification 已被置为 STATUS_DISMISSED、其余仍停留在 pending，破坏了「run 收尾/停止时一次性把本工作流的 pending 问题批量失效」这个契约——调用方拿到 Ok(已处理条数) 后也无法分辨哪些真正完成了。建议在外层用 `conn.transaction()` 把整个循环包起来，所有 notif_resolve 走事务句柄，并在 commit 时统一落盘；任一失败整体回滚，调用方可重新尝试。

select! 的超时/停止分支返回 Expired 之后才执行 `question_waiters.remove(&qid)`；期间应答端可能已完成 brief/audit 写入并尝试取走 tx，最终引擎已经按假设继续（不再 rx）。文件头注释明确把这种情况描述为「run 已死后才送达的回答：档案仍落（重跑生效），唤醒静默跳过」，但用户视角看到的是「我点了提交、模型却按假设走」——这条边界目前没有任何面向用户的反馈。建议在 WaitOutcome::Expired 这条返回文案里明确一句「你的回答已记录到档案，下次工作流重跑时生效」，或在通知卡片上挂一个状态标签，避免用户误以为提交失败。

The module-wide `#![allow(clippy::await_holding_lock)]` is too broad: only the four `scheduler_e2e_*` tests need it, yet it silently permits any future test in this file to hold a sync Mutex across `.await` without warning. comments.content: Each call to `mock_handle` does `Box::leak(Box::new(tauri::test::mock_app()))`, intentionally leaking one full `tauri::App` per test. Across the four `scheduler_e2e_*` tests this leaks four Apps for the process lifetime; the leaked App outlives the handle, so any `Drop`-based teardown inside the App never runs (masking teardown bugs and growing memory in CI loops). Consider constructing the mock App once per test and returning both `(App, AppHandle)`, or wrap the leaked App in a test-scoped guard.

`bot_log_tail_since` silently returns an empty string when the log file is truncated, rotated, or simply smaller than `offset` (e.g. by external cleanup between `bot_log_len()` and the read). The subsequent `tail.contains(needle)` assertions then fail with misleading diagnostics that look like the audit line was never written, rather than reporting the real cause. Add a length check that fails loudly when `offset > data.len()`.

Mock executors that panic on unexpected tool use end with an unreachable `ToolResult::ok(...)` under `#[allow(unreachable_code)]`. This pattern depends on the executor signature staying unchanged and silently couples the panic site to a type-only expression that must stay in sync with `ToolResult`'s shape. Prefer making the panic terminal (drop the fabricated value, or return `unreachable!()`), so the executor's return type is produced only on the live branch.

`run_task_in_chat_with` creates the bot session before invoking the runner, and the resulting `exec_traces` row stores that generated `session_id`. comments.content: **`useDropdownTop`: ResizeObserver setup race when refs are null at first effect run.** The branch is gated on `(rootRef.current || btnRef.current)`, so if neither ref has been populated yet (forwarded refs to lazily/conditionally mounted children, portal targets, etc.) the observer is skipped and only `window.resize` is subscribed. Because the dep array tracks ref *identity* rather than `.current`, and React does not re-run effects when `.current` mutates, the observer is never retroactively installed once the refs eventually populate. Subsequent button/root size changes (icon swap, async font load, width jitter — exactly what the comment promises to handle) will leave `top` stale until the window is resized. The fallback was meant only for environments without ResizeObserver, but the condition conflates the two cases.

**`useDropdownTop`: dependency array reacts to ref object identity, not ref contents.** `[rootRef, btnRef]` in deps means the effect re-runs whenever the parent passes fresh ref objects (inline object literals, non-`useRef` refs). Combined with the mount race above, even a parent that *does* swap to a new ref-object after mount will tear down and re-subscribe — but a ref whose `.current` mutates from `null` to a real node without an identity change will never trigger a re-subscription. The dep array gives a false sense of correctness: it does not capture what the effect actually depends on (the presence of observed DOM nodes), and provides no reactive hook for the post-mount population case.

comments.content: Prototype-chain safety: `LOBE_ICONS` and `PROVIDER_ALIASES` are plain `Record` objects that inherit from `Object.prototype`, so lookup with vendor names like `constructor`, `toString`, `valueOf`, `hasOwnProperty`, `__proto__`, etc. resolves to the inherited function/object instead of `undefined`. `slugIcon` is declared `string | null`, but `slugIcon("constructor")` actually returns the inherited `Function` constructor. Downstream code that uses the result as a URL (e.g. ``) will receive a non-string and break at runtime. Use `Object.create(null)` or `Map` for both tables (and add an own-property guard inside `slugIcon` / `resolveLobeIcon`).

Hardcoded business-data mapping: per project rules, business-related hardcoded strings are prohibited. `PROVIDER_ALIASES` is a large manually-maintained mapping of external models.dev provider keys and LobeHub slugs, with no validation that keys still exist upstream or that target slugs actually resolve in `LOBE_ICONS`. Any rename in models.dev or the LobeHub icon set silently degrades to a missing/null icon. Either generate this table from a script that consumes the same source of truth as `scripts/sync-lobe-icons.mjs`, or at minimum add a build-time check that every alias target exists in `LOBE_ICONS`.

Eager glob inflates module graph: `import.meta.glob(..., { eager: true, query: "?url", import: "default" })` registers every SVG URL in the SettingsPage module graph and prevents tree-shaking, so all synced LobeHub icons are emitted as references regardless of which providers are actually configured. Consider switching to a lazy/codepoint-on-demand glob (omit `eager`) and resolving the URL on demand, or only globby the subset the alias table can ever resolve to, to keep the settings-page chunk small.

Normalization miss for additional provider-name suffixes: `normalizeVendorName` only strips the exact English suffixes `token plan`, `coding plan`, and `step plan`. Real models.dev / display-name variants like `token-plan`, `coding-plan`, `step-plan` (hyphenated), or Chinese suffixes such as `套餐` / `计划` / `计费` will not be stripped and will leave the lookup key un-aliased, causing a `null` icon for otherwise-known providers. Extend the suffix regex (or build it from a configurable list) so hyphenated and Chinese variants are normalized consistently.

Pure-function contract violated: header states "纯函数，无 React/DOM 依赖（单测锚点）", but `toGraphologyGraph` defaults `now = Date.now()`. Layout (and `nodeSize` for `doing` tasks) becomes non-deterministic between calls, breaking snapshot-style unit tests and any retry/regenerate path that should be idempotent. Recommend requiring `now` as a parameter (or accepting it as `number` with no default) so the caller controls the clock — `GraphPage` already knows when it's building the graph.

Semantic mismatch between sector placement and anchor wiring. `groupOfNode` assigns each node to the FIRST matching tag group (`break` on first hit), so the node is positioned inside that group's sector. The later `membersByGroup` pass, however, walks every tag and registers the node under EVERY group it touches — so the same node receives `TAG_EDGE_WEIGHT` star edges to anchors of groups whose sector it does NOT occupy. Under FA2 these cross-sector anchors will pull nodes out of their intended sector, contradicting the documented "同标签（同义组）节点铺在专属扇区内" invariant. Either unify to one traversal with a single rule (e.g. first-match wins, consistent with sector placement), or document the intentional many-anchor behavior and adjust the initial placement to match.

Duplicate pass over `built.nodes` for tag-group membership: the initial `groupOfNode` loop and the anchor-construction `membersByGroup` loop walk the same `(node, tags)` pairs and compute overlapping maps with slightly different semantics (see previous comment). Unifying into one traversal that records both `nodeId → firstGroup` and `group → members[]` would halve work on tag-heavy graphs and prevent the two maps from drifting apart again.

NaN-color fallback in `resolveOwnerColor`: `Number(ownerKey.slice(6))` returns `NaN` for any non-numeric suffix, and `NaN % OWNER_PALETTE.length` is `NaN`, so `OWNER_PALETTE[NaN]` is `undefined`. The function then returns `undefined` to the Sigma renderer, which will surface as a WebGL uniform error rather than a visible "this is broken" signal. Validate the suffix is a finite integer and fall back to a safe default (e.g. `OWNER_PALETTE[0]` or `palette.t5`).

Silent owner collision in `ownerColorKey`: when an owner is missing from the injected `ownerOrder` map (e.g. a new owner added after the chips were computed, or a data inconsistency), the `?? 0` fallback maps it to `"owner:0"` — identical to whatever first-listed owner lives at index 0 in `OWNER_PALETTE`. Two distinct people will then render with the exact same color in the "owner" coloring mode, masking the bug. Surface this with a developer-visible warning or throw (mirroring the explicit "single source of truth" promise in the header). At minimum, return a reserved sentinel like `"owner:unknown"` and pick a distinct color in `resolveOwnerColor`.

Magic-number coupling in sector angular spread: `((j % 12) - 5.5) * (sector.width / 14)` uses 12 angular slots but divides by 14 — the 2-slot gap is the intended edge margin between sectors, but it is undocumented and fragile. With `groupMemberCount > 12`, the modulo wraps so j=0/12/24 stack at the same angle, and any future tweak to "12" without updating "14" (or vice versa) silently changes the gap. Hoist both numbers into named constants (e.g. `SECTOR_SLOTS = 12`, `SECTOR_SLOT_DIVISOR = 14`) with a one-line comment, or derive both from a single base value so the relationship is explicit.

The ref is not cleared after invoking the cleanup, so a consumer that calls the registered cleanup during normal drag-end (without manually nulling the ref) will trigger a second invocation on unmount. Since the cleanup typically removes window listeners, resets the dragging flag, and releases pointer capture, re-running it on a state where those have already been torn down can throw (e.g., removing an already-removed listener, `releasePointerCapture` on an already-released element) or produce undefined behavior. Either null `dragCleanupRef.current` inside this unmount cleanup after calling it, or document that the caller must null the slot when it invokes the cleanup outside of unmount, so the callback remains effectively single-shot.

comments.content: Inconsistent error handling between read and write paths. `loadProfile` routes failures through `handleCommandError(..., { silent: true })` and rethrows, but `setProfileName`, `setProfileAvatar`, and `removeProfileAvatar` have no `.catch()` at all — failed writes surface as raw rejections to the caller and skip the shared UI error prompt the read path relies on. Either route write errors through `handleCommandError` (matching `loadProfile`) or document why the write path deliberately leaves reporting to its callers.

`profile-changed` listener writes `cache = e.payload` directly without consulting `loadGen`, so it bypasses the generation protocol used everywhere else. Combined with `adoptProfile`'s gen check, a write whose response resolves AFTER another writer's broadcast event (e.g. concurrent edits from a different window/挂件) can still satisfy `gen === loadGen` and overwrite newer state with its own response. Either gate the event handler by `loadGen` (and increment before applying, or skip when not the latest local op) or drop the gen check in `adoptProfile` — the two mechanisms are not currently consistent.

`notify()` iterates `subs` with `Set.prototype.forEach`, and a subscriber's callback can synchronously unsubscribe itself or a peer via the cleanup returned by `subscribeProfile`. Per the ES Set iteration semantics, values deleted before they are visited are skipped, so a subscriber that unsubscribes a later peer will silently drop that peer's notification on this tick. Snapshot the subscribers into an array (e.g. `for (const cb of [...subs]) cb();`) before invoking.

Misleading JSDoc on `adoptProfile`: it claims "递增代际使在飞 force 加载的旧快照失效" but the helper itself does not increment `loadGen` — the `++loadGen` happens in the callers (`setProfileName` / `setProfileAvatar` / `removeProfileAvatar`). The docstring also has a stray `*` mid-line. Anyone editing this helper will be misled about its responsibility; rewrite to describe only what the function actually does (guard the cache write + notify by current `loadGen`) and move the "caller must bump the generation" requirement to the callers.

The three write functions are byte-for-byte identical except for the command name. Extract the shared shape (gen bump + invoke + adoptProfile) into a single helper to keep the `loadGen` / `adoptProfile` protocol in one place — currently the invariant "every write must ++loadGen before invoke" is repeated three times and easy to break on a future addition.

Cross-webview state divergence: each Tauri webview has its own isolated localStorage, so `emit()` only broadcasts the change event — it does NOT write the new value into other webviews' localStorage. A widget opened after the main window set the flag to `true` will still read `false` from its own localStorage. The "self-heal on reload" comment is incorrect: reloading the widget re-reads the SAME webview's localStorage, not a synced value. Subscribers that re-read localStorage on the event will still get the wrong (default) value. Consider also persisting the value through a Tauri-side store / command, or having each webview initialize its localStorage from a shared source on startup.

Emit failure is silently swallowed: `emit(WORKFLOW_VISIBILITY_EVENT).catch(() => {})` discards every error with no logging. If the Tauri backend or the event channel is unavailable, cross-webview sync silently breaks and there is no diagnostic surface to detect it. At minimum, log to console (perhaps gated by import.meta.env.DEV), or expose a way for callers to subscribe to sync failures.
comments.existing_code: emit(WORKFLOW_VISIBILITY_EVENT).catch(() => {});

comments.content: Strict `"1"` truthiness silently masks corrupt or legacy state: `localStorage.getItem(...) === "1"` returns `false` for every value other than the exact string `"1"` (including `"true"`, `"yes"`, empty string from prior schema, or external tampering), with no warning. Combined with the cross-webview issue above, this can hide real misconfiguration. Consider validating the stored value (warn on unexpected values) or normalizing on read.

Permissive structural type on `isWorkflowTask`: the parameter type `{ origin?: "user" | "workflow" }` accepts any object with an optional `origin` field, so a task object from a different schema (e.g., `origin: "system"`, missing `origin` due to a refactor, or a completely unrelated shape) silently returns `false` instead of failing fast at compile time. A narrower type (e.g., importing the canonical Task type, or using a discriminated union) would catch schema drift and make the predicate's contract explicit.
comments.existing_code:
export const isWorkflowTask = (t: { origin?: "user" | "workflow" }): boolean =>
  t.origin === "workflow";

This is a clear placeholder that was never filled in (or was meant to be filled by a code generator). comments.content: loadTasksFromDb and loadWorkspaceFromDb implement the same "distinguish empty from read failure" contract but handle failures inconsistently: tasks only `console.error`, workspace calls `handleCommandError(..., { silent: true })` and also returns `{ok:false}`. Callers will surface the failure differently (silent console vs. silent alert + caller toast). Pick one pattern (e.g. always return `{ok:false}` and let the caller decide UX) and apply it to both.

exportTasksToFile, importTasksFromFile, and loadPeople are bare `await invoke(...)` with no try/catch — every other write/read in this file wraps the call and either alerts via `handleCommandError` or returns a discriminated `LoadXResult`. The comment on export/import says "alert 职责在 caller", but `loadPeople` has no such comment and any failure here surfaces as an uncaught promise rejection. Wrap these in the same pattern (at minimum a `handleCommandError` + rethrow) for consistency.

sortByOrder uses `(a.order ?? 0) - (b.order ?? 0)`. For any two items whose `order` is undefined (or both 0), the comparator returns 0 and Array.prototype.sort is only guaranteed stable since ES2019 — older WebViews / non-standard engines can reorder ties arbitrarily. Worse, two legitimately-equal orders (e.g. right after the integer re-sort in assignInsertOrder, or before any order has been assigned) will produce non-deterministic UI ordering across renders. Use a stable tiebreaker (id) and ideally a total order so behavior is identical everywhere.
comments.suggestion_code:
export const sortByOrder = <T extends { id: string; order?: number }>(items: T[]) =>
  [...items].sort((a, b) => (a.order ?? 0) - (b.order ?? 0) || a.id.localeCompare(b.id));
comments.existing_code:
export const sortByOrder = (tasks: Task[]) =>
  [...tasks].sort((a, b) => (a.order ?? 0) - (b.order ?? 0));

comments.content: The docstring for assignInsertOrder claims "只有被拖条目生成新对象" / "order 未变的条目保留原引用", but the integer re-sort branch returns `arr.map((t, i) => (t.order === i ? t : { ...t, order: i }))` — after this runs, every entry with `order === i` keeps its reference, but any entry whose stored `order` doesn't match its current index becomes a fresh object. So if a caller skips `diffTaskRows` and feeds this array directly to upsertTasks, all re-ordered siblings (not just the dragged one) get re-uploaded even though only their `order` field "changed". Either tighten the docstring, or route workspace callers through diffTaskRows.
